title: Bagging vs Boosting
text: Say it in 30s: Both are ensembles of many models, but they attack different errors. Bagging trains many strong, high-variance models (e.g. deep trees) in parallel on bootstrap samples and averages them — it reduces variance . Boosting trains weak, high-bias models (e.g. shallow trees) sequentially, each correcting the previous one s mistakes — it mainly reduces bias (and some variance). Bagging (e.g. Random Forest) Independent trees on resampled data; predictions averaged/voted. Random Forest adds feature subsampling to decorrelate trees. Robust, parallelizable, hard to overfit by adding trees. Boosting (e.g. AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost/LightGBM) Each learner focuses on the residuals/errors of the ensemble so far. Often the strongest tabular performers, but more tuning and can overfit if over-trained. Sequential → less parallelizable. One-liner: bagging = many independent opinions averaged (variance↓); boosting = a relay team fixing each other s mistakes (bias↓). See depth: Classification Methods (§6–7). Related: Bias-Variance Tradeoff , Overfitting Underfitting .

title: Classification Methods
heads: The Master Table — Every Classifier Side by Side
Naive Bayes — Fast and Great for Text
k-NN and SVM — Distance vs Margin
Trees, Forests, Boosting — Bagging vs Boosting
text: Classification — predicting a discrete label — is the single most common framing you ll be asked to reason about, and interviewers use it to probe whether you understand why one model beats another on a given dataset, not just how to call .fit() . We line every major classifier up side by side, split them into the two families that organize the whole field, then walk each one with its assumptions, strengths, and the questions it tends to attract. What you ll be able to say after this chapter Place any classifier in the generative vs discriminative split and say what it learns. Derive logistic regression from the log-odds and explain why it s the default baseline. Explain why Naive Bayes works despite a naive assumption that s almost always false . Contrast bagging vs boosting in one sentence and say which fights bias vs variance. Pick a classifier from the shape of the data: size, dimensionality, linearity, interpretability. # The Master Table — Every Classifier Side by Side Before any single method, hold the landscape in your head. The classifiers you ll be asked about differ along a few axes that actually predict their behavior: what they learn, whether the boundary is linear, how they scale, and how interpretable they are. Model Family Boundary Strengths Watch out for Logistic regression Discriminative Linear Usually well-calibrated probabilities, interpretable, fast Underfits nonlinear data Naive Bayes Generative Linear in log-space (multinomial/Bernoulli; Gaussian NB can be quadratic) Tiny data, text, very fast Independence assumption, poor calibration k-NN Discriminative (lazy) Nonlinear No training, simple Slow at predict, curse of dimensionality SVM Discriminative Linear or kernel Strong in high-dim, margin-based Slow on big data, no native probabilities Decision tree Discriminative Axis-aligned Interpretable, handles mixed types Overfits, unstable Random forest Discriminative (bagging) Nonlinear Robust, low tuning, strong default Larger, less interpretable Gradient boosting Discriminative (boosting) Nonlinear Often best on tabular Tuning-sensitive, slower to train Neural network Discriminative Arbitrary Crushes vision/text/audio Data-hungry, opaque, tuning Memory hook Two questions sort almost any classifier: does it model the data (generative) or just the boundary (discriminative)? and is the boundary a straight line or can it bend? Everything else is a footnote on cost and interpretability. Interview angle Walk me through which classifier you d try. Don t recite — reason from the data. The senior move: name a fast linear baseline (logistic regression), then a strong nonlinear default (gradient-boosted trees for tabular, a neural net for perceptual data), and justify each by the data s structure. Jumping straight to XGBoost without a baseline reads as junior. # Two Families: Generative vs Discriminative This split organizes the entire chapter, so it s worth one clean restatement. A discriminative model learns the boundary directly — p ( y ∣ x ) p(y \mid x) p ( y ∣ x ) , or just where the line goes. A generative model learns how each class produces data — p ( x ∣ y ) p(x \mid y) p ( x ∣ y ) and p ( y ) p(y) p ( y ) — then flips it with Bayes rule to classify. Discriminative Generative Learns p ( y ∣ x ) p(y \mid x) p ( y ∣ x ) — the boundary p ( x , y ) = p ( x ∣ y ) p ( y ) p(x, y) = p(x \mid y)\,p(y) p ( x , y ) = p ( x ∣ y ) p ( y ) — the full story Classifies by Which side of the line? Which class most likely generated this x x x ? Can sample / detect outliers? No Yes Data appetite Wants more data, hits lower error Works on small data if assumptions hold Examples Logistic regression, SVM, trees, NN Naive Bayes, GMM, LDA, HMM The practical takeaway is the Ng–Jordan result from Fundamentals : a generative model reaches its error floor with fewer samples but that floor is higher ; the matching discriminative model is slower to converge but ends up more accurate with enough data. So generative shines in the small-data regime, discriminative in the large-data regime. Memory hook Discriminative asks which side? Generative asks who made this? — it learns each class s recipe and picks the most plausible cook. # Logistic Regression — The Must-Know Baseline Despite the name, logistic regression is a classifier . It s the single most important model to be able to derive from scratch, because nearly every interview that touches classification touches it. The setup: a linear model produces a score z = w ⊤ x + b z = w^\top x + b z = w ⊤ x + b that lives anywhere on the real line, but a probability has to sit in [ 0 , 1 ] [0, 1] [ 0 , 1 ] . The sigmoid squashes it: σ ( z ) = 1 1 + e − z \sigma(z) = \dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} σ ( z ) = 1 + e − z 1 ​ . Read backwards, this says the model is linear in the log-odds : log ⁡ p 1 − p = w ⊤ x + b \log\frac{p}{1 - p} = w^\top x + b lo g 1 − p p ​ = w ⊤ x + b That single fact is the heart of the method — a one-unit change in a feature shifts the log-odds by its weight. It s trained by minimizing cross-entropy (log-loss), not squared error. The reason matters and gets asked: cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood under a Bernoulli model, it s convex in the weights (so any local optimum is global; with separable data the weights diverge unless regularized), and it punishes confident wrong predictions hard. Squared error on a sigmoid is non-convex and produces vanishing gradients when the model is confidently wrong — exactly when you most need a signal. Property Logistic regression Why it matters Output Usually well-calibrated probability Threshold it for any precision/recall tradeoff Boundary Linear in features Add interactions/polynomials for curves Loss Cross-entropy (convex) Global optimum, clean gradients Regularization L1 (sparse) or L2 (shrink) Controls overfitting, L1 selects features Memory hook Logistic regression is linear regression on the log-odds , then squashed by a sigmoid. Linear in log-odds, probability out. Interview angle Three near-certain questions: (1) Why sigmoid? — to map a real-valued score to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] [ 0 , 1 ] and make it linear in log-odds. (2) Why cross-entropy not MSE? — convexity + non-vanishing gradients + it s the Bernoulli MLE. (3) Is it linear? — the boundary is linear in features, even though the sigmoid is nonlinear. Getting (3) right separates people who memorized from people who understand. Go deeper (optional) For multiclass, logistic regression generalizes to softmax (multinomial) regression: one weight vector per class, normalized to a distribution. Softmax + cross-entropy is exactly the output layer of most neural-net classifiers — so what s the last layer of a classifier net? is the same idea you already know. # Naive Bayes — Fast and Great for Text Naive Bayes is the canonical generative classifier and a perennial interview favorite because its central paradox is so clean: it rests on an assumption that is almost always false, and it works anyway. It applies Bayes rule — p ( y ∣ x ) ∝ p ( y ) p ( x ∣ y ) p(y \mid x) \propto p(y)\,p(x \mid y) p ( y ∣ x ) ∝ p ( y ) p ( x ∣ y ) — and makes the naive assumption that all features are conditionally independent given the class. That lets it factor p ( x ∣ y ) p(x \mid y) p ( x ∣ y ) into a product of per-feature terms, which is why it trains in a single pass and handles tens of thousands of features (every word in a vocabulary) effortlessly. The assumption is obviously wrong — in text, New and York are not independent. But Naive Bayes only needs the correct class to get the highest score , not accurate probabilities. The dependencies often distort all classes scores in the same direction, so the argmax survives even when the probabilities themselves are badly miscalibrated. That s the resolution to the paradox, and the answer interviewers want. Variant Use on Models each feature as Multinomial NB Word counts (text) Count from a multinomial Bernoulli NB Binary presence/absence 0/1 per feature Gaussian NB Continuous features A normal distribution Two practical notes that come up: Laplace (add-one) smoothing is essential — without it, a single unseen word gives p = 0 p = 0 p = 0 and zeroes out the whole product. And NB probabilities are poorly calibrated (pushed toward 0 or 1 by the independence assumption), so trust its ranking and labels, not its confidence numbers. Memory hook Naive Bayes assumes every feature votes independently. The assumption is a lie, but the winner of the vote is usually still right — good classification, bad probabilities. Interview angle Why does Naive Bayes work if the independence assumption is false? The crisp answer: it only needs the right class to win the argmax, not calibrated probabilities; the errors are often shared across classes and cancel at the decision. Bonus points for mentioning Laplace smoothing and that it s a strong, near-free baseline for text. # k-NN and SVM — Distance vs Margin These two are usually taught together because they represent two opposite instincts about what makes a good boundary: be like your neighbors versus stay as far from everyone as possible . k-Nearest Neighbors is the laziest model there is — it does no training, just stores the data. To classify a point, it finds the k k k closest stored examples and takes a majority vote. Small k k k means a jagged, low-bias/high-variance boundary; large k k k smooths it out (higher bias, lower variance). Its weaknesses are exactly its design: prediction is slow (you compare against everything), it s memory-heavy, and it dies in high dimensions because distances become meaningless — the curse of dimensionality . It also demands feature scaling, since raw-scale features dominate the distance. Support Vector Machines take the opposite stance: among all lines that separate the classes, pick the one with the widest margin — the largest gap to the nearest points (the support vectors ). A wide margin is a built-in regularizer, which is why SVMs are strong in high-dimensional spaces like text. The kernel trick lets them draw nonlinear boundaries by implicitly mapping data to a higher-dimensional space without ever computing the coordinates — the RBF kernel is the common default. k-NN SVM Training None (lazy) Solve a convex optimization Idea Vote of nearest neighbors Maximize the margin Boundary Flexible, local Linear, or kernel for nonlinear Scales to big data? Predict is slow Training slow, predict fast Key knobs k k k , distance metric, scaling C C C (margin softness), kernel Memory hook k-NN: tell me who your neighbors are. SVM: draw the boundary down the widest empty street. One is lazy and local; the other is a global optimizer obsessed with the margin. Interview angle For k-NN expect what happens as k k k grows? (bias up, variance down) and why does it fail in high dimensions? (distances concentrate, neighbors stop being meaningful). For SVM expect what s a support vector? (a point on or inside the margin that defines the boundary) and what does the kernel trick buy you? (nonlinear boundaries without explicit high-dimensional features). Go deeper (optional) The SVM C C C parameter is the margin-softness knob: small C C C = wide, soft margin tolerating misclassifications (more bias, less variance); large C C C = narrow, hard margin fitting the training data tightly (less bias, more variance). It s the same bias-variance dial in margin clothing. # Trees, Forests, Boosting — Bagging vs Boosting Tree-based models dominate tabular data, and the progression from a single tree to forests to boosting is one of the most testable arcs in ML. A decision tree splits the feature space with a sequence of yes/no questions, choosing each split to most reduce impurity ( Gini or entropy for classification). It s wonderfully interpretable and handles mixed feature types with no scaling — but a single deep tree overfits badly and is unstable : change a few points and the whole tree can rearrange. That instability is the opening for ensembles. The two ways to combine many trees are the central contrast of this section. Bagging (Random Forest) Boosting (GBM / XGBoost) Trees are trained In parallel, independently Sequentially, each fixing the last Each tree sees A bootstrap sample (+ random feature subset at each split) The residual errors so far Primarily reduces Variance Bias Failure mode Slightly weaker than tuned boosting Overfits if over-trained / under-regularized Tuning burden Low (strong out of the box) Higher (learning rate, depth, rounds) Random forests grow many deep, decorrelated trees on bootstrap samples with random feature subsets, then average them. Averaging many high-variance, low-bias trees cancels the variance — a robust, low-maintenance default. Gradient boosting instead builds shallow trees one at a time, each trained on the previous ensemble s errors, steadily driving down bias. Tuned well (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost), boosting is usually the top performer on heterogeneous tabular data. Memory hook Bagging = a committee voting in parallel to cancel each other s mistakes (kills variance). Boosting = a relay team , each runner covering the last one s shortfall (kills bias). Interview angle The bagging-vs-boosting contrast is asked constantly. Nail the one-liner: bagging trains independent trees in parallel to reduce variance; boosting trains dependent trees sequentially on residuals to reduce bias. Follow-ups: why are random-forest trees deep but boosting trees shallow? (deep = low-bias high-variance, perfect for averaging; shallow = weak learners boosting corrects gradually) and which overfits more easily? (boosting, since it keeps fitting residuals). # Ensembles in Full Zooming out, the ensembles above are three instances of one principle: combine many models so their errors cancel. Worth knowing all the named patterns. Method How it combines Mainly helps Bagging Parallel models on bootstrap samples, then average/vote Variance Boosting Sequential models on residuals Bias Stacking A meta-model learns to blend base models predictions Both (if base models are diverse) Voting Hard (majority) or soft (average probabilities) Variance The condition for an ensemble to help is diversity : the base models must make different errors. Averaging ten copies of the same model gains nothing. This is why random forests inject randomness (bootstrap rows + random feature subsets) — to decorrelate the trees so their mistakes don t line up. Memory hook An ensemble only helps if its members are wrong in different ways . Diversity is the whole trick — identical experts add nothing; disagreeing experts cancel each other s blind spots. Go deeper (optional) Stacking/blending of diverse models wins many Kaggle competitions: train diverse base models (trees, linear, nets), then a meta-learner on their out-of-fold predictions. The subtlety is leakage — the meta-model must be trained on held-out base predictions, or it learns from data the base models already saw. # Which Classifier When The payoff of the chapter: matching a model to the data in front of you. This is the decision interviewers actually want to see you make. Situation Reach for Need a fast, interpretable baseline Logistic regression Text / very high-dimensional sparse data Naive Bayes or linear SVM Tabular data, want top accuracy Gradient boosting (XGBoost/LightGBM) Tabular data, want robust + low tuning Random forest Images, audio, language Neural network Small data, low dimensions, nonlinear k-NN or SVM (RBF) Need calibrated probabilities Logistic regression (usually well calibrated), or calibrate afterward Need to explain every prediction Single decision tree or logistic regression The meta-strategy: always start with a simple baseline (logistic regression or a shallow tree), measure it honestly, then escalate to a stronger model only if the baseline leaves accuracy on the table. The baseline also catches leakage — a too-good baseline score is a red flag, not a victory. Interview angle You have a tabular dataset with 50k rows and mixed feature types — what do you use? Strong answer: a logistic-regression baseline for a reference point and calibration, then gradient-boosted trees as the likely winner, justified by their fit to heterogeneous tabular data and their handling of nonlinearities and interactions without manual feature engineering. Then mention you d validate the choice empirically — No Free Lunch. # Cross-Cutting Skills (Asked of Senior Candidates) Beyond naming models, senior interviews probe a few skills that cut across all classifiers. Handling class imbalance. When one class is rare (fraud, disease), accuracy is useless and most classifiers drift toward the majority. Levers: resample (SMOTE / oversample minority, undersample majority), reweight the loss to penalize minority errors more, and — most importantly — change the metric to precision/recall, F1, or PR-AUC instead of accuracy. Multiclass from binary models. Models like SVM are natively binary. One-vs-Rest trains one classifier per class against all others ( k k k classifiers); One-vs-One trains one per pair ( k ( k − 1 ) / 2 k(k-1)/2 k ( k − 1 ) /2 classifiers, each on less data). Logistic regression and trees handle multiclass natively via softmax / multi-way splits. Calibration. A model can rank well but report dishonest probabilities (Naive Bayes, SVMs, deep nets often do). If you need the number 0.7 to mean 70% of the time, calibrate with Platt scaling or isotonic regression on held-out data (see Model Evaluation Validation ). Memory hook Three senior reflexes: imbalanced data → change the metric first, resampling/reweighting second. Binary-only model → wrap it in One-vs-Rest. Probabilities you ll act on → calibrate them. Rapid fire — Classification Two families: discriminative learns the boundary p ( y ∣ x ) p(y\mid x) p ( y ∣ x ) ; generative learns p ( x , y ) p(x,y) p ( x , y ) and can sample. Generative wins small-data, discriminative wins large-data. Logistic regression: linear in log-odds, sigmoid out, trained with convex cross-entropy. The boundary is linear; use it as the baseline. Naive Bayes: assumes conditional independence (false) but wins the argmax anyway; great for text; use Laplace smoothing; poorly calibrated. k-NN: lazy, local, dies in high dimensions, needs scaling. SVM: max-margin, strong in high-dim, kernel trick for nonlinearity. Trees overfit and are unstable. Bagging (random forest) = parallel trees killing variance; boosting (XGBoost) = sequential trees killing bias. Ensembles need diverse base models (wrong in different ways) to help. Pick by data: logistic baseline → boosting for tabular, NN for perceptual, NB/linear-SVM for text. Imbalance → change the metric (PR-AUC, F1) before resampling/reweighting. # One-Page Summary Concept The one thing to remember Two families Discriminative draws the boundary p ( y ∣ x ) p(y\mid x) p ( y ∣ x ) ; generative models p ( x , y ) p(x,y) p ( x , y ) and can sample. Logistic regression Linear in log-odds, sigmoid out, convex cross-entropy loss; the usually well-calibrated baseline. Why not MSE Cross-entropy is convex with non-vanishing gradients; it s the Bernoulli MLE. Naive Bayes Conditional-independence assumption is false but the argmax still wins; great, fast text baseline. k-NN Lazy, local, needs scaling, dies in high dimensions; k k k trades bias for variance. SVM Maximize the margin; kernel trick for nonlinear boundaries; strong in high dimensions. Trees Interpretable but overfit and unstable — the reason ensembles exist. Bagging vs boosting Bagging = parallel trees, kills variance (random forest). Boosting = sequential trees on residuals, kills bias (XGBoost). Ensembles Only help when base models are wrong in different ways — diversity is the trick. Which when Logistic baseline → boosting for tabular, NN for perceptual, NB/linear-SVM for text. Imbalance Change the metric first (PR-AUC, F1), then resample/reweight. # Related Logistic Regression Generative vs Discriminative Bagging vs Boosting Precision Recall Regression Methods

title: Decision Trees and Gradient Boosting
heads: CART: how a tree chooses a split
Instability and other limits of single trees
Feature importance: what the numbers mean and where they mislead
Why boosting overfits differently from bagging
Interpreting GBDT: SHAP and permutation importance
When GBDT beats deep nets on tabular data (hedged)
text:
Classical Models: from a single CART tree to forests to XGBoost-style boosting. Classification Methods and Bagging vs Boosting give the headline contrast (bagging reduces variance, boosting reduces bias). This chapter goes underneath it: how a tree actually chooses splits, why a single tree is unstable, what random forests really average, how gradient boosting is functional gradient descent, and how the major libraries differ in practice. These are the topics where senior interviewers probe for mechanism rather than slogans. What you ll be able to say after this chapter Compute Gini, entropy, information gain, and variance reduction for a split, and say when they differ. Explain cost-complexity pruning, and how trees handle categorical and missing values. Describe OOB error and why impurity-based importance is biased. Derive gradient boosting as gradient descent in function space, and write the second-order XGBoost leaf weight and gain. Compare XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost on split finding, tree growth, and categorical handling. Give a tuning order, explain early stopping, and say when GBDT tends to beat deep nets on tabular data (and when it may not). # CART: how a tree chooses a split A CART (Classification And Regression Tree) recursively partitions feature space with binary, axis-aligned splits x j ≤ t x_j\le t x j ​ ≤ t (or a subset test for a categorical feature). Each leaf predicts a constant: the class distribution (or majority class) for classification, the mean of y y y for regression. Growing is greedy: at each node, pick the split with the largest impurity decrease and recurse. Greedy means locally optimal, not globally optimal; finding the best tree is NP-complete. # Impurity measures For a node with class proportions p 1 , … , p C p_1,\dots,p_C p 1 ​ , … , p C ​ : Measure Formula Range (binary) Notes Gini G = 1 − ∑ c p c 2 G=1-\sum_c p_c^2 G = 1 − ∑ c ​ p c 2 ​ [ 0 , 0.5 ] [0,\,0.5] [ 0 , 0.5 ] Probability that two random draws from the node differ in class; cheap (no logs) Entropy H = − ∑ c p c log ⁡ 2 p c H=-\sum_c p_c\log_2 p_c H = − ∑ c ​ p c ​ lo g 2 ​ p c ​ [ 0 , 1 ] [0,\,1] [ 0 , 1 ] Information-theoretic; slightly more sensitive to small class proportions Misclassification error 1 − max ⁡ c p c 1-\max_c p_c 1 − max c ​ p c ​ [ 0 , 0.5 ] [0,\,0.5] [ 0 , 0.5 ] Not strictly concave, so often fails to reward a split that improves purity without changing the majority class; poor for growing Variance (regression) 1 n ∑ i ( y i − y ˉ ) 2  rac1n\sum_i(y_i- ar y)^2 n 1 ​ ∑ i ​ ( y i ​ − y ˉ ​ ) 2 ≥ 0 \ge0 ≥ 0 The node s mean squared error around its mean prediction Gini and entropy are both strictly concave and typically produce very similar trees; the choice rarely matters much in practice, and Gini is the common default for speed. # Split gain For a candidate split sending n L n_L n L ​ of n n n samples left and n R n_R n R ​ right, the impurity decrease is Δ = I ( parent ) − n L n I ( left ) − n R n I ( right ) . \Delta = I(	ext{parent})- rac{n_L}{n}I(	ext{left})- rac{n_R}{n}I(	ext{right}). Δ = I ( parent ) − n n L ​ ​ I ( left ) − n n R ​ ​ I ( right ) . With entropy as I I I , Δ \Delta Δ is the information gain (the reduction in label entropy from knowing the branch). With variance as I I I , Δ \Delta Δ is the variance reduction , equivalent to the reduction in sum of squared errors. Worked example: a node with 10 samples, 5 positive and 5 negative, so G = 0.5 G=0.5 G = 0.5 . A split yields left (4 positive, 1 negative; G = 1 − 0.64 − 0.04 = 0.32 G=1-0.64-0.04=0.32 G = 1 − 0.64 − 0.04 = 0.32 ) and right (1 positive, 4 negative; G = 0.32 G=0.32 G = 0.32 ). Then Δ = 0.5 − 0.5 ( 0.32 ) − 0.5 ( 0.32 ) = 0.18 \Delta=0.5-0.5(0.32)-0.5(0.32)=0.18 Δ = 0.5 − 0.5 ( 0.32 ) − 0.5 ( 0.32 ) = 0.18 . Finding the best threshold. For a numeric feature, sort the values and scan the candidate thresholds (midpoints between consecutive distinct values), updating left/right class counts incrementally. That costs O ( n log ⁡ n ) O(n\log n) O ( n lo g n ) per feature per node for the sort, or O ( n ) O(n) O ( n ) with presorted/binned data. Histogram-based libraries bin features into at most about 255 bins first and scan bins instead, which is the reason for their speed (see below). # Controlling size: pruning A tree grown until leaves are pure has low bias and high variance: it memorizes noise. Two controls: Pre-pruning (early stopping): limit max_depth , require min_samples_leaf or min_samples_split , require a minimum impurity decrease. Fast, but can stop too early, since a split with small immediate gain can enable a very useful later split (the XOR pattern, where no single split helps but two together separate the classes perfectly). Post-pruning, cost-complexity (weakest-link) pruning: grow a large tree T 0 T_0 T 0 ​ , then for a penalty α ≥ 0 \alpha\ge0 α ≥ 0 minimize R α ( T ) = R ( T ) + α ∣ T ∣ , R_\alpha(T)=R(T)+\alpha\,|T|, R α ​ ( T ) = R ( T ) + α ∣ T ∣ , where R ( T ) R(T) R ( T ) is the training error (or impurity-weighted loss) and ∣ T ∣ |T| ∣ T ∣ the number of leaves. As α \alpha α increases, repeatedly collapse the internal node whose removal increases error least per leaf removed, yielding a nested sequence of subtrees; choose α \alpha α by cross-validation (the 1-standard-error rule picks the smallest tree within one SE of the best). In practice with ensembles, individual trees are controlled by depth and leaf-size limits rather than tuned pruning. # Categorical and missing values Categorical features. A subset split on a K K K -level feature has 2 K − 1 − 1 2^{K-1}-1 2 K − 1 − 1 candidates. For binary classification and regression , a classical result shows the optimal subset split can be found by ordering the categories by mean response (or class-1 proportion) and scanning the K − 1 K-1 K − 1 split points along that order; some libraries (for example LightGBM, which sorts categories by gradient statistics, and R tree packages) exploit this. For multiclass the shortcut does not hold exactly. One-hot encoding works but makes sparse features that a tree can only isolate one level at a time, which is inefficient for high cardinality and dilutes importance across dummies. High cardinality raises overfitting risk: with many levels, some subset will split the training data well by chance. Splits on such features also get inflated impurity-based importance (see below). Target (mean) encoding replaces a level by a statistic of the target, but if computed on the same rows it leaks the label; it must be computed out-of-fold or with ordered schemes (the CatBoost idea below), plus smoothing toward the global mean. Missing values. Options: impute (simple, but loses the signal that data were missing); add a missingness indicator; CART-style surrogate splits (use another feature that mimics the primary split for rows where it is missing); or, as in XGBoost, LightGBM, and recent scikit-learn tree models, learn a default direction for missing values at each split by trying both and keeping the better gain. The last is convenient and exploits informative missingness, but if values are missing for a reason that differs between training and serving, the learned routing can be wrong, so verify the missingness mechanism is stable. # Instability and other limits of single trees High variance. A small change in data can change an early split and hence the whole tree below it. This is exactly why averaging (bagging) helps. Piecewise-constant, axis-aligned. A tree approximates a diagonal boundary or smooth trend with a staircase and needs many splits to do it; rotating the feature space can change performance a lot (a reason that engineered linear combinations or PCA features sometimes help trees). No extrapolation. A regression tree predicts a leaf mean, so outside the training range predictions are constant; trees should not be expected to follow a linear trend beyond the data (a concern in forecasting; see Time Series Stationarity ). Split-selection bias. Greedy impurity criteria prefer features with many possible splits (continuous or high-cardinality), which can select spurious features. Conditional inference trees correct this with significance tests; ensembles mitigate it partly. Interpretability is real for shallow trees and fades quickly with depth or ensembling. Interview angle Why is a single decision tree high variance? Greedy top-down splitting makes early decisions that condition everything below, and small perturbations in the data can flip them; a deep tree also has enough capacity to fit noise. The structural fix is averaging many perturbed trees (bagging) or limiting capacity (pruning). # Random forests in detail A random forest (Breiman) grows B B B trees, each on a bootstrap sample, and averages predictions (or votes). Two randomization sources decorrelate the trees: Bootstrap rows per tree. Each bootstrap sample draws n n n rows with replacement; the probability a given row is absent is ( 1 − 1 / n ) n → e − 1 ≈ 0.368 (1-1/n)^n	o e^{-1}\approx0.368 ( 1 − 1/ n ) n → e − 1 ≈ 0.368 , so each tree sees about 63.2 % 63.2\% 63.2% unique rows. Random feature subset at every split (not once per tree): only m try m_	ext{try} m try ​ of the p p p features are candidates at each node. Common heuristics are about p \sqrt p p ​ for classification and about p / 3 p/3 p /3 for regression, but treat these as starting points to tune (library defaults differ). Why the feature subsampling matters. If one feature is very strong, bootstrap alone leaves every tree splitting on it at the root, so ρ ho ρ stays high; restricting candidates per split lowers ρ ho ρ at a modest cost in each tree s strength. Lower m try m_	ext{try} m try ​ means more diversity but weaker trees; it is the central forest hyperparameter. Trees are typically grown deep (low bias), because averaging handles variance. Out-of-bag (OOB) error. Each row is out-of-bag for about 36.8 % 36.8\% 36.8% of the trees. Predict each row using only trees that did not train on it, and score those predictions. This gives an approximately unbiased generalization estimate without a separate validation set, which is convenient for tuning. Caveats: it assumes rows are i.i.d.; with grouped, temporal, or duplicated data the OOB estimate is optimistic because related rows land in other trees training sets (use group-aware or forward-chaining validation instead; see Cross-Validation ); and tuning heavily against OOB reintroduces optimism. Does adding trees overfit? For a forest, increasing B B B does not increase variance in the way depth does; error generally plateaus, so more trees is safe apart from compute and memory. The forest can still overfit through very deep trees with noisy labels and tiny leaves, so min_samples_leaf is a useful regularizer. Probabilities. The answer: the derivative of the loss with respect to the current predictions of each training example, which is the direction in function space that most reduces the loss. Each tree is a regression fit to that direction, and ν 
u ν is the step size. Squared loss turns the gradient into the plain residual; other losses give other targets. # Why boosting overfits differently from bagging Each stage fits the remaining error, so after enough rounds the ensemble starts fitting noise; test error typically follows a U-shape in the number of rounds, so the number of trees is a regularization knob (unlike forests). With small ν 
u ν the minimum is broader and later. Shallow trees (depth 3 to 8, depending on interactions) are preferred because each stage should be a weak, low-variance learner and because depth equals the maximum interaction order the model can express. # XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost All three implement regularized gradient-boosted decision trees with the same core idea; they differ in how they find splits, grow trees, and handle categoricals. Version details change over time, so treat the table as the typical design. Aspect XGBoost LightGBM CatBoost Split finding Exact greedy and histogram-based approximate (histogram method is the common choice for speed) Histogram-based : bin features to a small number of bins, accumulate G , H G,H G , H per bin Histogram-based; quantized features Tree growth Level-wise (depth-wise) by default; leaf-wise via a loss-guide policy Leaf-wise (best-first): split the leaf with the largest gain Symmetric (oblivious) trees: the same split condition across a whole level Categoricals Historically needs encoding; native support was added more recently Native: sorts categories by gradient statistics to find a good subset split Native with ordered target statistics Missing values Learned default direction Learned default direction Handled natively with configurable modes Speed tricks Sparsity-aware splits, column blocks, regularized objective Histogram subtraction, GOSS (keep large-gradient rows, sample small ones), EFB (bundle mutually exclusive sparse features) GPU-friendly oblivious trees; ordered boosting (a bias fix, mainly used on smaller data) Typical regularization max_depth , min_child_weight , lambda , alpha , gamma num_leaves , min_data_in_leaf , lambda_l1/l2 , min_gain_to_split depth , l2_leaf_reg , strong defaults Out-of-box strength Reliable and widely used Fast on large data Often strong with little tuning, especially with categoricals Histogram splits. Instead of sorting values per node, bin each feature once (about 256 bins by default in many setups) and, for each node, build a ( G , H ) (G,H) ( G , H ) histogram per feature; best split per feature is then a scan over bins, so cost scales with bins rather than rows. A child s histogram can be derived by subtracting its sibling s from the parent s, nearly halving the work. The price is quantization: thresholds are limited to bin edges, usually a negligible accuracy loss. Leaf-wise versus level-wise. Level-wise growth expands all nodes at a depth, producing balanced trees with a bounded size by depth. Leaf-wise growth always splits the single most beneficial leaf, reaching lower loss for the same number of leaves but giving unbalanced trees that can overfit on small datasets; hence the main complexity control is num_leaves plus min_data_in_leaf , not max_depth alone. Rule of thumb: keep num_leaves well below 2 max_depth 2^{	ext{max\_depth}} 2 max_depth . CatBoost s ordered target statistics. Plain target encoding uses the row s own label in computing its encoding, causing target leakage (the model sees a feature computed from the answer). CatBoost imposes a random permutation of the rows and encodes each row using only the labels of rows earlier in that permutation, e.g. ∑ prior rows with level c y + a p count + a  rac{\sum_{	ext{prior rows with level }c}y+a\,p}{	ext{count}+a} count + a ∑ prior rows with level c ​ y + a p ​ with prior p p p and weight a a a . Ordered boosting extends this idea to the gradient computation itself to reduce prediction shift (the bias from computing residuals on the same rows used to fit the model). Symmetric trees act as a regularizer and make inference fast. # Key hyperparameters and tuning order Hyperparameter Effect Direction when overfitting learning_rate ( ν 
u ν ) Step size per tree Lower (and raise rounds) n_estimators / rounds Capacity of the ensemble Use early stopping max_depth / num_leaves Interaction depth, tree complexity Lower min_child_weight / min_data_in_leaf Minimum evidence per leaf Raise subsample (rows), colsample_* (features) Randomization and variance reduction Lower (for example toward 0.6 to 0.9) lambda (L2), alpha (L1), gamma / min_gain_to_split Penalize leaf weights, complexity Raise scale_pos_weight / class weights Reweights positives Use with care; changes calibration A sensible tuning order , from largest effect to finest: Fix a sensible objective and metric, and set a moderately high learning rate (about 0.05 to 0.1) with early stopping to find the right number of rounds quickly. Tune tree complexity: max_depth or num_leaves , then min_child_weight / min_data_in_leaf . Tune randomization: row and column subsampling. Tune regularization: λ \lambda λ , α \alpha α , γ \gamma γ . Lower the learning rate (for example to 0.01 to 0.03), raise the number of rounds with early stopping, and refit. Use random or Bayesian search rather than grids; the ranges above are heuristics that depend on the dataset size and noise level, so treat them as starting points. For imbalanced problems, choose the evaluation metric first (PR-AUC or log loss) and consider class weighting only if the ranking, not the calibrated probability, is the goal. # Early stopping Hold out a validation set (or use CV folds); at each round compute the validation metric and stop when it fails to improve for early_stopping_rounds rounds, then keep the best iteration. Details that matter: The validation set is used for model selection , so its score is optimistically biased; report final performance on a separate test set (or nested validation). The split must mirror deployment: time-based for temporal data, group-based when rows cluster by entity, otherwise leakage makes early stopping choose too many rounds. In CV, per-fold best iterations differ; use the mean or median when refitting on all data, perhaps with a small increase for the larger training set. A noisy validation metric on small data can stop prematurely; use a patient early_stopping_rounds and a low learning rate. # Interpreting GBDT: SHAP and permutation importance SHAP assigns each feature a Shapley value: its average marginal contribution to the prediction over all orderings of features, which satisfies local accuracy (the contributions plus a base value sum to the prediction), missingness , and consistency . TreeSHAP computes exact Shapley values for tree ensembles in polynomial time, in contrast to the exponential cost of the brute-force definition. Practical points: Local (per-prediction) explanations aggregate into global ones (mean absolute SHAP), and dependence plots show effect shape and interactions. Missing features must be defined: the interventional version breaks dependence using a background dataset, the path-dependent version follows the trees own cover statistics. With correlated features the two can differ: the path-dependent version can assign nonzero credit to a feature the model never splits on, while the interventional version evaluates the model on off-manifold combinations; state which one is used. SHAP explains the model s behavior , not causal effects, and is for the model s output scale (log-odds for classifiers), which may differ from probability scale. Permutation importance (on held-out data) measures performance dependence directly and is model-agnostic; use it to sanity-check SHAP or gain-based rankings, and group correlated features when permuting. # When GBDT beats deep nets on tabular data (hedged) Gradient-boosted trees are commonly the strongest or near-strongest family on medium-sized, heterogeneous tabular data (a few thousand to a few hundred thousand rows with mixed numeric/categorical features), and published benchmark comparisons have found tuned tree ensembles competitive with or better than standard deep architectures in that regime, with much less tuning. Plausible reasons, which are explanatory hypotheses rather than settled laws: Tabular targets are often irregular and non-smooth in the features, and trees represent sharp, axis-aligned thresholds naturally while smooth networks have a bias toward low-frequency functions. Uninformative features are common; trees split selection is comparatively robust to them, while networks use all inputs. Features have heterogeneous meaning and scale (no spatial or sequential structure to exploit), the case where convolution or attention priors give little. Trees need little preprocessing (no scaling, native handling of missing values), are fast to train, and tune relatively easily. Conditions that can shift the balance toward neural networks: very large datasets; multimodal inputs (text, image, sequences) feeding the tabular model; the need for end-to-end learned embeddings of high-cardinality entities; multi-task or transfer settings; or very small datasets where pretrained tabular models may help. Ensembling a GBDT with a network often beats either alone. The honest interview position is: start with a regularized linear baseline and a tuned GBDT, and move to deep models when data type, scale, or the need for learned representations justifies the cost; verify with a proper validation scheme on your data rather than relying on a benchmark. Interview angle A strong hedged answer to Why not just use a neural network? : On mid-sized tabular data with mixed types, tuned GBDTs are often as good or better, train faster, and need little preprocessing; benchmark both anyway, and consider a network if there is a lot of data, unstructured inputs, or a need for learned embeddings. # One-Page Summary Concept Key point CART Greedy, binary, axis-aligned splits; leaf = class distribution or mean; optimal tree is NP-complete. title: Generative vs Discriminative
text: Say it in 30s: Discriminative models learn the boundary directly — P(y | x) — they only answer which class. Generative models learn each class s shape — P(x | y) and P(y) — then use Bayes rule to derive P(y | x), so they can also generate new x. The canonical pair Logistic Regression (discriminative) vs Naive Bayes (generative). Discriminative usually wins with ample data (optimizes the thing you care about). Generative wins with little data or when you need to sample, detect outliers, or handle missing features. Examples Discriminative: logistic regression, SVMs, most neural net classifiers, random forests. Generative: Naive Bayes, GMMs, HMMs, and modern generative models (VAEs, diffusion, LLMs). Trap: generative in the classic sense (models P(x,y)) is a superset idea that also covers today s generative AI — be ready to bridge both meanings. See depth: Classification Methods (§2), Fundamentals (§1). Related: Logistic Regression , Maximum Likelihood Estimation .

title: Logistic Regression
text: Say it in 30s: A linear classifier that outputs a probability. It puts a linear combination of features through a sigmoid to get P(y=1), and is trained by minimizing cross-entropy (= maximum likelihood under a Bernoulli model). Despite the name, it s classification. Why it s the must-know baseline Outputs probabilities (usually reasonably well calibrated, unless heavily regularized, reweighted/resampled or misspecified), not just labels. Interpretable : a weight is the change in log-odds per unit feature; exp(weight) is an odds ratio. Convex loss → any local optimum is global (unique if strictly convex, i.e. full-rank X or L2-regularized), fast to train. The discriminative counterpart to Naive Bayes. Key points Decision boundary is linear; use feature engineering or kernels for nonlinearity. Regularize with L1 (sparse) or L2 (stable) — same penalties as linear regression. Multiclass via softmax (a.k.a. multinomial logistic regression). Trap: it can t separate XOR-like data without nonlinear features. Underfits genuinely nonlinear boundaries. See depth: Classification Methods (§3), TensorGym Study Notes . Related: Cross-Entropy Loss , Generative vs Discriminative , Gradient Descent , Precision Recall .
