title: Regression Methods
heads: The four classical assumptions (and what breaks)
Regularization: OLS vs Ridge vs Lasso vs Elastic Net
Choosing features and going beyond a straight line
text: Notation used throughout n n n = examples, p p p = features, X X X = n × ( p + 1 ) n\times(p+1) n × ( p + 1 ) design matrix (first column of 1s for the intercept). w w w = coefficient vector, y ^ = X w \hat{y} = Xw y ^ ​ = X w , residual e = y − y ^ e = y - \hat{y} e = y − y ^ ​ , λ \lambda λ = regularization strength. ε \varepsilon ε = true noise term, σ 2 \sigma^2 σ 2 = noise variance. # Linear regression: the straight line Analogy. Linear regression is a recipe with fixed ingredient prices. The prediction is a shopping bill: each feature (quantity) times its coefficient (unit price), plus a base charge (intercept). Training = figuring out the prices that best explain past bills. Model: y ^ = w 0 + w 1 x 1 + w 2 x 2 + ⋯ + w p x p = X w \hat{y} = w_0 + w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + \dots + w_px_p = Xw y ^ ​ = w 0 ​ + w 1 ​ x 1 ​ + w 2 ​ x 2 ​ + ⋯ + w p ​ x p ​ = X w Assumed truth: y = X w + ε y = Xw + \varepsilon y = X w + ε , with noise ε \varepsilon ε . How to read a coefficient (say it precisely in interviews): w j w_j w j ​ = expected change in y y y for a one-unit increase in x j x_j x j ​ , holding all other features fixed . Holding others fixed is exactly what breaks under multicollinearity — correlated features can t be moved independently, so individual coefficients become unstable and uninterpretable. Standardize features → coefficients become comparable importance per standard deviation. Why it s everyone s baseline: Closed-form training, exact reproducibility, interpretable coefficients with confidence intervals, fast at serving time, and a strong sanity check — if a deep model can t beat linear regression, the features (not the architecture) are the problem. Closed form Finding the optimal parameters directly via a mathematical formula, without an iterative optimization process like gradient descent. # How it finds the line (OLS) Analogy. Stretch vertical rubber bands from every data point to a rigid rod. Each band pulls with force proportional to its stretch (squared-error physics). OLS is where the rod settles — the equilibrium of all the pulls. One point dragged far away (an outlier) pulls linearly harder (its energy grows quadratically) and tilts the whole rod: that s MSE sensitivity from Loss Functions , now geometric. Figure 1 — OLS minimizes the sum of squared vertical residuals Objective (ordinary least squares): minimize the residual sum of squares RSS ( w ) = ∥ y − X w ∥ 2 = ∑ i ( y i − x i ⊤ w ) 2 \text{RSS}(w) = \lVert y - Xw\rVert^2 = \sum_i (y_i - x_i^\top w)^2 RSS ( w ) = ∥ y − X w ∥ 2 = i ∑ ​ ( y i ​ − x i ⊤ ​ w ) 2 This is MSE from Loss Functions , summed. Derivation → normal equations (do this on a whiteboard once): ∇ w RSS = − 2 X ⊤ ( y − X w ) = 0 ⇒ X ⊤ X w = X ⊤ y ⇒ w ^ = ( X ⊤ X ) − 1 X ⊤ y \nabla_w\,\text{RSS} = -2X^\top(y - Xw) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; X^\top X w = X^\top y \;\Rightarrow\; \hat{w} = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y ∇ w ​ RSS = − 2 X ⊤ ( y − X w ) = 0 ⇒ X ⊤ X w = X ⊤ y ⇒ w ^ = ( X ⊤ X ) − 1 X ⊤ y The solution exists when X ⊤ X X^\top X X ⊤ X is invertible — i.e. no perfect multicollinearity, n ≥ p n \ge p n ≥ p . Geometric view (the elegant answer): y ^ = X w ^ \hat{y} = X\hat{w} y ^ ​ = X w ^ is the orthogonal projection of y y y onto the column space of X X X . Residual vector e e e is perpendicular to every column: X ⊤ e = 0 X^\top e = 0 X ⊤ e = 0 — the same statement as the normal equations. Two ways to solve it: Method Cost When Normal equations / QR or Cholesky O ( n p 2 + p 3 ) O(np^2 + p^3) O ( n p 2 + p 3 ) p p p small–medium ( ≲ 10 4 \lesssim 10^4 ≲ 1 0 4 ); exact Gradient descent / SGD O ( n p ) O(np) O ( n p ) per epoch p p p huge, n n n huge, streaming; approximate Gauss–Markov theorem (the why OLS credential): IF errors have zero mean, constant variance, and no correlation, THEN OLS is BLUE : the B est (minimum-variance) L inear U nbiased E stimator. Note what s NOT required: normality. Normality is only needed for exact small-sample t-tests/CIs. Also know: ridge (below) deliberately gives up U (unbiased) to reduce variance — and usually wins on test error. That s the bias–variance trade from Fundamentals , in one sentence. # The four classical assumptions (and what breaks) Analogy. The assumptions are the warranty card, not the on/off switch. The line still fits if you violate them — but the warranty (unbiased coefficients, trustworthy p-values and intervals) is void, often silently. The four (mnemonic LINE) + the practical fifth: # Assumption Meaning Diagnostic What breaks if violated Fix L Linearity E [ y ∣ x ] E[y\mid x] E [ y ∣ x ] really is X w Xw X w residuals vs fitted: curve pattern coefficients biased — model is just wrong transforms, polynomials, splines, interactions I Independence of errors errors don t influence each other Durbin–Watson; residuals vs time show waves SEs too small → fake significance time-series models; clustered/robust SEs N Normality of errors ε ∼ \varepsilon \sim ε ∼ Gaussian Q–Q plot small-sample p-values/CIs off (predictions fine) rarely fatal; bootstrap; large n n n → CLT rescues you E Equal variance (homoscedasticity) Var ⁡ ( ε ) \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon) Var ( ε ) constant across x x x funnel in residuals vs fitted; Breusch–Pagan wrong SEs → wrong inference; inefficient log-transform y y y , WLS, robust (White/HC) SEs + No perfect multicollinearity no feature is a linear combo of others VIF, condition number ( X ⊤ X ) − 1 (X^\top X)^{-1} ( X ⊤ X ) − 1 blows up → huge, sign-flipping coefficients drop/combine features, PCA, ridge Figure 2 — Residual-plot signatures: healthy, funnel, curve, waves Multicollinearity — the deep-dive interviewers love: VIF j = 1 1 − R j 2 \text{VIF}_j = \dfrac{1}{1 - R_j^2} VIF j ​ = 1 − R j 2 ​ 1 ​ , where R j 2 R_j^2 R j 2 ​ comes from regressing feature j j j on all other features. Rule of thumb: VIF 5 – 10 \text{VIF} 5\text{–}10 VIF 5 – 10 → trouble. Symptoms: great R 2 R^2 R 2 but no individual feature significant; coefficients flip sign when you add/remove a feature; tiny data changes swing coefficients wildly. Key subtlety: multicollinearity inflates coefficient variance but barely hurts predictions . If you only predict, you can often ignore it; if you must explain, you can t. Cleanest fix: ridge — ( X ⊤ X + λ I ) (X^\top X + \lambda I) ( X ⊤ X + λ I ) is always invertible (see Regularization ). Production issues. Silent heteroscedasticity: revenue-prediction errors grow with customer size. Point forecasts look fine; the ± bands are fiction for big accounts. Fix: model log ⁡ ( revenue ) \log(\text{revenue}) lo g ( revenue ) , or use quantile regression for honest intervals. Duplicated features in a feature store: two teams register near-identical signals (e.g. 7-day and weekly averages) → multicollinearity → an important feature shows a negative coefficient in the explanation dashboard and stakeholders panic. Fix: VIF audit + ridge. Extrapolation: linear models happily predict far outside the training range (a house with 50 bathrooms). Clamp inputs and monitor feature ranges in serving. # Regularization: OLS vs Ridge vs Lasso vs Elastic Net Analogy (recap from Loss Functions ). Airline L1 charges per item → you drop items (sparse). Airline L2 charges by weight squared → everything lighter, nothing dropped. Elastic Net is a codeshare of both. The four estimators, one table: Objective Solution Sparsity Best at OLS ∥ y − X w ∥ 2 \lVert y-Xw\rVert^2 ∥ y − X w ∥ 2 ( X ⊤ X ) − 1 X ⊤ y (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y ( X ⊤ X ) − 1 X ⊤ y ✗ n ≫ p n \gg p n ≫ p , clean, low collinearity Ridge ∥ y − X w ∥ 2 + λ ∥ w ∥ 2 2 \lVert y-Xw\rVert^2 + \lambda\lVert w\rVert_2^2 ∥ y − X w ∥ 2 + λ ∥ w ∥ 2 2 ​ ( X ⊤ X + λ I ) − 1 X ⊤ y (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y ( X ⊤ X + λ I ) − 1 X ⊤ y ✗ shrinks only correlated features; p p p close to or above n n n ; pure prediction Lasso ∥ y − X w ∥ 2 + λ ∥ w ∥ 1 \lVert y-Xw\rVert^2 + \lambda\lVert w\rVert_1 ∥ y − X w ∥ 2 + λ ∥ w ∥ 1 ​ no closed form — coordinate descent + soft-thresholding ✓ exact zeros feature selection; believe few features matter Elastic Net ∥ y − X w ∥ 2 + λ ( α ∥ w ∥ 1 + ( 1 − α ) ∥ w ∥ 2 2 ) \lVert y-Xw\rVert^2 + \lambda(\alpha\lVert w\rVert_1 + (1-\alpha)\lVert w\rVert_2^2) ∥ y − X w ∥ 2 + λ ( α ∥ w ∥ 1 ​ + ( 1 − α ) ∥ w ∥ 2 2 ​ ) coordinate descent ✓ + grouping correlated features AND want sparsity Figure 3 — Coefficient paths vs λ \lambda λ : ridge shrinks smoothly, lasso zeroes one by one Facts to volunteer in an interview: λ \lambda λ is chosen by cross-validation ; λ = 0 \lambda = 0 λ = 0 recovers OLS; λ → ∞ \lambda \to \infty λ → ∞ kills all coefficients (intercept survives — never penalized). Standardize features first — both penalties are unit-sensitive. Ridge keeps correlated twins together with similar weights; lasso picks one twin ~arbitrarily and zeroes the other → unstable feature selection story; Elastic Net fixes this (grouping effect). p n p n p n : OLS is undefined ( X ⊤ X X^\top X X ⊤ X singular); ridge still works; lasso selects at most n n n features. Bayesian one-liner: ridge = Gaussian prior, lasso = Laplace prior, MAP estimation (see Maximum Likelihood Estimation ). Degrees of freedom: ridge s effective dof = ∑ i d i 2 d i 2 + λ p = \sum_i \dfrac{d_i^2}{d_i^2+\lambda} p = ∑ i ​ d i 2 ​ + λ d i 2 ​ ​ p ( d i d_i d i ​ = singular values of X X X ) — shrinkage spends fewer parameters than it has. # Polynomial regression Analogy. A polynomial degree is a bendiness dial on a ruler. Degree 1: rigid ruler. Degree 3: gentle flex that traces the trend. Degree 15: cooked spaghetti that passes through every point — including the noise — and flails wildly at the edges. The key conceptual trick: Polynomial regression IS linear regression — on expanded features: y ^ = w 0 + w 1 x + w 2 x 2 + ⋯ + w d x d \hat{y} = w_0 + w_1x + w_2x^2 + \dots + w_d x^d y ^ ​ = w 0 ​ + w 1 ​ x + w 2 ​ x 2 + ⋯ + w d ​ x d . Linear in linear model means linear in the parameters w w w , not in x x x . Same OLS solver, same normal equations, same everything. Figure 4 — Degree is the bias–variance dial: underfit / right / overfit What to know: Degree ↑ \uparrow ↑ ⇒ bias ↓ \downarrow ↓ , variance ↑ \uparrow ↑ — the cleanest concrete instance of the bias–variance tradeoff ( Bias-Variance Tradeoff ). Train error always falls with degree; test error is U-shaped. Pick degree by CV. High-degree pathologies: wild oscillation near the data edges (Runge phenomenon), and explosive extrapolation outside the range. x , x 2 , x 3 x, x^2, x^3 x , x 2 , x 3 are strongly correlated → multicollinearity → standardize, use orthogonal polynomial bases, and regularize (poly features + ridge is a strong combo). Better-behaved alternative: splines — piecewise low-degree polynomials joined smoothly at knots → local flexibility without global oscillation. Feature count explodes with interactions: full degree- d d d expansion of p p p features ≈ ( p + d d ) \approx \binom{p+d}{d} ≈ ( d p + d ​ ) terms → regularization becomes mandatory. # Scoring: R² and adjusted R² Analogy. R 2 R^2 R 2 answers: how much better is your model than the laziest possible one? The lazy baseline predicts the mean y ˉ \bar{y} y ˉ ​ for everyone. R 2 R^2 R 2 = the fraction of the baseline s error your model eliminated. Definitions: SS res = ∑ i ( y i − y ^ i ) 2 \text{SS}_{\text{res}} = \sum_i(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 SS res ​ = ∑ i ​ ( y i ​ − y ^ ​ i ​ ) 2 (your model s leftover error); SS tot = ∑ i ( y i − y ˉ ) 2 \text{SS}_{\text{tot}} = \sum_i(y_i - \bar{y})^2 SS tot ​ = ∑ i ​ ( y i ​ − y ˉ ​ ) 2 (baseline s error). R 2 = 1 − SS res SS tot (fraction of variance explained) R^2 = 1 - \frac{\text{SS}_{\text{res}}}{\text{SS}_{\text{tot}}} \qquad \text{(fraction of variance explained)} R 2 = 1 − SS tot ​ SS res ​ ​ (fraction of variance explained) R adj 2 = 1 − ( 1 − R 2 ) ⋅ n − 1 n − p − 1 (pays a price per feature) R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1 - (1 - R^2)\cdot\frac{n - 1}{n - p - 1} \qquad \text{(pays a price per feature)} R adj 2 ​ = 1 − ( 1 − R 2 ) ⋅ n − p − 1 n − 1 ​ (pays a price per feature) The facts interviewers actually probe: Claim Truth R 2 ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] R^2 \in [0, 1] R 2 ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] ? Only in-sample with an intercept. On test data R 2 R^2 R 2 can be negative — worse than predicting the mean. Adding any feature changes R 2 R^2 R 2 ? In-sample R 2 R^2 R 2 never decreases when you add a feature, even pure noise — that s why it can t do model selection. Adjusted R 2 R^2 R 2 fixes that? It penalizes p p p , so it can fall when a feature adds nothing — better, but still in-sample; CV is the real judge. High R 2 R^2 R 2 = good model? No: leakage, overfitting, or just low-noise data. Low R 2 R^2 R 2 can still be valuable (finance lives at R 2 ≈ 0.01 R^2 \approx 0.01 R 2 ≈ 0.01 ). R 2 R^2 R 2 for nonlinear models? The = squared correlation ( y , y ^ ) (y, \hat{y}) ( y , y ^ ​ ) identity holds only for linear-with-intercept OLS; report MSE/MAE for general models. Relationship to the metrics chapter: R 2 R^2 R 2 is a rescaled MSE — same ranking of models on the same data; it adds interpretability, not new information (see Model Evaluation Validation ). # Choosing features and going beyond a straight line Analogy. Feature selection is hiring for a small team: each new hire must justify a salary (complexity). Stepwise hiring by interviews alone (in-sample fit) hires charming frauds; you want references from outside the room (cross-validation, information criteria). Feature selection — three families: Family Idea Examples Cost / risk Filter rank features before modeling correlation, mutual information cheap; ignores interactions Wrapper search subsets by model performance forward/backward stepwise expensive; overfits the search; inference after selection is invalid Embedded selection happens inside training lasso , tree importances one shot; lasso = the principled stepwise Model-size criteria, one line each: AIC = 2 k − 2 ln ⁡ L ^ = 2k - 2\ln\hat{L} = 2 k − 2 ln L ^ (prediction-oriented); BIC = k ln ⁡ n − 2 ln ⁡ L ^ = k\ln n - 2\ln\hat{L} = k ln n − 2 ln L ^ (heavier penalty, consistency-oriented; picks smaller models for large n n n ). Beyond a straight line (staying in linear-model land): Transforms: log ⁡ ( x ) \log(x) lo g ( x ) , x \sqrt{x} x ​ , log ⁡ ( y ) \log(y) lo g ( y ) — fix skew and multiplicative effects. Log- y y y means coefficients become % effects: Δ y ≈ 100 ⋅ w j % \Delta y \approx 100\cdot w_j\% Δ y ≈ 100 ⋅ w j ​ % per unit x j x_j x j ​ . Interactions: add x 1 ⋅ x 2 x_1\cdot x_2 x 1 ​ ⋅ x 2 ​ when one feature s effect depends on another (price sensitivity differs by region). Polynomials / splines: splines = piecewise polynomials with smooth knots — flexible AND stable. GAMs: y = ∑ j f j ( x j ) y = \sum_j f_j(x_j) y = ∑ j ​ f j ​ ( x j ​ ) — each feature gets its own smooth curve; still additive → still explainable feature by feature. When to leave linear land: heavy feature interactions you can t enumerate → gradient-boosted trees ( Classification Methods ); raw signal inputs (text/images) → deep learning. Production issues. Stepwise + p-values in prod reports: selection invalidates classic inference (the features were chosen because they looked significant — winner s curse). Use lasso for selection, then refit OLS on the chosen set ( relaxed lasso ) and validate out-of-sample. Target leakage via feature engineering: a days_since_last_payment feature computed with future knowledge gives R 2 = 0.99 R^2 = 0.99 R 2 = 0.99 offline, garbage online. Every feature must be computable at prediction time. Schema drift: a transform pipeline (log, interactions) trained against one feature scale silently breaks when an upstream team changes units. Version the preprocessing artifact with the model. # Decision table Situation Method One-line why Baseline, n ≫ p n \gg p n ≫ p , want interpretation OLS BLUE under Gauss–Markov; exact CIs if errors are also normal Correlated features / unstable coefficients Ridge ( X ⊤ X + λ I ) − 1 (X^\top X+\lambda I)^{-1} ( X ⊤ X + λ I ) − 1 always exists; variance ↓ \downarrow ↓ Many features, few matter Lasso exact zeros = built-in selection Correlated features AND want sparsity Elastic Net L1 sparsity + L2 grouping p n p n p n Ridge / lasso / Elastic Net OLS undefined; lasso caps at n n n features Curved relationship, one or few features Polynomial (low degree) or splines + CV linear in parameters; degree = bias–variance dial Outliers in y y y Huber / quantile regression robust losses on a linear model Asymmetric cost / need intervals Quantile regression pinball loss; τ \tau τ from cost ratio Counts Poisson regression (GLM) right noise model, log link Skewed positive target log ⁡ ( y ) \log(y) lo g ( y ) + OLS multiplicative errors; remember exp ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \exp(\cdot) exp ( ⋅ ) gives the median Nonlinear interactions everywhere Gradient-boosted trees leave linear land knowingly # 60-second interview answers Question Answer in one breath Derive OLS? Minimize ∥ y − X w ∥ 2 \lVert y-Xw\rVert^2 ∥ y − X w ∥ 2 ; set gradient − 2 X ⊤ ( y − X w ) = 0 -2X^\top(y-Xw) = 0 − 2 X ⊤ ( y − X w ) = 0 → normal equations X ⊤ X w = X ⊤ y X^\top Xw = X^\top y X ⊤ X w = X ⊤ y → w ^ = ( X ⊤ X ) − 1 X ⊤ y \hat{w} = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y w ^ = ( X ⊤ X ) − 1 X ⊤ y ; geometrically, project y y y onto X X X s column space. Why can t you trust R 2 R^2 R 2 going up? In-sample R 2 R^2 R 2 rises with ANY added feature; use adjusted R 2 R^2 R 2 , AIC/BIC, or best: cross-validation. And test-set R 2 R^2 R 2 can be negative. Multicollinearity — symptoms and fix? Inflated coefficient variance, sign flips, big R 2 R^2 R 2 with no significant features; detect with VIF = 1 / ( 1 − R j 2 ) \text{VIF} = 1/(1-R_j^2) VIF = 1/ ( 1 − R j 2 ​ ) ; fix with ridge, dropping/combining features, or PCA. Predictions are mostly fine; interpretation is not. Ridge vs lasso? Ridge: L2, closed form, shrinks, handles collinearity, never zeros. Lasso: L1, soft-thresholding, exact zeros, selection, unstable with correlated twins. Elastic Net blends. Is polynomial regression linear? Yes — linear in the parameters. It s OLS on expanded features; linear model never meant linear in x x x . When is OLS BLUE? Gauss–Markov: zero-mean, homoscedastic, uncorrelated errors → best linear unbiased estimator. Normality NOT required (only for exact small-sample inference). Why does ridge beat OLS on test error? It trades a little bias for a big variance cut — minimizing test MSE = = = bias² + variance + noise, not unbiasedness. # Common traps → fixes Trap Fix Judging models by in-sample R 2 R^2 R 2 adjusted R 2 R^2 R 2 at minimum; cross-validation for real Regularizing unstandardized features scale first, inside the CV pipeline Penalizing the intercept don t Interpreting coefficients under collinearity check VIF before telling a coefficient story p-values after stepwise selection invalid; use holdout validation or post-selection inference Trusting a linear model outside training range monitor input ranges; clamp; flag extrapolations log-transforming y y y then exponentiating naively you get the median, not the mean (Jensen); add the smearing / σ 2 / 2 \sigma^2/2 σ 2 /2 correction if you need the mean Fitting degree-15 polynomial because train error fell test error is U-shaped; pick degree by CV; prefer splines Connects backward: Loss Functions supplies the losses (MSE, Huber, quantile) and penalties (L1/L2). Connects forward: Classification Methods (logistic regression = this + sigmoid + CE), Model Evaluation Validation . # Related Regularization Bias-Variance Tradeoff Gradient Descent Classification Methods

title: Support Vector Machines
text: Say it in 30s: An SVM finds the decision boundary that separates the classes with the widest possible margin — the hyperplane as far as possible from the nearest points of each class. Those nearest points are the support vectors and are the only ones that define the boundary. The kernel trick lets it draw nonlinear boundaries by computing dot products in a higher-dimensional space without ever building that space. Key points Boundary is a hyperplane w·x + b = 0 ; classify with sign(w·x + b) , labels coded y ∈ {+1, −1} . Fix the scale so on-margin support vectors satisfy y(w·x + b) = 1 (in the soft margin, violators have y(w·x + b) 1 ); then the half-margin is 1/||w|| , full margin 2/||w|| . Hard margin: minimize ½||w||² s.t. yᵢ(w·xᵢ + b) ≥ 1 . Minimizing ||w|| = maximizing the margin. Soft margin (real data): minimize ½||w||² + C·Σξᵢ s.t. yᵢ(w·xᵢ + b) ≥ 1 − ξᵢ , ξᵢ ≥ 0 . Slack ξ allows violations. C is the bias-variance knob: large C → punish violations hard (narrow margin, overfit risk); small C → tolerate violations (wider margin, more regularized). Kernel trick: the dual depends on the data only through dot products xᵢ·xⱼ , so replace them with a kernel K(xᵢ, xⱼ) to get a nonlinear boundary cheaply. Common kernels: RBF (Gaussian), polynomial, linear. Common follow-ups / traps What s the margin? → distance from the boundary to the nearest points ( 1/||w|| ; full margin width 2/||w|| ); SVM maximizes it. Which points matter? → only the support vectors; far-away points don t move the boundary. Why does the kernel trick work? → optimization needs only pairwise dot products, never the explicit high-dimensional features. What does C do? → trades margin width against training violations; it s the regularization parameter. Don t say SVM just draws a boundary — the defining idea is the maximum-margin boundary. See depth: Classification Methods . Related: Logistic Regression , Regularization , Bias-Variance Tradeoff .

title: Data Preprocessing & Feature Engineering
heads: Resampling shifts the prior, and calibration breaks
text: Data Features: what happens to the data before the model sees it, and why most surprisingly good offline results trace back to this stage. In most applied settings the model family matters less than the data handling around it. A gradient-boosted tree trained on leaky features will beat a carefully tuned model trained on clean ones, and then fail in deployment. This chapter covers the pipeline in the order it should be built: split first, then clean, encode, transform, balance, and select, with every fitted step living inside the training fold. The recurring theme is a single rule: anything learned from data must be learned from training data only. What you ll be able to say after this chapter Describe a leakage-safe pipeline and name the four leakage families with a detection tip for each. Distinguish MCAR, MAR, and MNAR, and pick an imputation strategy with a missing-indicator when missingness is informative. State which model families need feature scaling and why trees do not. Implement target encoding with out-of-fold statistics and smoothing. Explain how resampling and class weights shift predicted probabilities, and how to correct for it. Compare filter, wrapper, and embedded feature selection, and say where each can leak. # Split Hygiene: Train, Validation, Test Each split has a single job, and mixing jobs is the root of most optimistic estimates. Split Job Touched how often Train Fit parameters (weights, tree splits) and every preprocessing statistic (means, vocabularies, encodings) Constantly Validation Choose hyperparameters, features, thresholds, model family Many times (this is what makes it optimistic over time) Test One unbiased estimate of final performance Once, after all decisions are frozen With cross-validation, the validation role rotates across folds and a separate test set is still kept aside when the number of model-selection decisions is large. See Cross-Validation for nested CV, which separates selection from estimation when data is scarce. Practical rules: Split before any fitting. Even harmless steps such as computing a column mean or fitting a vocabulary belong after the split. Match the split to deployment. If the model will score future rows, split by time. If it will score new users, entities, or sites, split by group. A random split is only appropriate when the deployment distribution of new rows is exchangeable with the training rows. Stratify when classes are rare , so that every fold contains enough positives to estimate metrics (stratification stabilizes estimates; it does not fix leakage). Deduplicate first. Exact and near-duplicate rows (repeated scrapes, augmentations, re-submitted records) that straddle the split inflate scores. Freeze the test set. Each look at test performance that informs a decision converts it into a second validation set. Interview angle How would you split the data? is rarely about percentages. The strong answer starts from the unit of generalization : what will be new at prediction time (a later date, a new customer, a new device)? Then the split mirrors that, and the preprocessing is fit inside the training portion only. # Data Leakage Leakage is any pathway by which information unavailable at prediction time influences training or evaluation. The symptom is an offline score that is too good and a production score that is not. Four families cover most cases. Family Mechanism Typical example Detection tips Target leakage A feature encodes the label or is produced after the outcome Number of collections calls as a feature for loan default; a discharge code predicting a diagnosis Single feature with implausibly high importance or single-feature AUC near 1; ask of each feature when is this value written, relative to the prediction time? Train-test contamination Information from held-out rows enters fitting Scaling or imputing on the full dataset; selecting features on all data; target encoding without cross-fitting; duplicates across splits Compare a pipeline fit on train only against one fit on all data; check duplicate and near-duplicate overlap between splits Temporal leakage Future information is used to predict the past Random split on time-ordered data; rolling features computed with the current or future rows; labels that mature after the cutoff Re-run with a forward-chaining split and see whether the score drops; verify that every feature has an event timestamp not later than the prediction timestamp Group leakage Correlated rows from the same entity are on both sides Multiple images per patient, many sessions per user, several rows per household Evaluate with grouped splits; a large gap between random-CV and group-CV scores indicates entity memorization Further patterns worth knowing: Label-derived features. Aggregates (such as per-user conversion rate) that include the current row s label. Selection and survivorship bias in the label. Labels that exist only for rows that passed an earlier filter (for example, loan outcomes exist only for approved applicants). This is a bias in the training distribution rather than leakage in the strict sense, but it produces the same offline-online gap. Preprocessing order. Resampling or augmenting before splitting places near-copies of a row in both train and validation. Identifier leakage. Row IDs, file names, or timestamps that correlate with the label because of how the data was collected. A useful smell test If one feature dominates importance, or a quick model reaches near-perfect accuracy on a problem that is known to be hard, the likely explanation is a leak rather than a modelling success. Inspect that feature s definition and timestamp before celebrating. Go deeper (optional) Leakage can also be introduced by the evaluation loop. Repeatedly choosing among many candidate models on the same validation set overfits to it, and the winner s score is an optimistically biased estimate. The cure is a fresh holdout or nested CV, as covered in Model Evaluation Validation . # Missing Data Before choosing a fix, ask why values are missing. Rubin s taxonomy describes the dependence between the missingness indicator M M M and the data, split into observed values X o b s X_{obs} X o b s ​ and missing values X m i s X_{mis} X mi s ​ . Mechanism Definition Example Consequence MCAR (completely at random) P ( M ∣ X ) = P ( M ) P(M \mid X) = P(M) P ( M ∣ X ) = P ( M ) Sensor packet loss unrelated to anything Dropping rows is unbiased (but loses power); most imputers behave acceptably MAR (at random) P ( M ∣ X ) = P ( M ∣ X o b s ) P(M \mid X) = P(M \mid X_{obs}) P ( M ∣ X ) = P ( M ∣ X o b s ​ ) Income missing more often for younger respondents, and age is recorded Model-based imputation conditional on observed variables can be unbiased; complete-case analysis generally is biased MNAR (not at random) P ( M ∣ X ) P(M \mid X) P ( M ∣ X ) depends on X m i s X_{mis} X mi s ​ itself High earners decline to report income No purely data-driven fix is guaranteed; need domain assumptions, sensitivity analysis, or a missing-indicator that captures the pattern MAR versus MNAR cannot be established from the observed data alone, since the difference lies in the unobserved values. The choice is a modelling assumption supported by domain knowledge. # Options Approach How Strengths Limits Drop rows / columns Complete-case analysis Simple Biased unless MCAR; can discard most of the data if many columns are partly missing Constant / mean / median Fill with a training-set statistic Fast, keeps all rows Shrinks variance and attenuates correlations; median is more robust to skew Group-wise statistics Fill with the mean within a segment Uses structure Segment sizes must be adequate; the group means come from training data kNN / iterative (chained equations) Predict each feature from the others Captures relationships (supports MAR) Costly; must be fit inside folds; a single imputation understates uncertainty Multiple imputation Draw several completed datasets, pool results Propagates imputation uncertainty Mostly used for inference; heavier for prediction pipelines Native handling Gradient-boosted trees learn a default direction for missing values at each split No imputation step, can exploit informative missingness Library-dependent; linear and distance-based models still need imputed values Missing indicator Add a binary column m j = 1 [ x j missing ] m_j = \mathbb{1}[x_j \text{ missing}] m j ​ = 1 [ x j ​ missing ] alongside imputation Lets the model use missingness as signal (relevant under MNAR or MAR-with-signal) Doubles columns for each affected feature; can add noise if missingness is uninformative Interview angle A solid default: impute with a training-fold median (numeric) or a dedicated missing level (categorical), and add a missing indicator for features where missingness is plausibly informative. Then check, with a model trained on the indicators alone, whether missingness predicts the label. The statement it depends on the mechanism is correct but is only the opening line; follow it with what to do in each case. Pitfalls: imputing before the split leaks statistics; imputing the target is a different problem and is rarely appropriate; and train and serving pipelines must apply the same imputation values (see ML in Production Monitoring ). # Scaling and Normalization Two common transformations, both fit on training data and then applied unchanged to validation, test, and serving data: z = x − μ t r a i n σ t r a i n x ′ = x − x m i n x m a x − x m i n z = \frac{x - \mu_{train}}{\sigma_{train}} \qquad\qquad x = \frac{x - x_{min}}{x_{max} - x_{min}} z = σ t r ain ​ x − μ t r ain ​ ​ x ′ = x ma x ​ − x min ​ x − x min ​ ​ Standardization (left) yields zero mean and unit variance on the training set; min-max (right) maps to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] [ 0 , 1 ] on the training set and can fall outside that range at test time. Robust scaling replaces mean and standard deviation with median and IQR, which reduces sensitivity to outliers. Model family Is scaling needed? Reason Decision trees, random forests, gradient-boosted trees Generally no Splits depend only on the ordering of values; monotone transformations leave the tree unchanged Linear / logistic regression (unregularized, closed-form) Not for fit quality Predictions are invariant to feature scale, but coefficients change units Regularized linear models (ridge, lasso, elastic net) Yes The penalty acts on coefficient size, so features on larger scales are penalized less; see Regularization Gradient descent training (linear models, neural networks) Yes, in practice Badly scaled features produce ill-conditioned loss surfaces and slow or unstable optimization kNN, k-means, RBF-kernel SVM Yes Distances are dominated by the largest-scale feature PCA Yes (usually standardize) Variance is scale-dependent; otherwise the largest-unit feature dominates the leading components. See Eigenvectors, PCA and SVD Naive Bayes (Gaussian) Not required Per-feature class-conditional parameters absorb scale Warning The statistics must come from the training fold. Fitting a scaler on the entire dataset before splitting leaks the mean and variance of held-out rows. The effect is typically small for large data and larger for small samples or heavy-tailed features, but it is avoidable at no cost. Batch normalization and layer normalization inside neural networks are a learned, in-model form of the same idea; they do not replace input standardization in every setting but reduce the sensitivity to it. # Categorical Encoding Encoding Description Good for Watch out for One-hot One binary column per level Linear models, neural networks, low-cardinality features Width grows with cardinality; unseen levels at serving time need a rule (all-zero or other ) Ordinal / integer Map levels to integers Truly ordered categories; tree models in some cases Imposes a spurious order and spacing on nominal variables for linear and distance-based models Frequency / count Replace level with its training frequency High cardinality, quick baseline Distinct levels with equal counts collide; frequency may drift over time Target (mean) encoding Replace level with a statistic of the label High-cardinality features with real label signal Leakage if computed with the row s own label; needs smoothing and cross-fitting Hashing Hash level into k k k buckets Very high or open-ended cardinality, streaming vocabularies Collisions merge unrelated levels; not invertible; signed hashing reduces collision bias Learned embeddings Dense vector per level, trained with the model Very high cardinality in neural models; levels with shared structure Needs enough examples per level; rare and new levels need fallback buckets # Target encoding without leakage The naive version replaces category c c c with the training mean of y y y among rows in c c c . For the row itself, that mean contains its own label, and for rare categories the row s label dominates. The model then learns that the encoding is nearly the label, which fails on new data. Two corrections, normally applied together: Smoothing (shrinkage) pulls small categories toward the global mean y ˉ \bar y y ˉ ​ : μ ^ c = n c y ˉ c + m y ˉ n c + m \hat\mu_c = \frac{n_c\,\bar y_c + m\,\bar y}{n_c + m} μ ^ ​ c ​ = n c ​ + m n c ​ y ˉ ​ c ​ + m y ˉ ​ ​ where n c n_c n c ​ is the count in category c c c , y ˉ c \bar y_c y ˉ ​ c ​ its mean label, and m m m a smoothing strength (a hyperparameter tuned on validation). With n c ≪ m n_c \ll m n c ​ ≪ m the encoding is close to the global mean; with n c ≫ m n_c \gg m n c ​ ≫ m it is close to the category mean. This is the posterior mean under a simple Beta-Binomial or Gaussian prior view. Cross-fitting (out-of-fold encoding). Split the training data into K K K folds. For rows in fold k k k , compute the encoding from the other K − 1 K-1 K − 1 folds. At validation, test, and serving time, use the encoding fitted on all of the training data. Leave-one-out variants exist but can leak through the row-removal arithmetic (the encoding of a row shifts deterministically with its own label), so the K K K -fold form is the safer default. For time-ordered data, replace the folds with an expanding window so that each row is encoded using only earlier rows. Interview angle Mention both halves: smoothing handles rare levels, cross-fitting handles self-leakage. Also state that nested validation matters: the encoding is part of the model, so it must be refit inside each outer CV fold. Unseen categories at serving time need an explicit fallback (the global mean for target encoding, an unknown bucket for embeddings or one-hot). Rare levels are commonly grouped into an other level using a minimum-count threshold set on training data. # Numeric Transforms Log and power transforms. For positive, right-skewed variables (income, counts, durations), log ⁡ ( x ) \log(x) lo g ( x ) or log ⁡ ( 1 + x ) \log(1+x) lo g ( 1 + x ) compresses the tail and turns multiplicative relationships into additive ones. This often helps linear and distance-based models and stabilizes variance; tree models are invariant to monotone transforms of an input, so the transform matters mainly for the target or for combination features. A target log-transform changes what the model optimizes (errors on the log scale), and predictions transformed back via exp ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \exp(\cdot) exp ( ⋅ ) estimate the conditional median rather than the mean under symmetric log-scale noise. Box-Cox and Yeo-Johnson are parametric families that fit the exponent from training data. Binning (discretization). Equal-width or quantile bins turn a number into ordered categories. Pros Cons Lets a linear model fit a piecewise-constant nonlinearity Discards within-bin information; creates discontinuities at edges Reduces the influence of outliers Bin edges are learned from training data and drift over time Can help interpretability and monotonic constraints Many bins add parameters; trees already choose their own thresholds For models that can learn nonlinearities natively (trees, neural networks), explicit binning is often unnecessary. For linear models, splines are a smoother alternative. Other common transforms: clipping to a range, rank or quantile transform (maps to a uniform or normal shape; robust to outliers but loses distances), ratios and differences between features (rate per exposure), and cyclical encoding of periodic features such as hour of day via ( sin ⁡ ( 2 π t / T ) , cos ⁡ ( 2 π t / T ) ) (\sin(2\pi t/T), \cos(2\pi t/T)) ( sin ( 2 π t / T ) , cos ( 2 π t / T )) so that hour 23 and hour 0 are adjacent. # Outliers First separate errors (a negative age, a sensor stuck at its maximum) from rare but valid extremes (a genuinely large purchase). Errors are fixed or removed; valid extremes often carry the signal in fraud and risk problems. Technique Notes IQR rule: flag points beyond Q 1 − 1.5 I Q R Q_1 - 1.5\,\mathrm{IQR} Q 1 ​ − 1.5 IQR or Q 3 + 1.5 I Q R Q_3 + 1.5\,\mathrm{IQR} Q 3 ​ + 1.5 IQR Robust, univariate, a heuristic threshold rather than a law z-score thresholding Mean and standard deviation are themselves inflated by outliers; the median absolute deviation version is sturdier Winsorizing / clipping at percentiles Keeps the row, limits leverage; percentiles come from training data Robust losses (Huber, quantile) Reduce sensitivity without altering the data; see Regression Methods Isolation forest, local outlier factor Multivariate anomalies, useful for audit rather than automatic deletion Removing outliers from the evaluation set while keeping them in production flatters the metric. Any cleaning rule is applied to training data; the same transformation (clipping bounds, not deletion) is applied at serving. # Class Imbalance When one class is rare (fraud, disease, churn), accuracy is uninformative and training objectives are dominated by the majority. The first move is to choose metrics suited to the problem (PR-AUC, recall at a precision target, cost-weighted loss); see ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC and Precision Recall . Rebalancing techniques are a second tool and are not required in every case. Strong classifiers trained with a proper scoring rule on imbalanced data often rank well already, and the main issue is choosing a decision threshold. Lever Mechanism Effect on ranking Effect on probabilities Class weights Multiply the loss of minority examples by w w w Can change the fitted model, especially for flexible ones Shifts predicted probabilities upward; they no longer estimate the true event rate Random undersampling Drop majority rows Faster training; discards information Shifts probabilities upward Random oversampling Duplicate minority rows Can overfit duplicates (see leakage note below) Shifts probabilities upward SMOTE and variants Synthesize minority points by interpolating between neighbors Can help weak learners in low dimension Shifts probabilities; see pitfalls Threshold moving Change the cutoff on the score, leaving training untouched Ranking unchanged Probabilities untouched; the decision changes Cost-sensitive loss / focal loss Weight by difficulty or by error cost Model-dependent Probabilities generally miscalibrated # Resampling shifts the prior, and calibration breaks Suppose the true positive rate is low and negatives are kept with probability β \beta β (undersampling). Writing p p p for the true posterior and p s p_s p s ​ for the posterior under the resampled distribution, the odds scale by 1 / β 1/\beta 1/ β : p s 1 − p s = 1 β ⋅ p 1 − p ⟹ p = β p s β p s − p s + 1 \frac{p_s}{1-p_s} = \frac{1}{\beta}\cdot\frac{p}{1-p} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p = \frac{\beta\,p_s}{\beta\,p_s - p_s + 1} 1 − p s ​ p s ​ ​ = β 1 ​ ⋅ 1 − p p ​ ⟹ p = β p s ​ − p s ​ + 1 β p s ​ ​ Equivalently, on the logit scale the model trained on resampled data is offset by − ln ⁡ β -\ln\beta − ln β relative to the true logit, and the correction adds ln ⁡ β \ln\beta ln β back. A positive-class weight w w w in a well-specified model shifts the logit by roughly + ln ⁡ w +\ln w + ln w in the same spirit. The correction is exact only when the model is correctly specified for the posterior; for misspecified or flexible overfit models, recalibration on untouched validation data (Platt scaling or isotonic regression, see Model Evaluation Validation ) is more reliable than an analytic correction. Interview angle The sentence that distinguishes strong answers: If scores will be read as probabilities (expected-loss decisions, ranking by expected value, thresholds from a cost matrix), the resampled model must be recalibrated on data with the true class prior. If only the ranking matters, resampling does not affect that argument. # SMOTE pitfalls Apply after the split and only to training folds. Synthesizing before splitting places points interpolated from validation rows into training, which is a form of leakage. Distance-based. SMOTE interpolates in feature space, so it needs scaled numeric features and does not apply directly to categorical features (variants such as SMOTE-NC exist). High dimensions and noise. Neighborhoods become uninformative as dimension grows (see the curse of dimensionality below), and interpolation between a minority point and a mislabeled neighbor can place synthetic samples inside the majority region. Evaluate on the original distribution. The validation and test sets keep the true class ratio, or metrics no longer describe production. Gains are often modest against class weights or threshold tuning with a strong learner; compare against those baselines rather than assuming resampling helps. # Feature Selection Selection reduces variance, cost, and latency, and can improve interpretability. Three families: Family How it works Examples Strengths Limits Filter Score each feature independently of the final model Correlation, mutual information, χ 2 \chi^2 χ 2 , ANOVA F-test, variance threshold Fast, model-agnostic Ignores interactions and redundancy among features (two near-duplicate features both score well) Wrapper Search subsets, scoring each with the actual model Forward selection, backward elimination, recursive feature elimination (RFE) Accounts for interactions and the model s behavior Expensive; high risk of overfitting the validation scores when many subsets are tried Embedded Selection happens during training L1 / lasso (zeroes coefficients), tree split usage, elastic net Cheap, tuned to the model Model-specific; correlated features can be selected arbitrarily Cautions: Selection is part of the model. If features are chosen using labels on the full dataset and the model is then cross-validated, the CV estimate is optimistic, often severely when features far outnumber samples. Run selection inside each training fold. Impurity-based tree importances are biased toward high-cardinality and continuous features. Permutation importance (shuffle one feature in held-out data and measure the drop) is less biased but can understate a feature when correlated copies exist, since the model leans on the other copy. Stability matters: if selected subsets change a lot between folds, the ranking is unreliable. Lasso selects among correlated features somewhat arbitrarily; elastic net groups them more smoothly. See Regularization . # Feature Crosses and Interactions A cross combines features so that a model can express their joint effect: a product x 1 x 2 x_1 x_2 x 1 ​ x 2 ​ for numeric features, or a Cartesian combination such as (city, hour_bucket) for categoricals. Linear and logistic models cannot represent an interaction unless one is supplied, so crosses are the main way to add expressiveness. Trees learn interactions through successive splits; neural networks learn them through hidden layers, so manual crosses help less (though explicit crosses over very sparse high-cardinality IDs can still help memorization). Cost: crossing categorical features multiplies cardinality, so data per cell shrinks; hashing the crossed feature into a fixed number of buckets bounds the width, at the price of collisions. Ratios and differences (clicks per impression, spend relative to the account s median) are a lightweight form of interaction, often more robust than raw products. # Time and Lag Features Time-aware features are the most frequent source of both strong signal and temporal leakage. Feature type Construction Leakage guard Lags Value at t − k t-k t − k Use only values with timestamps strictly before the prediction time Rolling statistics Mean, std, min, max over a window Shift the window so that it excludes the current row (window ends at t − 1 t-1 t − 1 ) Expanding / entity aggregates Count or mean over all history for a user Compute point-in-time, as of each row s timestamp, not from the final table Calendar Hour, day of week, holiday flag Encode periodic features cyclically; holidays are known in advance and are safe Recency / frequency Time since last event, events in the last 7 days Define last relative to the prediction timestamp Differences and growth rates x t − x t − k x_t - x_{t-k} x t ​ − x t − k ​ , x t / x t − k x_t / x_{t-k} x t ​ / x t − k ​ Same cutoff rule as lags; handle zeros in denominators Two further rules apply. First, joins must be point-in-time ( as-of ) : joining a slowly changing attribute (a user s plan tier) by key alone gives the current value rather than the value at the event, which leaks the future. Second, the label horizon defines the cutoff : with a label such as churns within 30 days , features must be frozen at the prediction date and rows whose label window has not yet closed must be excluded or handled as censored. For stationarity and forecasting-specific validation, see Time Series Stationarity and Cross-Validation . # Curse of Dimensionality As the number of features d d d grows with fixed n n n , several things degrade: Sparsity. To keep the same sample density, n n n must grow exponentially in d d d . Nonparametric estimators such as kNN or kernel methods converge at rates that deteriorate with d d d (for twice-differentiable targets, the mean squared error of kernel regression decays like n − 4 / ( d + 4 ) n^{-4/(d+4)} n − 4/ ( d + 4 ) ). Distance concentration. For many data distributions, the ratio between the distances to the nearest and farthest neighbors approaches 1 as d d d increases, so nearest carries little information for distance-based methods. The effect is stronger when features are independent and noisy than when the data lie near a low-dimensional manifold. Volume geometry. Most of the volume of a d d d -dimensional ball lies in a thin shell near its surface, since the fraction of volume within radius ( 1 − ϵ ) r (1-\epsilon)r ( 1 − ϵ ) r is ( 1 − ϵ ) d (1-\epsilon)^d ( 1 − ϵ ) d . Overfitting capacity. With d ≥ n d \ge n d ≥ n a linear model can interpolate the training labels; regularization, dimension reduction, or feature selection is needed. Mitigations: regularization, feature selection, dimensionality reduction (PCA, autoencoders, embeddings), and more data. Real data frequently lies near a lower-dimensional structure, which is why high-dimensional models can still generalize, but the argument is empirical for each dataset rather than guaranteed. Go deeper (optional) Adding irrelevant features hurts distance-based methods quickly and hurts regularized or tree-based methods more slowly. A quick diagnostic is to append a few random noise columns and see whether the model assigns them importance; high noise-column importance signals overfitting. # Pipeline Checklist: Leakage-Safe Workflow Encapsulate every fitted step in a single pipeline object so that fitting, cross-validation, and serving share the same code. Define prediction time and label horizon. For each feature, write down when its value becomes known. Deduplicate and choose the split by time, group, or random-stratified according to the unit of generalization. Set aside the test set; do not touch it. Fit all preprocessing on the training portion only: imputers, scalers, encoders, vocabularies, binning edges, outlier bounds, feature selectors. Cross-fit any step that uses the label (target encoding, supervised selection, stacking features). Resample or reweight inside training folds only; keep validation and test at the natural class ratio. Tune hyperparameters, thresholds, and calibration on validation data; if probabilities matter, recalibrate on data with the true prior. Sanity-check for leaks: feature importance review, single-feature AUC, a time-forward or group-wise re-split, shuffled-label test (the score should fall to chance). Evaluate once on the test set with metrics matching the business decision. Ship the fitted pipeline as one artifact and log the training-data snapshot and statistics so that serving reproduces the same transforms (see ML in Production Monitoring ). Interview angle A concise way to summarize this checklist: Every number the pipeline learns comes from training rows only, every step that uses the label is cross-fitted, and the validation scheme mirrors how the model will meet new data. # One-Page Summary Topic Key idea Splits Train fits everything learned; validation selects; test is touched once. Split by the unit of generalization (time, group, random). Leakage Target, train-test contamination, temporal, group. Detect with timestamp audits, single-feature AUC, re-splits, shuffled-label tests. Missingness MCAR / MAR / MNAR; MAR vs MNAR is an assumption. Impute with training statistics, add indicators when missingness is informative; trees can handle missing natively. Scaling Needed for distance-based, regularized, gradient-trained, and PCA; not for trees. Fit on train only. Encoding One-hot for low cardinality; target encoding needs smoothing n c y ˉ c + m y ˉ n c + m \frac{n_c \bar y_c + m\bar y}{n_c+m} n c ​ + m n c ​ y ˉ ​ c ​ + m y ˉ ​ ​ plus out-of-fold fitting; hashing and embeddings for huge cardinality. Numeric Log for right skew; binning trades information for robustness; cyclical encoding for periodic features. Outliers Separate errors from signal; clip with training bounds; robust losses. Imbalance Metrics first; class weights, resampling, or threshold moving next. Resampling shifts the prior, so recalibrate: p = β p s β p s − p s + 1 p = \frac{\beta p_s}{\beta p_s - p_s + 1} p = β p s ​ − p s ​ + 1 β p s ​ ​ . SMOTE only on training folds. Selection Filter (fast), wrapper (costly, overfits), embedded (L1, trees). Run inside CV folds. Crosses Needed by linear models; trees and nets learn interactions. Hashing bounds width. Time features Lag and rolling windows end before the prediction time; point-in-time joins. High dimension Sparsity and distance concentration hurt local methods; regularize, reduce, or add data. # Related MOC - Data Features Model Evaluation Validation for calibration, metrics, and splitting Cross-Validation for nested and time-series splits Classification Methods for imbalance in the model context Regularization and Bias-Variance Tradeoff ML in Production Monitoring for training-serving skew

The head: GAP → Dense → Softmax → Loss
text: A CNN slides small learnable pattern detectors ( filters / kernels ) across an image. Early layers find edges, deeper layers find textures, parts, then whole objects. Convolution is just sliding-window pattern matching with learned weights. The whole game is: spatial size shrinks, channel depth grows , then a head maps features to classes. # Image as a tensor An image is a tensor of shape H × W × C H \times W \times C H × W × C (height, width, channels). Grayscale C = 1 C=1 C = 1 , RGB C = 3 C=3 C = 3 . After the first layer, channels stop being colors and become feature maps (one per filter). # The convolution operation A filter is a small weight grid (e.g. 3 × 3 3\times3 3 × 3 ) that spans all input channels. A 3 × 3 3\times3 3 × 3 filter over a 3-channel input is 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 3\times3\times3 = 27 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 weights + 1 +1 + 1 bias. Slide it; at each position multiply weights by the covered pixels, sum, add bias → one pixel of one output feature map. out ( i , j ) = b + ∑ d i ∑ d j ∑ c in ( i + d i , j + d j , c ) ⋅ w ( d i , d j , c ) \text{out}(i,j) = b + \sum_{d_i}\sum_{d_j}\sum_{c} \text{in}(i+d_i,\, j+d_j,\, c)\cdot w(d_i, d_j, c) out ( i , j ) = b + d i ​ ∑ ​ d j ​ ∑ ​ c ∑ ​ in ( i + d i ​ , j + d j ​ , c ) ⋅ w ( d i ​ , d j ​ , c ) Two properties make this cheap and powerful: Parameter sharing — the same weights are reused at every location. One edge detector works everywhere; you store it once. Local connectivity — each output depends only on a small patch (its receptive field ). One filter → one feature map. Use many filters (say 64) → 64 output channels. # The four knobs Stride S S S — how many pixels the filter jumps each step. S = 1 S=1 S = 1 keeps size; S = 2 S=2 S = 2 roughly halves each spatial dim (downsampling). Padding P P P — a border (usually zeros) added so the output size is controllable and border pixels are treated fairly. valid : P = 0 P=0 P = 0 , output shrinks. same : pad so output size = = = input size (at S = 1 S=1 S = 1 ). For odd kernel K K K : P = K − 1 2 P = \frac{K-1}{2} P = 2 K − 1 ​ → K = 3 ⇒ P = 1 K{=}3 \Rightarrow P{=}1 K = 3 ⇒ P = 1 , K = 5 ⇒ P = 2 K{=}5 \Rightarrow P{=}2 K = 5 ⇒ P = 2 . Kernel size K K K — the window edge length. Number of filters — sets the output depth (channels). # Output-size formula (memorize) O = ⌊ W − K + 2 P S ⌋ + 1 O = \left\lfloor \frac{W - K + 2P}{S} \right\rfloor + 1 O = ⌊ S W − K + 2 P ​ ⌋ + 1 Applied independently to height and width. Spatial size comes from this formula; depth comes from the number of filters . Example: 3 input channels, 3 × 3 3\times3 3 × 3 , 64 filters → ( 3 ⋅ 3 ⋅ 3 + 1 ) ⋅ 64 = 28 ⋅ 64 = 1,792 (3\cdot3\cdot3 + 1)\cdot 64 = 28 \cdot 64 = 1{,}792 ( 3 ⋅ 3 ⋅ 3 + 1 ) ⋅ 64 = 28 ⋅ 64 = 1 , 792 . Note it does not depend on image height/width — parameter sharing paying off. # Inside one Conv block The repeating unit. One 3 × 3 3\times3 3 × 3 layer sees 3 × 3 3\times3 3 × 3 ; stack two → 5 × 5 5\times5 5 × 5 ; three → 7 × 7 7\times7 7 × 7 . title: Gated Recurrent Unit
text: A GRU is a streamlined LSTM : same core trick (gated, mostly-additive memory so gradients survive), but with one memory line instead of two and two gates instead of three. Fewer parameters → trains faster, needs less data, often just as good. # The setup No separate cell state — just one memory vector h h h — and two sigmoid gates. # The two gates Update gate ( σ \sigma σ ) — the main one. A single slider doing the forget and input jobs together: toward 1 = keep old memory, ignore new; toward 0 = drop old memory, take in new. Keeping is the opposite of adding (if you keep 70%, you take 30% new). Holding it near 1 across steps is what preserves long-range memory and the gradient. Reset gate ( σ \sigma σ ) — decides how much of the past to ignore when drafting the new candidate memory. Lets the cell start fresh when the current input begins something new and old context would be noise. One step in words: reset gate decides how much past to fold into a candidate new memory → update gate decides how much of that candidate to swap in versus how much old memory to keep. # Forward math (defined bottom-up) Symbols: σ \sigma σ squashes to ( 0 , 1 ) (0,1) ( 0 , 1 ) (a dial), tanh ⁡ \tanh tanh to ( − 1 , 1 ) (-1,1) ( − 1 , 1 ) (signed content), ⊙ \odot ⊙ = elementwise multiply, [ h t − 1 , x t ] [h_{t-1},x_t] [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ] = concatenation, each W W W = a learned matrix. h h h is the single memory state. Define the two dials and the candidate first — each reads [ h t − 1 , x t ] [h_{t-1},x_t] [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ] : Update dial z t = σ ( W z [ h t − 1 , x t ] ) z_t = \sigma(W_z[h_{t-1},x_t]) z t ​ = σ ( W z ​ [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ]) — how much old memory to keep Reset dial r t = σ ( W r [ h t − 1 , x t ] ) r_t = \sigma(W_r[h_{t-1},x_t]) r t ​ = σ ( W r ​ [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ]) — how much past to use when drafting Candidate h ~ t = tanh ⁡ ( W h [ r t ⊙ h t − 1 , x t ] ) \tilde h_t = \tanh\big(W_h[\,r_t \odot h_{t-1},\, x_t\,]\big) h ~ t ​ = tanh ( W h ​ [ r t ​ ⊙ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ] ) — note the past is filtered by r t r_t r t ​ before drafting Then blend old memory and candidate with the single update dial: h t = z t ⊙ h t − 1 + ( 1 − z t ) ⊙ h ~ t h_t = z_t \odot h_{t-1} + (1 - z_t)\odot \tilde h_t h t ​ = z t ​ ⊙ h t − 1 ​ + ( 1 − z t ​ ) ⊙ h ~ t ​ (PyTorch convention: z z z near 1 keeps the old memory.) Gradient: the leading term is ∂ h t ∂ h t − 1 ≈ diag ⁡ ( z t ) \dfrac{\partial h_t}{\partial h_{t-1}} \approx \operatorname{diag}(z_t) ∂ h t − 1 ​ ∂ h t ​ ​ ≈ diag ( z t ​ ) , so holding z t ≈ 1 z_t \approx 1 z t ​ ≈ 1 keeps the gradient highway open — same additive trick as the LSTM, with one dial instead of separate forget/input gates. # Inside one GRU cell Inputs x t x_t x t ​ and h t − 1 h_{t-1} h t − 1 ​ feed both gates and the candidate. The reset gate filters the past before the candidate is drafted; the update gate blends candidate vs. old memory at the very end. Convention here matches the note and PyTorch: z near 1 keeps the old memory , so the candidate h ~ \tilde h h ~ gets weight ( 1 − z ) (1-z) ( 1 − z ) . Some textbooks flip this; the math is identical, only the label on the dial moves. (Caveat: the candidate above is the original Cho form tanh ⁡ ( W [ r ⊙ h , x ] ) \tanh(W[r\odot h, x]) tanh ( W [ r ⊙ h , x ]) ; PyTorch applies the reset gate after the hidden matmul: n = tanh ⁡ ( W i n x + b i n + r ⊙ ( W h n h + b h n ) ) n=\tanh(W_{in}x+b_{in}+r\odot(W_{hn}h+b_{hn})) n = tanh ( W in ​ x + b in ​ + r ⊙ ( W hn ​ h + b hn ​ )) .) # The step, as a sequence # Stacking GRUs Real models rarely use one layer. You stack them: the hidden-state sequence from layer 1 becomes the input sequence to layer 2, and so on. Two directions of information flow, and they don t mix: Sideways (through time): each layer keeps its own hidden state h h h and passes it to its future self at the next timestep. Layer 1 and layer 2 each have a separate memory line. Upward (through depth): at each timestep, a layer s output is fed as the input to the layer above it. Lower layers tend to pick up short, local patterns; higher layers compose them into longer-range structure. Only the top layer s outputs are usually read for predictions. More layers add representational depth but cost compute and can overfit on small data — same tradeoff as stacking anything. num_layers in PyTorch s nn.GRU does exactly this stacking for you. # LSTM vs GRU LSTM GRU Memories 2 (cell + hidden) 1 (merged) Gates 3 (forget, input, output) 2 (update, reset) Params more fewer Strength slight edge on very long / complex sequences faster, leaner, less data Neither changes the loss ( cross-entropy ). In practice: try both, pick by validation. GRU is a sensible default for speed or limited data; LSTM when sequences are long and complex. # 30-second answer A GRU merges the LSTM s two memories into one and uses two gates: an update gate (keep-old vs take-new in a single dial) and a reset gate (how much past to use when forming the candidate). Same gradient-saving idea as the LSTM, with less machinery. # See also Long Short-Term Memory — the fuller version Recurrent Neural Networks — the base cell both upgrade Cross-Entropy Loss · Gradient Descent

title: Graph Neural Networks
text: A GNN learns from data that lives on a graph — entities (nodes) wired together by relations (edges) — instead of a grid (images, CNNs ) or a sequence (text, RNNs ). The core trick is message passing : each node repeatedly updates its own vector by mixing in its neighbors vectors. Stack k k k rounds and a node sees everything within k k k hops. # The setup A graph is nodes plus edges. Every node v v v starts with a feature vector x v x_v x v ​ (its raw attributes). The model learns from the features and the wiring — that s the whole reason to reach for a graph model rather than a plain MLP over the features alone. Three things a GNN can predict, depending on where you read out: node level — a label per node (fraud user, spam page) edge level — does a link exist / what kind (recommendation, knowledge graph) graph level — one label for the whole graph (molecule property) # Message passing — the engine Let h v ( k ) h_v^{(k)} h v ( k ) ​ be node v v v s vector after layer k k k , with h v ( 0 ) = x v h_v^{(0)} = x_v h v ( 0 ) ​ = x v ​ . One layer is three functions: Message — for each neighbor u u u , build a message m u → v = MSG ( h u , h v , e u v ) m_{u\to v} = \text{MSG}(h_u, h_v, e_{uv}) m u → v ​ = MSG ( h u ​ , h v ​ , e uv ​ ) , where e u v e_{uv} e uv ​ is an optional edge feature. Aggregate — collapse all neighbor messages into one vector with a permutation-invariant operator (sum, mean, or max — the result can t depend on neighbor order): a v = AGG ( { m u → v : u ∈ N ( v ) } ) a_v = \text{AGG}(\{m_{u\to v} : u \in \mathcal N(v)\}) a v ​ = AGG ({ m u → v ​ : u ∈ N ( v )}) . Update — fold the aggregate back into the node: h v ( k ) = UPDATE ( h v ( k − 1 ) , a v ) h_v^{(k)} = \text{UPDATE}(h_v^{(k-1)}, a_v) h v ( k ) ​ = UPDATE ( h v ( k − 1 ) ​ , a v ​ ) . Every architecture below is just a different choice of these three functions. # GCN — the equation worth memorizing H ( k ) = σ ( D ~ − 1 / 2 A ~ D ~ − 1 / 2 H ( k − 1 ) W ( k ) ) H^{(k)} = \sigma\big(\tilde D^{-1/2}\,\tilde A\,\tilde D^{-1/2}\,H^{(k-1)}\,W^{(k)}\big) H ( k ) = σ ( D ~ − 1/2 A ~ D ~ − 1/2 H ( k − 1 ) W ( k ) ) A ~ = A + I \tilde A = A + I A ~ = A + I — adjacency with self-loops (so a node includes itself). D ~ \tilde D D ~ — diagonal degree matrix of A ~ \tilde A A ~ . W ( k ) W^{(k)} W ( k ) — the only learned parameter in the layer; σ \sigma σ — a nonlinearity (ReLU). Per node: h v ( k ) = σ ⁣ ( ∑ u ∈ N ( v ) ∪ { v } 1 d ~ v d ~ u W ( k ) h u ( k − 1 ) ) h_v^{(k)} = \sigma\!\Bigg(\sum_{u \in \mathcal N(v)\cup\{v\}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tilde d_v\,\tilde d_u}}\, W^{(k)} h_u^{(k-1)}\Bigg) h v ( k ) ​ = σ ( u ∈ N ( v ) ∪ { v } ∑ ​ d ~ v ​ d ~ u ​ ​ 1 ​ W ( k ) h u ( k − 1 ) ​ ) So GCN s message weight is pure geometry ( 1 / d ~ v d ~ u 1/\sqrt{\tilde d_v\tilde d_u} 1/ d ~ v ​ d ~ u ​ ​ ) — no learned per-edge importance, which is its main weakness. The symmetric normalization down-weights high-degree hub neighbors and keeps the operator s eigenvalues real and bounded (which both stabilizes training and, as below, causes oversmoothing). # GAT — learn the weights Replace the fixed coefficient with a learned attention weight α v u \alpha_{vu} α v u ​ : h v ( k ) = σ ⁣ ( ∑ u α v u W h u ( k − 1 ) ) , α v u = exp ⁡ ( e v u ) ∑ w exp ⁡ ( e v w ) , e v u = LeakyReLU ( a ⊤ [ W h v ∥ W h u ] ) h_v^{(k)} = \sigma\!\Bigg(\sum_{u} \alpha_{vu}\, W h_u^{(k-1)}\Bigg), \qquad \alpha_{vu} = \frac{\exp(e_{vu})}{\sum_{w} \exp(e_{vw})}, \quad e_{vu} = \text{LeakyReLU}\big(a^\top[Wh_v \,\Vert\, Wh_u]\big) h v ( k ) ​ = σ ( u ∑ ​ α v u ​ W h u ( k − 1 ) ​ ) , α v u ​ = ∑ w ​ exp ( e v w ​ ) exp ( e v u ​ ) ​ , e v u ​ = LeakyReLU ( a ⊤ [ W h v ​ ∥ W h u ​ ] ) Now the weight depends on the content of the two nodes, not just structure. Essentially a transformer -style attention where the adjacency matrix is the attention mask. Usually multi-head. # GraphSAGE — the scalable template h v ( k ) = σ ( W ⋅ [ h v ( k − 1 ) ∥ AGG ( { h u ( k − 1 ) } ) ] ) h_v^{(k)} = \sigma\Big(W \cdot \big[\,h_v^{(k-1)} \,\Vert\, \text{AGG}(\{h_u^{(k-1)}\})\,\big]\Big) h v ( k ) ​ = σ ( W ⋅ [ h v ( k − 1 ) ​ ∥ AGG ({ h u ( k − 1 ) ​ }) ] ) It concatenates self with the neighbor aggregate (keeps node identity), and samples a fixed number of neighbors instead of using all — that s what makes it run on billion-edge graphs and work inductively on unseen nodes. # GIN — maximally expressive h v ( k ) = MLP ( k ) ⁣ ( ( 1 + ϵ ) h v ( k − 1 ) + ∑ u ∈ N ( v ) h u ( k − 1 ) ) h_v^{(k)} = \text{MLP}^{(k)}\!\Big((1+\epsilon)\,h_v^{(k-1)} + \sum_{u\in\mathcal N(v)} h_u^{(k-1)}\Big) h v ( k ) ​ = MLP ( k ) ( ( 1 + ϵ ) h v ( k − 1 ) ​ + u ∈ N ( v ) ∑ ​ h u ( k − 1 ) ​ ) Uses sum , not mean or max, on purpose: mean can t tell { A , B } \{A,B\} { A , B } from { A , A , B , B } \{A,A,B,B\} { A , A , B , B } , max can t tell { A , B } \{A,B\} { A , B } from { A , A , B } \{A,A,B\} { A , A , B } . Only sum is injective over a multiset (preserves counts). This is the link to the Weisfeiler-Lehman test — GIN hits the 1-WL expressiveness ceiling. Sum is needed to reach the 1-WL ceiling; mean or max fall below it. # The three side by side A spectrum: structure decides everything (GCN) → content decides (GAT) → preserve maximum structural info (GIN). Cost: GCN ≈ GIN GAT; expressiveness order is GCN GAT/GraphSAGE GIN (for structure). None dominates: GAT often wins on feature-rich graphs, GIN on molecules, GCN is a shockingly hard baseline for the compute. # Depth, outputs, and oversmoothing One layer = see direct neighbors; two layers = neighbors of neighbors. Depth = reach. Then pool the final embeddings into the right readout head. Oversmoothing (the reason GNNs stay shallow, 2–4 layers): strip weights/nonlinearity and a layer is repeated multiplication by A ^ = D ~ − 1 / 2 A ~ D ~ − 1 / 2 \hat A = \tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde A\tilde D^{-1/2} A ^ = D ~ − 1/2 A ~ D ~ − 1/2 , so k k k layers ≈ A ^ k H \approx \hat A^k H ≈ A ^ k H . The eigenvalues of A ^ \hat A A ^ live in ( − 1 , 1 ] (-1,1] ( − 1 , 1 ] with the leading one at exactly 1 1 1 , so every other component is shrunk by λ k → 0 \lambda^k \to 0 λ k → 0 . All node embeddings collapse toward the dominant eigenvector — they become indistinguishable. This is why just add layers (which works for CNNs/transformers) actively hurts here. Residual connections, normalization, and jumping-knowledge layers fight this. Oversquashing — a related failure: a node s exponentially growing receptive field gets crammed into a fixed-size vector, so long-range dependencies get lost. # Training: losses, activations, batching There is no special GNN loss . The GNN produces embeddings; a readout head turns them into predictions, and the loss follows the head and task level (see Cross-Entropy Loss ). Node / graph classification — cross-entropy (softmax + CE for multi-class, sigmoid + BCE for binary/multi-label). In the transductive setting, compute the loss only over labeled training nodes even though message passing uses the whole graph. Regression (molecule property, ETA) — MSE or MAE / Huber. Link prediction — the one with a GNN-specific flavor. Score a candidate edge ( u , v ) (u,v) ( u , v ) from the two embeddings (dot product h u ⊤ h v h_u^\top h_v h u ⊤ ​ h v ​ or an MLP on [ h u ∥ h v ] [h_u \Vert h_v] [ h u ​ ∥ h v ​ ] ), then train with negative sampling + BCE or a margin/ranking loss (BPR, max-margin). # Negative sampling Link prediction has ∼ N 2 \sim N^2 ∼ N 2 possible pairs but only a few million real edges, so almost everything is a non-edge . You can t compute the loss over all negatives (intractable + hopelessly imbalanced — predict no edge everywhere and score 99.9999%). Instead, for each positive edge sample a handful of negatives (typically 1:1 to 1:5 ), usually by fixing u u u and drawing a random w w w it isn t linked to. Train the scorer to output high for real edges, low for sampled fakes . Same trick appears in word2vec (avoids a full-vocab softmax), recommendations/retrieval, and contrastive learning. The detail interviewers probe: Hard negative mining — sample negatives the model currently scores high (plausible fakes) for a stronger gradient than uniform-random easy negatives. Frequency/degree-based sampling (word2vec used freq 0.75 ^{0.75} 0.75 ) to avoid over-sampling popular nodes. False-negative noise — a sampled negative may be a true-but-missing link; usually tolerated because it s rare. One-liner: negative sampling approximates an impossibly large negative set with a small representative (or deliberately hard) sample, turning all-vs-all into positive-vs-few-negatives. # Activations Nothing exotic. ReLU is the default σ \sigma σ between layers. LeakyReLU is a fixed architectural choice inside GAT s attention scoring ; ELU is a common GAT alternative. At the head: softmax (multi-class), sigmoid (binary / multi-label / link probability), linear (regression). The aggregator (sum/mean/max) is the pooling operator, not an activation, and must stay permutation-invariant. # The engineering gotchas Normalization — vanilla BatchNorm is awkward (batch = variable-size set of nodes/graphs); use LayerNorm , GraphNorm , or PairNorm (PairNorm is designed to fight oversmoothing ). Deeper GNNs = normalization + residuals + jumping-knowledge. Self-loops — A ~ = A + I \tilde A = A + I A ~ = A + I so a node keeps its own features in the aggregation. Pooling for graph-level tasks — sum vs mean has the same expressiveness tradeoff as AGG (sum keeps size/count, mean normalizes it away); GIN recommends sum. Mini-batching is not row-slicing — either neighbor sampling (GraphSAGE) or subgraph batching (Cluster-GCN, GraphSAINT) for graphs too big for memory. Edge features — plain GCN/GAT use node features only; thread e u v e_{uv} e uv ​ through the message function (general MPNN ), or use R-GCN for typed edges in knowledge graphs (one weight matrix per relation). Optimizer — just Adam, nothing GNN-specific. # Use cases production Recommendations — Pinterest PinSage (GraphSAGE on the pin–board graph) is the classic deployed example; Uber Eats, Alibaba similar. Fraud / abuse — fraud rings are graph structure; isolated features miss them. Payments, marketplaces. Molecules / drug discovery — graph-level property prediction on molecular graphs. Maps / logistics — Google used a GNN for ETA prediction over the road graph. Knowledge graphs — link prediction, entity resolution (R-GCN handles typed edges). # Where they fail Oversmoothing / oversquashing — limits depth and long-range reach (above). Scalability — neighbor explosion: a k k k -hop neighborhood can be most of the graph. Sampling helps but adds variance. Dynamic graphs — most GNNs assume a static graph; real graphs change constantly, and serving fresh embeddings is a real eng problem. Often don t beat simpler baselines — a tuned MLP + hand-engineered graph features frequently matches published GNN wins. If the signal is in node features, not topology, a GNN is overkill. Always benchmark a non-graph baseline first. # Metrics Depends on the task level (see Precision Recall , ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC ): Node / graph classification — accuracy, F1, AUC-ROC, AUC-PR (use PR for fraud — heavy class imbalance). Link prediction — AUC plus ranking metrics: Hits@k, MRR (mean reciprocal rank), MAP. Recommendation — Recall@k, NDCG@k, MRR. Regression (molecules, ETA) — MAE, RMSE. # One-line recall A GNN layer only chooses how to weight a neighbor (MSG), how to combine weighted neighbors (AGG), and how to fold that into the node (UPDATE). GCN fixes weights by degree, GAT learns them by content, GraphSAGE samples + concatenates, GIN sums and proves that s maximal. Everything else is plumbing. # See also Convolutional Neural Networks — convolution on a grid; GNN generalizes it to arbitrary graphs Recurrent Neural Networks — attention link to GAT Gradient Descent — how the weights W W W are trained ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC · Precision Recall — the classification metrics above Cross-Entropy Loss — the usual node/graph classification loss

title: Long Short-Term Memory
text: An LSTM is an RNN cell that fixes vanishing gradients by adding a second memory line — the cell state — that information rides along with only gentle edits (keep + add) instead of being fully overwritten every step. Learned gates (sigmoid dials, 0→1) decide what to erase, what to write, and what to read. The name says it: it makes short-term memory able to act long-term. # The two memories Cell state c c c — the long-term memory. A conveyor belt running across all steps. It mostly gets multiplied (forget) and added to (input), never fully rewritten. That additive path is why information and gradients survive long gaps. Hidden state h h h — the short-term memory / working output. What the cell exposes right now to predict and pass forward. A vanilla RNN has only h h h (hence it forgets). The LSTM s innovation is the added c c c line. # What a gate is A gate is a tiny layer that outputs a number between 0 and 1 via sigmoid — a dial. 0 = block, 1 = let through. You multiply the dial against some information. The network learns to set the dial from context (it sees the new input x t x_t x t ​ and previous output h t − 1 h_{t-1} h t − 1 ​ ). # The three gates Forget gate ( σ \sigma σ ) — multiplies the belt to decide what to erase . Near 1 = keep the memory; near 0 = wipe it. (New subject in the sentence → drop the old one.) Input gate ( σ \sigma σ paired with a tanh ⁡ \tanh tanh candidate) — decides what new content to add to the belt. The tanh ⁡ \tanh tanh proposes candidate content; the sigmoid decides how much of it to write. Output gate ( σ \sigma σ ) — decides how much of the belt to read out as the hidden state h t h_t h t ​ . One step in words: look at x t x_t x t ​ and h t − 1 h_{t-1} h t − 1 ​ → forget some of the belt → add new content to the belt → read a filtered view as the output. # Forward math (defined bottom-up) Symbols: σ \sigma σ squashes to ( 0 , 1 ) (0,1) ( 0 , 1 ) (a dial), tanh ⁡ \tanh tanh to ( − 1 , 1 ) (-1,1) ( − 1 , 1 ) (signed content), ⊙ \odot ⊙ = elementwise multiply, [ h t − 1 , x t ] [h_{t-1},x_t] [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ] = concatenation, each W W W = a learned matrix. c c c = cell-state belt, h h h = hidden state. Define the four pieces first — each just reads [ h t − 1 , x t ] [h_{t-1},x_t] [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ] : Forget dial f t = σ ( W f [ h t − 1 , x t ] ) f_t = \sigma(W_f[h_{t-1},x_t]) f t ​ = σ ( W f ​ [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ]) — how much of the old belt to keep Input dial i t = σ ( W i [ h t − 1 , x t ] ) i_t = \sigma(W_i[h_{t-1},x_t]) i t ​ = σ ( W i ​ [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ]) — how much new content to write Candidate g t = tanh ⁡ ( W g [ h t − 1 , x t ] ) g_t = \tanh(W_g[h_{t-1},x_t]) g t ​ = tanh ( W g ​ [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ]) — the proposed new content (signed → tanh) Output dial o t = σ ( W o [ h t − 1 , x t ] ) o_t = \sigma(W_o[h_{t-1},x_t]) o t ​ = σ ( W o ​ [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ]) — how much of the belt to expose Then assemble — update the belt (keep some old, add some new), then read it out: c t = f t ⊙ c t − 1 + i t ⊙ g t c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot g_t c t ​ = f t ​ ⊙ c t − 1 ​ + i t ​ ⊙ g t ​ h t = o t ⊙ tanh ⁡ ( c t ) h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(c_t) h t ​ = o t ​ ⊙ tanh ( c t ​ ) Gradient highway: because the belt update is additive , ∂ c t ∂ c t − 1 ≈ diag ⁡ ( f t ) \dfrac{\partial c_t}{\partial c_{t-1}} \approx \operatorname{diag}(f_t) ∂ c t − 1 ​ ∂ c t ​ ​ ≈ diag ( f t ​ ) — just the forget gate, not a tanh ⁡ ′ W \tanh W tanh ′ W matrix. Chained across time it s ∏ i diag ⁡ ( f i ) \prod_i \operatorname{diag}(f_i) ∏ i ​ diag ( f i ​ ) ; if the net learns f i ≈ 1 f_i \approx 1 f i ​ ≈ 1 the gradient survives undimmed (the constant error carousel ). # Why it fixes vanishing gradients In a plain RNN the backward chain multiplied tanh ⁡ ′ ⋅ W \tanh \cdot W tanh ′ ⋅ W at every hop and collapsed to ~0. In an LSTM the cell-state s backward term is roughly just the forget-gate value . If the network learns to hold that gate near 1, the gradient flows back across many steps almost undimmed. The gates create a near-multiplication-free highway for the gradient. # Stacking layers Stack LSTMs by feeding one layer s hidden-state sequence as the input sequence to the layer above. The wrinkle vs. a plain RNN stack: each layer carries two lines sideways through time — the cell state c c c and the hidden state h h h — but only h h h is passed upward to the next layer. The c c c belt is private to its layer and never leaves it. So depth and time stay orthogonal: c c c and h h h flow left-to-right within a layer; only h h h flows bottom-to-top across layers. Top layer s h h h is read for predictions. num_layers in PyTorch s nn.LSTM builds this for you. # 30-second answer An LSTM adds a long-term cell-state belt alongside the short-term hidden state, and three sigmoid gates (forget = erase, input = write, output = read). The belt carries memory by keep-and-add rather than overwrite, so both information and gradients survive long sequences. It does not change the loss ( cross-entropy stays the same) — only the memory-update machinery. # See also Recurrent Neural Networks — the base cell LSTM upgrades Gated Recurrent Unit — the leaner cousin (1 memory, 2 gates) Cross-Entropy Loss · Gradient Descent
