title: PyTorch
heads: Weights  bias are linear; activations are nonlinear
Is the update layer-by-layer or all at once?
Does layer 's update account for layer 's update?
text: ML + PyTorch study notes: weights, activations, and how backprop actually updates a network. # Weight initialization Initial weights are random and small (bias often 0, though nn.Linear draws it randomly too). Random, not zero — if all weights start equal, every neuron computes the same thing and gets the same update forever (the symmetry problem ). Randomness lets neurons specialize. Small, not huge — too big → signal/gradients explode (NaN); too small → they vanish (learns slowly). Principled inits scale randomness by layer fan: Xavier/Glorot (fan_in + fan_out; sigmoid/tanh) or He/Kaiming (fan_in; ReLU). nn.Linear uses a Kaiming-uniform variant by default (≈U(±1/√fan_in), bias also random); call nn.init.xavier_* or kaiming_* explicitly for tanh or ReLU. Set torch.manual_seed(42) for reproducible runs. # Weights bias are linear; activations are nonlinear A neuron has two parts: z = X W + b (linear: weights = slope, bias = intercept) a = activation ( z ) (nonlinear) z = XW + b \quad \text{(linear: weights = slope, bias = intercept)} \qquad a = \text{activation}(z) \quad \text{(nonlinear)} z = X W + b (linear: weights = slope, bias = intercept) a = activation ( z ) (nonlinear) Weights and bias do plain linear math ( y = m x + c y = mx + c y = m x + c ). Both are learned, both updated by gradient descent. The activation function is what s nonlinear (and it s fixed, not learned). Why needed: stacking linear layers with no activation collapses to one linear equation. Activations let the network model curves/complex patterns. Mental model: linear step → bend → linear step → bend → … # How weights are updated (gradient descent) One formula: w new = w old − ( η × gradient ) w_{\text{new}} = w_{\text{old}} - (\eta \times \text{gradient}) w new ​ = w old ​ − ( η × gradient ) Gradient = direction steepness of how loss changes with the weight. positive → increasing the weight raises loss → decrease it. negative → increasing the weight lowers loss → increase it. Either way you move opposite the gradient → hence the minus sign ( descent ). Learning rate η \eta η = step size. too big → overshoot, bounce around, diverge. too small → painfully slow. Hill analogy: gradient points steepest uphill; you step downhill (opposite) repeatedly until you reach the valley (low loss). Optimizers: plain SGD uses the formula directly; Adam adapts the step size per weight, but the core move opposite the gradient logic is the same. # How gradients are calculated (backpropagation) Backprop = the chain rule applied backwards through the network. In words: if A affects B and B affects C, then A s effect on C = = = (A→B) × \times × (B→C). Just multiply the links. # Worked single-neuron example Setup: x = [ 1 , 4 ] x = [1, 4] x = [ 1 , 4 ] , y = 0 y = 0 y = 0 , w = [ 0.5 , 0.5 ] w = [0.5, 0.5] w = [ 0.5 , 0.5 ] , b = 0 b = 0 b = 0 . z = 0.5 ⋅ 1 + 0.5 ⋅ 4 = 2.5 , p = σ ( 2.5 ) = 0.924 z = 0.5\cdot1 + 0.5\cdot4 = 2.5, \qquad p = \sigma(2.5) = 0.924 z = 0.5 ⋅ 1 + 0.5 ⋅ 4 = 2.5 , p = σ ( 2.5 ) = 0.924 Chain for w 1 w_1 w 1 ​ : w 1 → z → p → Loss \;w_1 \to z \to p \to \text{Loss} w 1 ​ → z → p → Loss . ∂ L ∂ w 1 = ∂ L ∂ p ⋅ ∂ p ∂ z ⋅ ∂ z ∂ w 1 = p − y p ( 1 − p ) ⋅ p ( 1 − p ) ⋅ x 1 = ( p − y ) x 1 \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_1} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial p}\cdot\frac{\partial p}{\partial z}\cdot\frac{\partial z}{\partial w_1} = \frac{p-y}{p(1-p)}\cdot p(1-p)\cdot x_1 = (p - y)\,x_1 ∂ w 1 ​ ∂ L ​ = ∂ p ∂ L ​ ⋅ ∂ z ∂ p ​ ⋅ ∂ w 1 ​ ∂ z ​ = p ( 1 − p ) p − y ​ ⋅ p ( 1 − p ) ⋅ x 1 ​ = ( p − y ) x 1 ​ The p ( 1 − p ) p(1-p) p ( 1 − p ) cancels. Plugging in: ∂ L ∂ w 1 = ( 0.924 − 0 ) ⋅ 1 = 0.924 , ∂ L ∂ w 2 = ( 0.924 ) ⋅ 4 = 3.70 , ∂ L ∂ b = 0.924 \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_1} = (0.924 - 0)\cdot 1 = 0.924, \quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_2} = (0.924)\cdot 4 = 3.70, \quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b} = 0.924 ∂ w 1 ​ ∂ L ​ = ( 0.924 − 0 ) ⋅ 1 = 0.924 , ∂ w 2 ​ ∂ L ​ = ( 0.924 ) ⋅ 4 = 3.70 , ∂ b ∂ L ​ = 0.924 # Why the gradient is per-weight Every weight shares the same error term ( p − y ) (p - y) ( p − y ) but is multiplied by its own input x i x_i x i ​ . Different input → different gradient. ( w 2 w_2 w 2 ​ s input was 4, so its gradient is 4× w 1 w_1 w 1 ​ s.) # General per-weight formula gradient for a weight = ( error signal at its neuron ) × ( input flowing through it ) \text{gradient for a weight} = (\text{error signal at its neuron}) \times (\text{input flowing through it}) gradient for a weight = ( error signal at its neuron ) × ( input flowing through it ) Same error × input shape at every layer, however deep. # Multi-layer: why back For an earlier-layer weight the chain is longer (more links multiplied). The front part of that product is shared by all weights feeding a neuron, so backprop computes it once at the output and passes it backward as an error signal δ \delta δ . Working right-to-left avoids recomputing shared pieces — that s the efficiency trick. # Division of labor in PyTorch forward pass → compute prediction, autograd records every operation. loss.backward() → chain-rule backwards, store one gradient per weight in weight.grad . opt.step() → use the gradients to nudge every weight simultaneously. # Is the update layer-by-layer or all at once? All at once, at the end. No weight changes during backprop. 1. forward pass - compute predictions using CURRENT weights 2. backward pass - compute the GRADIENT for every weight in every layer (last layer - first layer, but ONLY computing numbers) 3. opt.step() - NOW update every weight in every layer SIMULTANEOUSLY The weights are frozen during the entire forward + backward pass. Backprop going right-to-left is only about computing gradients efficiently, not about updating in stages. # Does layer t t t s update account for layer t + 1 t+1 t + 1 s update? No. Every gradient is computed w.r.t. the current (old) weights , assuming all other weights stay fixed. Each gradient answers: If I nudge this one weight a tiny bit and everything else stays put, how does the loss change? Then opt.step() nudges every weight at once — each under the assumption the others didn t move. # Doesn t that overcorrect? It can — and the learning rate is what keeps it safe. A gradient is only exactly true for an infinitesimally small step (it s a local linear approximation). The interaction between two layers updates is a higher-order effect: small × small = tiny 2 \text{small} \times \text{small} = \text{tiny}^2 small × small = tiny 2 → negligible when steps are small. weight change ≈ small , inter-layer interaction ≈ small × small = tiny 2 \text{weight change} \approx \text{small}, \qquad \text{inter-layer interaction} \approx \text{small} \times \text{small} = \text{tiny}^2 weight change ≈ small , inter-layer interaction ≈ small × small = tiny 2 So a small learning rate keeps the everyone else held fixed assumption valid. Any mismatch this round is re-measured and corrected next round. This is partly why too large a learning rate diverges : big steps make the layers interfere strongly, the assumption breaks, the overcorrection actually happens, and loss bounces/explodes. # Mental model One iteration = a single synchronized step where every layer moves as if the others didn t. Deliberately wrong but self-correcting: many small approximate steps, re-measuring all gradients each time, beats one big perfect jump. Over many iterations the whole network converges together. (Fancier optimizers, batch-norm, second-order methods exist partly to handle these inter-layer interactions better — plain gradient descent just relies on small steps + repeat. ) # Quick reference: the whole picture 1. Get data (pandas) - preprocess (fit on train only) - convert to tensors 2. Init weights randomly (small) 3. For each epoch: forward: guess = activation(X·W + b) loss: measure wrongness backward: chain-rule back - gradient per weight (error × input) step: new = old − lr × gradient (every weight at once) 4. Loss curve slides down = learning 5. Evaluate on validation (eval mode, no_grad) # Related Gradient Descent Cross-Entropy Loss Logistic Regression TensorGym Study Notes

title: Recurrent Neural Networks
text: An RNN reads a sequence one item at a time, keeping a memory (hidden state) that summarizes everything seen so far. It predicts the next item from that memory. The whole game: one cell, one set of weights, reused at every step , with the memory passed forward and rewritten each step. Its fatal flaw is forgetting — the trace of early items fades, so it can t learn long-range dependencies. LSTMs and GRUs fix exactly that. # The core computation (one step) At each step t t t the cell takes the new input x t x_t x t ​ and the previous memory h t − 1 h_{t-1} h t − 1 ​ , and produces the new memory: h t = tanh ⁡ ( W x h x t + W h h h t − 1 + b ) h_t = \tanh(W_{xh}\, x_t + W_{hh}\, h_{t-1} + b) h t ​ = tanh ( W x h ​ x t ​ + W hh ​ h t − 1 ​ + b ) y ^ t = softmax ( W h y h t ) \hat{y}_t = \text{softmax}(W_{hy}\, h_t) y ^ ​ t ​ = softmax ( W h y ​ h t ​ ) Read it as two streams meeting: the input s contribution ( W x h x t W_{xh} x_t W x h ​ x t ​ ) plus the memory s contribution ( W h h h t − 1 W_{hh} h_{t-1} W hh ​ h t − 1 ​ ), added together, then squashed by tanh ⁡ \tanh tanh into ( − 1 , 1 ) (-1, 1) ( − 1 , 1 ) . The squash is a pressure valve — it stops the memory from exploding over a long sequence and adds the non-linearity that makes the net expressive. There are a few distinct weight matrices, each with its own job: W x h W_{xh} W x h ​ — maps the input into memory space. W h h W_{hh} W hh ​ — maps old memory to new memory (the recurrence). W h y W_{hy} W h y ​ — maps memory to an output prediction. Notation key σ \sigma σ = sigmoid, squashes any number to ( 0 , 1 ) (0,1) ( 0 , 1 ) (a dial ); tanh ⁡ \tanh tanh = squashes to ( − 1 , 1 ) (-1,1) ( − 1 , 1 ) (signed content). ⊙ \odot ⊙ = elementwise multiply (two vectors, slot by slot) — distinct from matrix-vector multiply like W h h h t − 1 W_{hh}h_{t-1} W hh ​ h t − 1 ​ . [ h t − 1 , x t ] [h_{t-1},x_t] [ h t − 1 ​ , x t ​ ] = concatenation (glue the two vectors into one). Subscripts t , k , i t,k,i t , k , i are timestep indices. Caution: in tanh ⁡ ′ ( z i ) \tanh (z_i) tanh ′ ( z i ​ ) the z i z_i z i ​ is the pre-activation (the stuff inside the tanh), unrelated to the GRU update gate z t z_t z t ​ . # Weight sharing (the defining feature) The same W x h , W h h , W h y W_{xh}, W_{hh}, W_{hy} W x h ​ , W hh ​ , W h y ​ are reused at every time step. Same matrices across layers means across time — step 2 does not get fresh weights, it reuses step 1 s. Consequences: The model handles sequences of any length without adding parameters. It s one cell that loops , not a stack of distinct layers. The nodes in a drawing are the same cell at different times. # One evolving memory, not many There is one memory that takes a new value each step. h 1 , h 2 , h 3 h_1, h_2, h_3 h 1 ​ , h 2 ​ , h 3 ​ are not separate memories — they are snapshots of the same memory over time, like frames of a video. Each step reads the memory it was handed, computes a fresh updated version, and passes it forward . A node does not keep a private memory; the memory flows through each node, getting rewritten as it goes (note-passing down a row of people). # Stacking layers Don t confuse unrolling over time (the same one cell reused at each step) with stacking layers (genuinely different cells with their own weights, piled on top of each other). You can do both at once: stack layers, and unroll the whole stack over time. The hidden-state sequence from layer 1 becomes the input sequence to layer 2. Two flows that don t mix: each layer carries its own hidden state sideways through time, and at each timestep a layer s output feeds up as the next layer s input. Only the top layer s outputs are read for predictions. Note that stacking does not fix forgetting — without gates, each layer s sideways memory still fades, which is the whole reason LSTM / GRU exist. # Loss Next-item prediction uses cross-entropy , summed over the sequence: L = ∑ t = 1 T L t , L t = − log ⁡ y ^ t [ correct item ] L = \sum_{t=1}^{T} L_t, \qquad L_t = -\log \hat{y}_t[\text{correct item}] L = t = 1 ∑ T ​ L t ​ , L t ​ = − lo g y ^ ​ t ​ [ correct item ] The pipeline is softmax then cross-entropy : softmax ( p i = e z i / ∑ j e z j p_i = e^{z_i}/\sum_j e^{z_j} p i ​ = e z i ​ / ∑ j ​ e z j ​ ) turns raw scores into probabilities; cross-entropy ( − log ⁡ p correct -\log p_{\text{correct}} − lo g p correct ​ ) measures how little probability you gave the right answer. They are two consecutive operations, easy to conflate — the divide by the sum lives in softmax, the log lives in cross-entropy. # Training: Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT) BPTT is ordinary backprop — applied to the RNN. The full cycle for one batch: Forward — run all steps, save h 1 … h T h_1 \dots h_T h 1 ​ … h T ​ , compute the loss. (memory changes here; weights frozen) Unroll — lay the loop out as a chain of repeated cells, one box per step, so it looks like a normal deep network. Backward — walk from the loss back through the chain, computing a gradient contribution at each step. (memory frozen; gradients computed here) Update — the optimizer ( SGD/Adam ) nudges the weights once , using the summed gradient. (weights change here) Unrolling = stretching the loop memory → [cell] → memory → [cell] → ... into a row [step1] → [step2] → [step3] so the chain rule applies like in any feedforward net. The one thing BPTT adds over plain backprop: because the weights are shared across steps, each step gives a gradient contribution for the same W W W , so you sum them across time , then update once. (You can t update mid-walk — step 3 s gradient assumed the old W W W .) Compute vs. update Gradients are computed at every node; the weights are updated only once, after summing all the per-step contributions. BPTT computes gradients, the optimizer spends them. # Why long-range learning fails (vanishing gradients) To send the gradient from a late step t t t back to an early step k k k , it must pass through every step in between, multiplying a Jacobian at each hop: ∂ h t ∂ h k = ∏ i = k + 1 t diag ⁡ ⁣ ( tanh ⁡ ′ ( z i ) ) W h h \frac{\partial h_t}{\partial h_k} = \prod_{i=k+1}^{t} \operatorname{diag}\!\big(\tanh (z_i)\big)\, W_{hh} ∂ h k ​ ∂ h t ​ ​ = i = k + 1 ∏ t ​ diag ( tanh ′ ( z i ​ ) ) W hh ​ This product of ( t − k ) (t-k) ( t − k ) terms is the killer: tanh ⁡ ′ ≤ 1 \tanh \le 1 tanh ′ ≤ 1 always (near 0 when saturated) → multiplying many sub-1 numbers drives the result toward 0 ( vanishing ). W h h W_{hh} W hh ​ raised to the power ( t − k ) (t-k) ( t − k ) scales like its largest singular value λ \lambda λ : λ 1 \lambda 1 λ 1 (with tanh ⁡ ′ ≤ 1 \tanh \le 1 tanh ′ ≤ 1 ) ⇒ \Rightarrow ⇒ vanish; λ 1 \lambda 1 λ 1 is necessary (not sufficient) for the gradient to explode . So early steps contribute almost nothing to the summed gradient — they re heard but they whisper. The loss function (cross-entropy) is fine; the problem is purely getting the signal back through a long multiplicative chain. Truncated BPTT (only unroll the last N N N steps) is the common practical workaround, at the cost of not learning very long dependencies. # 30-second answer An RNN is one cell with shared weights and a single evolving memory; it blends the new input with the carried-over memory and squashes with tanh ⁡ \tanh tanh at each step. Trained with BPTT (backprop on the unrolled, weight-shared chain, summing the shared weights gradients across time). It fails on long sequences because the backward signal is a product of many Jacobians that vanishes (or explodes) — which is the whole motivation for LSTM / GRU gated memory. # See also Cross-Entropy Loss — the output loss (Objectives Losses) Gradient Descent — the optimizer that applies BPTT s gradients (Math) Convolutional Neural Networks — the other core architecture; uses ReLU, RNNs use tanh/sigmoid Next: LSTM GRU — gated fixes for vanishing gradients

title: TensorGym Study Notes
heads: dim — which axis the operation runs along
keepdim=True — preserve the collapsed axis as size 1
squeeze / unsqueeze — remove / add a size-1 dimension
argmax — index of the max, not the value
torch.cat — join tensors along an axis
Softmax (turns logits into a probability distribution)
text: A cheat-sheet of the concepts covered while working through the TensorGym exercises ( Colab notebook ). # dim — which axis the operation runs along The number you pass to sum , mean , max , softmax , etc. is the axis that gets collapsed. For a 2D tensor of shape [rows, cols] : dim=0 → travel down the rows → one result per column dim=1 → travel across the columns → one result per row x = torch.tensor([[ 1. , 2 , 3 ], [ 4 , 5 , 6 ]]) # shape [2, 3] torch. sum (x, dim= 0 ) # [5, 7, 9] (per column) torch. sum (x, dim= 1 ) # [6, 15] (per row) Rule of thumb: if the answer should have one number per column, use dim=0 ; per row, dim=1 . # keepdim=True — preserve the collapsed axis as size 1 Keeps shape [2, 1] instead of [2] so it broadcasts back against the original. m = torch. max (x, dim= 1 , keepdim= True ).values # shape [2, 1] x - m # works element-wise per row thanks to broadcasting # squeeze / unsqueeze — remove / add a size-1 dimension v = torch.tensor([ 1 , 2 , 3 ]) # [3] v.unsqueeze( 1 ) # [[1],[2],[3]] shape [3, 1] (column vector) v.unsqueeze( 0 ) # [[1, 2, 3]] shape [1, 3] (row vector) y = torch.tensor([[ 1 ],[ 2 ],[ 3 ]]) # [3, 1] y.squeeze() # [1, 2, 3] shape [3] squeeze only removes dimensions of size 1. keepdim=True is like a built-in unsqueeze . # argmax — index of the max, not the value a = torch.tensor([ 10 , 50 , 30 ]) torch. max (a) # 50 (the value) torch.argmax(a) # 1 (the position). Ties - first occurrence. Same in NumPy. With a dim / axis it returns the argmax along that axis. # torch.cat — join tensors along an axis torch.cat((A[:, :i], A[:, i+ 1 :]), dim= 1 ) # drop column i (join left right blocks) dim=1 joins side-by-side (columns); dim=0 stacks vertically (rows). @ is shorthand for torch.matmul . # dtype gotcha Integer literals make int tensors. mean / var error on int tensors, and mixed-dtype matmul fails. Cast with x = x.float() up front when inputs come from integer lists. # Variance: population ( / N /N / N ) vs unbiased ( / ( N − 1 ) /(N-1) / ( N − 1 ) ) torch.var(x) # default: / (N-1) unbiased (Bessel s correction) torch.var(x, unbiased= False ) # / N population Manual: 1 N ∑ ( x − x ˉ ) 2 \frac{1}{N}\sum (x - \bar{x})^2 N 1 ​ ∑ ( x − x ˉ ) 2 (population) or divide by N − 1 N-1 N − 1 (unbiased). Use population when your data is the whole set (batch norm, standardize); N − 1 N-1 N − 1 when estimating from a sample. # Z-score standardization (per feature/column) x std = x − μ σ 2 + ϵ x_{\text{std}} = \frac{x - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}} x std ​ = σ 2 + ϵ ​ x − μ ​ mean = x.mean(dim= 0 , keepdim= True ) var = x.var(dim= 0 , unbiased= False , keepdim= True ) x_std = (x - mean) / torch.sqrt(var + 1e-8 ) # 1e-8 for numerical safety # Softmax (turns logits into a probability distribution) A logit = raw, unbounded model score before normalization. On paper, softmax ( x ) i = e x i ∑ j e x j \text{softmax}(x)_i = \dfrac{e^{x_i}}{\sum_j e^{x_j}} softmax ( x ) i ​ = ∑ j ​ e x j ​ e x i ​ ​ . m = logits. max (dim= 1 , keepdim= True ).values # subtract max for numerical stability e = torch.exp(logits - m) probs = e / e. sum (dim= 1 , keepdim= True ) # each row sums to 1 The max-subtraction does not change the result (softmax is shift-invariant) — it just prevents exp overflow. # Sigmoid logistic regression σ ( z ) = 1 1 + e − z \sigma(z) = \dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} σ ( z ) = 1 + e − z 1 ​ squashes any real z z z to ( 0 , 1 ) (0, 1) ( 0 , 1 ) ; a logit of 0 → probability 0.5. logits = X @ w + b probs = torch.sigmoid(logits) # 1 / (1 + e^-z) preds = (probs = 0.5 ). float () # threshold for class labels # Normalization layers (normalize activations, not weights) All re-center/re-scale the values flowing between layers; they differ in what they average over: Method Averages over Batch-size dependent? Batch norm the batch, per feature ( dim=0 ) Yes — noisy for tiny batches Layer norm all features of one example No — used in transformers Group norm feature groups, per example No Batch norm (across the batch / rows): mean = data.mean(dim= 0 ) var = data.var(dim= 0 , unbiased= False ) # BN uses the biased (N) variance out = (data - mean) / torch.sqrt(var + epsilon) The mean/var are statistics computed from data each pass — not learned. Only the weights and the norm s learnable γ \gamma γ (scale) / β \beta β (shift) are updated by gradient descent. Placement is usually: linear → norm → activation (ReLU). # Scaled dot-product attention Attention ( Q , K , V ) = softmax ⁣ ( Q K ⊤ d k ) V \text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V Attention ( Q , K , V ) = softmax ( d k ​ ​ Q K ⊤ ​ ) V scores = (query @ key.T) / math.sqrt(query.size(- 1 )) # size(-1) = d_k, the last dim weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=- 1 ) # each query s weights sum to 1 output = weights @ value # weighted blend of value rows Weight the values = weighted average of the value vectors using the softmax weights. Masked version: set blocked positions to a large negative before softmax so they get ~0 weight: scores = scores.masked_fill(mask == 0 , - 1e9 ) # LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) Freeze the big base weight; learn only a narrow rank- r r r bottleneck B A BA B A . Order matters (matrices aren t square): A A A projects down (in → r r r ), B B B projects up ( r r r → out). title: Training Deep Networks
heads: The Training Loop in One Picture
LayerNorm and why transformers use it
text:
Deep Learning: how a network actually gets trained, and how to tell when it is not. Gradient Descent gives the basic loop: compute a gradient, step against it. This chapter is what sits on top of that loop in practice: which optimizer, how the learning rate changes over time, how weights are initialized, what normalization layers do, how to keep gradients numerically healthy, how to scale training across devices, and how to debug a run that is not learning. Most why is my training broken questions reduce to a short list of causes covered here. What you ll be able to say after this chapter Write the update rules for SGD with momentum, RMSProp, Adam and AdamW, and say what each term fixes. Explain why weight decay and L2 regularization are the same thing in SGD but different in Adam. Justify warmup and cosine decay, and say how the learning rate should change with batch size (under stated assumptions). Derive the Xavier and He variance rules from a one-layer argument. State BatchNorm s train/eval difference, and why transformers use LayerNorm. Give a debugging order: overfit a tiny batch, then read the loss curves. # The Training Loop in One Picture Every run repeats the same cycle: forward pass, loss, backward pass, optimizer step. All the topics below act on one of those stages. A solid answer: Adam adapts a per-parameter step and usually converges faster with less tuning, especially for transformers and sparse gradients; SGD with momentum has half the optimizer memory and, with a well-tuned schedule, is often competitive or better on generalization for convolutional vision models. State the condition ( often , with tuning ) rather than a blanket winner. Then volunteer the AdamW point: decoupled decay matters because L2 in Adam is rescaled by the adaptive denominator. Go deeper Adam s memory is 2 × 2	imes 2 × the parameters on top of weights and gradients; in mixed-precision training the optimizer states plus an fp32 master copy of the weights dominate memory (see the distributed section). Variants such as Adafactor reduce second-moment memory by factorizing the matrix v v v . # Learning-Rate Schedules and Warmup A constant learning rate is rarely optimal. Early on, large steps make fast progress; later, the noise in mini-batch gradients keeps the iterate bouncing around the minimum unless the step shrinks. A large learning rate at step 0 can push a transformer into a bad region from which it recovers slowly or not at all. Warmup ramps the learning rate linearly from near zero over the first several hundred to several thousand steps, which gives v ^ \hat v v ^ time to stabilize and lets activations settle. Warmup is more important for Adam-style optimizers, deep post-LN transformers and large batch sizes than for small shallow nets with SGD. Pre-LN placement (below) reduces, but does not always remove, the need for it. # Finding a learning rate A learning-rate range test (increase η \eta η exponentially over a short run and plot loss against η \eta η ) shows a region where loss falls fastest; a value somewhat below where loss begins to rise is a reasonable starting point. This is a heuristic: the best peak value for a full schedule can differ from what the short test suggests. Common mistakes Setting the decay horizon T T T shorter than the actual run (so the rate hits the floor early and the run stalls), restarting from a checkpoint without restoring scheduler and optimizer state (the schedule or Adam moments silently reset), and tuning η \eta η on a schedule different from the one used in the final run. # Batch Size Effects Batch size B B B trades gradient noise against hardware efficiency. Gradient noise. The variance of the mini-batch gradient decreases roughly as 1 / B 1/B 1/ B . Small batches give noisy steps that can act as implicit regularization; large batches give accurate steps but do less learning per example once the batch exceeds the critical batch size beyond which more parallelism stops reducing the number of steps proportionally. Throughput. Larger batches use accelerators more efficiently up to a memory or compute limit. Learning-rate scaling. For SGD, a common heuristic is the linear scaling rule : multiply η \eta η by k k k when multiplying B B B by k k k , combined with warmup. The reasoning: k k k small steps of size η \eta η with independent noisy gradients are approximately one step of size k η k\eta k η on the averaged gradient, as long as the loss does not change much within those k k k steps. This holds approximately for moderate k k k and breaks at large batch. For Adam, a square-root scaling ( η ∝ B \eta \propto \sqrt{B} η ∝ B ​ ) is often suggested instead; both are rules of thumb to be validated. Generalization gap. Very large batches without adjusting the learning rate or schedule have been observed to generalize worse; much of the gap can be closed by retuning, so it is not a fixed law. Gradient accumulation simulates a large batch on limited memory: run k k k micro-batches, sum their gradients (scaling the loss by 1 / k 1/k 1/ k ), then step once. This matches a batch of k B kB k B for the gradient, but not for layers whose statistics depend on the batch, such as BatchNorm, which still sees only the micro-batch. Interview angle If asked you doubled the batch size, what else changes? mention the learning rate (scale, with warmup, as a starting point), the number of steps per epoch (so schedule lengths expressed in steps need updating), and BatchNorm statistics if per-device batch changes. # Weight Initialization The goal is to keep the scale of activations (forward) and gradients (backward) roughly constant across depth at the start of training. Otherwise signals decay to zero or explode exponentially in the number of layers. # Derivation intuition Consider one linear unit y = ∑ i = 1 n i n w i x i y = \sum_{i=1}^{n_{in}} w_i x_i y = ∑ i = 1 n in ​ ​ w i ​ x i ​ , with weights i.i.d., zero mean, variance V a r ( w ) \mathrm{Var}(w) Var ( w ) , inputs i.i.d. with zero mean and variance V a r ( x ) \mathrm{Var}(x) Var ( x ) , and weights independent of inputs. Then V a r ( y ) = n i n V a r ( w ) V a r ( x ) . \mathrm{Var}(y) = n_{in}\,\mathrm{Var}(w)\,\mathrm{Var}(x). Var ( y ) = n in ​ Var ( w ) Var ( x ) . To keep V a r ( y ) = V a r ( x ) \mathrm{Var}(y) = \mathrm{Var}(x) Var ( y ) = Var ( x ) we need V a r ( w ) = 1 / n i n \mathrm{Var}(w) = 1/n_{in} Var ( w ) = 1/ n in ​ .
