Every unit in a layer would receive identical gradients and remain identical forever (the symmetry is never broken). Random init breaks it. Residual networks often zero-initialize (or scale down) the final layer of each residual branch so every block starts as the identity, which keeps early training stable at great depth. Transformers commonly scale output projections by something like 1 / 2 L 1/\sqrt{2L} 1/ 2 L ​ for a similar reason. Go deeper The derivation assumes independence and zero-mean inputs; it describes the variance at initialization only. It does not guarantee anything once training moves the weights, which is part of why normalization layers are used in addition to careful init. # BatchNorm For a feature, BatchNorm normalizes over the mini-batch (and spatial positions for convolutions): x ^ = x − μ B σ B 2 + ϵ , y = γ x ^ + β \hat x =  rac{x-\mu_B}{\sqrt{\sigma_B^2+\epsilon}}, \qquad y = \gamma\,\hat x +  eta x ^ = σ B 2 ​ + ϵ ​ x − μ B ​ ​ , y = γ x ^ + β with learned scale γ \gamma γ and shift β  eta β so the layer can recover the identity if useful. Train vs eval is the classic trap. Training Evaluation / inference Statistics used Mean and variance of the current mini-batch Running averages accumulated during training Depends on other examples in the batch Yes No Running stats updated Yes: μ r u n ← ( 1 − m ) μ r u n + m μ B \mu_{run} \leftarrow (1-m)\mu_{run} + m\mu_B μ r u n ​ ← ( 1 − m ) μ r u n ​ + m μ B ​ No Consequences: Forgetting model.eval() makes predictions depend on whatever else is in the batch, and with batch size 1 the batch variance is degenerate. Very small batches give noisy statistics and a train/inference mismatch; alternatives are GroupNorm or synchronized BatchNorm across devices. Fine-tuning with a tiny batch is a common situation to freeze BatchNorm statistics. Distribution shift between train and serving data shows up as stale running statistics. Why it helps is still discussed. The original explanation was reduced internal covariate shift ; later empirical work argues the main effect is a smoother loss landscape, which allows larger learning rates. State it as makes optimization better conditioned and permits higher learning rates and leave the mechanism as debated. # LayerNorm and why transformers use it LayerNorm normalizes across the feature dimension of each token independently: x ^ = x − μ σ 2 + ϵ , μ , σ 2 computed over the d features of one example/token \hat x =  rac{x-\mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2+\epsilon}},\quad \mu,\sigma^2 	ext{ computed over the } d 	ext{ features of one example/token} x ^ = σ 2 + ϵ ​ x − μ ​ , μ , σ 2 computed over the d features of one example/token BatchNorm LayerNorm Normalizes over Batch (and space), per feature Features, per example/token Train/eval difference Yes (running stats) None Batch-size sensitivity High for small batches None Works with variable-length sequences Awkward: padding and length distort statistics Yes: each token is handled alone Typical home CNNs Transformers, RNN-style models Transformers use LayerNorm because sequence lengths vary, batches can be small relative to the model, per-token statistics avoid mixing padded positions and other examples, and inference (often batch size 1, autoregressive) must behave identically to training. RMSNorm, which drops mean-centering and rescales by the root mean square only, is a cheaper variant used in many recent large language models. Pre-LN vs post-LN. Post-LN places the norm after the residual addition (original transformer); Pre-LN places it inside the branch before the sublayer, leaving the residual path as an unnormalized identity. Pre-LN gradients are often better behaved at depth and training is typically less dependent on warmup, with slightly lower final quality reported in some settings. Interview angle A crisp one-liner: BatchNorm normalizes across examples, so it couples the batch and needs running stats at inference. LayerNorm normalizes across features within each example, so it behaves identically in train and eval, which suits variable-length sequences and small or size-1 batches. # Dropout During training, each activation is zeroed independently with probability p p p . This discourages co-adaptation of units and can be viewed as training an ensemble of thinned subnetworks. Inverted dropout scales the surviving activations by 1 / ( 1 − p ) 1/(1-p) 1/ ( 1 − p ) at training time: h ~ = m ⊙ h 1 − p , m i ∼ Bernoulli ( 1 − p ) 	ilde h =  rac{m \odot h}{1-p},\qquad m_i\sim	ext{Bernoulli}(1-p) h ~ = 1 − p m ⊙ h ​ , m i ​ ∼ Bernoulli ( 1 − p ) so E [ h ~ ] = h \mathbb{E}[	ilde h] = h E [ h ~ ] = h . At inference nothing changes: dropout is switched off and no rescaling is needed. (The original formulation instead left training alone and multiplied weights by 1 − p 1-p 1 − p at test time; the two are equivalent in expectation.) Practical notes: Dropout is a regularizer, so it helps mainly when the model overfits; with abundant data and short training (many large language model pretraining runs), it is often set to zero. Using dropout and BatchNorm together can interact poorly because dropout changes activation variance between train and eval ( variance shift ); common practice is to place dropout after the normalization, or to prefer one. Forgetting model.eval() leaves dropout active at inference and produces noisy predictions. Monte Carlo dropout leaves it on intentionally to sample an approximate predictive distribution. # Vanishing and Exploding Gradients Backpropagation multiplies Jacobians layer by layer. For depth L L L , ∂ L ∂ h 0 = ∂ L ∂ h L ∏ l = 1 L ∂ h l ∂ h l − 1 .  rac{\partial L}{\partial h_0} =  rac{\partial L}{\partial h_L}\prod_{l=1}^{L} rac{\partial h_l}{\partial h_{l-1}}. ∂ h 0 ​ ∂ L ​ = ∂ h L ​ ∂ L ​ l = 1 ∏ L ​ ∂ h l − 1 ​ ∂ h l ​ ​ . If the typical singular values of the Jacobians are below 1, the product shrinks exponentially (vanishing); if above 1, it grows exponentially (exploding). Recurrent networks are the extreme case because the same matrix is multiplied once per time step. Cause Mechanism Mitigation Saturating activations (sigmoid, tanh) Derivative ≤ 0.25 \le 0.25 ≤ 0.25 for sigmoid, near 0 in the tails ReLU-family or GELU; sensible init Poor init Jacobian scale ≠ 1 
e 1  = 1 Xavier / He Depth without shortcuts Product of many Jacobians Residual connections Recurrence Same weight matrix repeated Gated cells (LSTM/GRU), gradient clipping Dying ReLU Unit stuck at negative pre-activation, gradient zero Lower learning rate, Leaky ReLU, better init # Residual connections A residual block computes h l = h l − 1 + F ( h l − 1 ) h_{l} = h_{l-1} + F(h_{l-1}) h l ​ = h l − 1 ​ + F ( h l − 1 ​ ) . Its Jacobian is I + ∂ F / ∂ h I + \partial F/\partial h I + ∂ F / ∂ h , so the identity term provides a gradient path that does not shrink with depth; the gradient from the top reaches early layers through the sum of many paths of different lengths. Blocks also only need to learn a correction to the identity, and zero-initializing the branch output starts the network as an identity map. # Gradient clipping Clipping bounds the update when a rare batch produces a huge gradient. Clip by global norm: if ∥ g ∥ 2 c \|g\|_2 c ∥ g ∥ 2 ​ c , replace g ← g ⋅ c / ∥ g ∥ 2 g \leftarrow g\cdot c/\|g\|_2 g ← g ⋅ c /∥ g ∥ 2 ​ . This keeps the direction and caps the magnitude; it is the usual choice, with c c c around 1 for many transformer recipes (tune per model). Clip by value: clamp each element into [ − c , c ] [-c, c] [ − c , c ] , which changes the direction. Clipping treats the symptom (spiky gradients) and is cheap insurance for RNNs and large-model training. If clipping activates on most steps, the learning rate or init is likely too aggressive. With mixed precision and loss scaling, unscale gradients before computing the norm. # Mixed Precision Training in 16-bit formats cuts memory and increases throughput on supporting hardware. Format Bits (sign/exp/mantissa) Range Precision Notes fp32 1/8/23 Wide High Baseline fp16 1/5/10 Narrow (max about 65,504) Moderate Underflow of small gradients; needs loss scaling bf16 1/8/7 Same as fp32 Lower Rarely needs loss scaling; less mantissa precision The standard recipe keeps an fp32 master copy of the weights and optimizer states, runs forward/backward in 16-bit, and applies updates in fp32. Small updates ( η g \eta g η g much smaller than the weight) would be rounded away in 16-bit weights, which is why the master copy matters. Loss scaling (fp16) multiplies the loss by a large factor S S S before backward so small gradients remain representable, then divides gradients by S S S before the step; dynamic scaling reduces S S S when infs/NaNs appear and skips that step. Operations sensitive to range or accumulation (softmax, layer norm statistics, large reductions, the loss) are usually kept in fp32. Symptoms A loss that suddenly becomes NaN in fp16 often means overflow (loss scale too high, or an unnormalized activation). Repeated skipped steps with a collapsing loss scale point to a genuinely unstable run, not a scaling bug. # Distributed Training at a Glance Strategy What is split Communication Use when Data parallel The batch; each device holds a full model replica All-reduce of gradients each step The model fits on one device; goal is throughput Sharded data parallel (ZeRO / FSDP-style) Optimizer states, then gradients, then parameters across data-parallel ranks All-gather of parameters, reduce-scatter of gradients Replicas do not fit; memory is the limit Tensor (model) parallel Individual layers matrices across devices Frequent, per-layer collectives; needs fast interconnect A single layer is too large; usually within a node Pipeline parallel Consecutive layers into stages on different devices Activations between stages; micro-batching to fill the pipeline Model too deep for one device; across nodes Key ideas: Synchronous data parallel with N N N devices and per-device batch B B B behaves like single-device training with batch N B NB N B , so the batch-size and learning-rate considerations above apply. Pipeline parallelism has bubbles where stages idle; splitting the batch into micro-batches reduces the idle fraction. Memory per parameter in mixed-precision Adam is roughly 16 bytes ( 2 2 2 weights + 2 2 2 gradients + 4 4 4 master weights + 4 + 4 4+4 4 + 4 moments); activations come on top and can be traded for compute via activation checkpointing (recompute instead of store). Large runs usually combine several of these (data x tensor x pipeline). Interview angle Pick the strategy from the bottleneck: fits in memory then data parallel; does not fit then shard states (FSDP/ZeRO) before reaching for tensor/pipeline; very large layers or models then add tensor and pipeline parallelism, keeping tensor parallel inside the fast interconnect domain. # Debugging Checklist Debug in this order. Each step isolates a different failure class. Check the data and labels. Visualize a few samples with their labels after all preprocessing. Verify the train/validation split has no leakage, label shapes and dtypes are right, and normalization statistics come from the training set. Check the initial loss. For K K K -class classification with a sensible init, the starting cross-entropy should be close to ln ⁡ K \ln K ln K (for example about 2.30 2.30 2.30 for 10 classes). A very different value suggests a bug in the loss, label encoding, or output scale. Overfit a tiny batch. Train on 8 to 32 examples with regularization off and no augmentation. The loss should go to near zero. If it does not, the problem is a bug (wrong loss/labels, frozen parameters, missing zero_grad , learning rate far off, detached graph), not a lack of data or capacity. Confirm the model is in the right mode. model.train() for training and model.eval() for evaluation, which affects dropout and BatchNorm. Scale up one change at a time. Full data, then regularization, then augmentation, then schedule. Adding several changes at once hides the cause of a regression. Monitor diagnostics. Per-layer gradient norms and update-to-weight ratios (often around 10 − 3 10^{-3} 1 0 − 3 is cited as a rough healthy order of magnitude), activation statistics, fraction of dead ReLUs, and the learning rate actually applied. Compare against a baseline. A simple model (linear, small MLP) establishes the achievable score and detects pipeline bugs that a complex model would mask. # Reading loss curves Observation Likely cause Check or fix Train loss flat from step 0 Learning rate far too low, frozen params, dead activations, labels uninformative Overfit a tiny batch; check gradients are non-zero Loss decreases then diverges or NaN Learning rate too high, no warmup, overflow, bad data point Lower η \eta η , add warmup and clipping, check for NaN inputs Train loss falls, validation loss rises Overfitting More data/augmentation, regularization, early stopping, smaller model Both train and validation high, plateau Underfitting or optimization problem Larger model, longer training, higher learning rate, better features Train much better than validation immediately Leakage differences or distribution mismatch between splits; or eval-mode difference Audit the split; check eval() behavior Validation better than train Dropout/augmentation active only during training; train loss averaged over the epoch while validation measured at the end Compare under identical conditions Noisy, jagged loss Small batch or high learning rate Smooth the plot, increase batch or lower η \eta η Sudden spikes mid-training Rare bad batches, Adam second-moment instability at high η \eta η Clipping, lower peak η \eta η , raise ϵ \epsilon ϵ or lower β 2  eta_2 β 2 ​ (e.g. 0.95, used in some large-model recipes), skip the batch, inspect data Loss plateaus then drops later Normal for some tasks (grokking-like phases, learning-rate drops) Do not stop early without checking the schedule Go deeper Silent bugs are more common than exotic ones: shuffling inputs and labels separately, applying augmentation to validation data, computing the loss on padded positions, a softmax applied twice (logits passed to a loss that already applies it), and the last-batch size mismatch. These all produce curves that look almost plausible. # One-Page Summary Topic Key facts SGD / momentum Momentum averages gradients and damps oscillation in steep directions; check the ( 1 − β ) (1- eta) ( 1 − β ) convention across libraries Adam First moment + second moment with bias correction; per-parameter normalized step; ϵ \epsilon ϵ matters in low precision AdamW Weight decay applied directly to weights, not through the adaptive denominator; L2 in Adam under-regularizes high-gradient weights Schedules Warmup (stabilizes v ^ \hat v v ^ and early activations) then cosine or linear decay; keep scheduler state in checkpoints Batch size Noise ∝ 1 / B \propto 1/B ∝ 1/ B ; scale η \eta η (linear for SGD, often sqrt for Adam) as a starting heuristic, with warmup Init V a r ( w ) = 1 / n i n \mathrm{Var}(w)=1/n_{in} Var ( w ) = 1/ n in ​ keeps forward variance; He = 2 / n i n =2/n_{in} = 2/ n in ​ for ReLU; Xavier = 2 / ( n i n + n o u t ) =2/(n_{in}+n_{out}) = 2/ ( n in ​ + n o u t ​ ) BatchNorm Batch stats in training, running stats in eval; sensitive to small batches LayerNorm Per-token feature normalization; no train/eval gap; suits transformers and variable lengths Dropout Inverted scaling 1 / ( 1 − p ) 1/(1-p) 1/ ( 1 − p ) in training; off at inference Gradients Vanishing/exploding from Jacobian products; residuals, init, normalization, gated cells; clip by global norm Mixed precision 16-bit compute, fp32 master weights; loss scaling for fp16; bf16 has fp32 range Distributed DP (replicas), sharded DP (memory), tensor (layer split), pipeline (stage split) Debugging Initial loss ≈ ln ⁡ K \approx \ln K ≈ ln K ; overfit a tiny batch first; change one thing at a time # Related Gradient Descent PyTorch Cross-Entropy Loss Regularization Overfitting Underfitting Recurrent Neural Networks Long Short-Term Memory Convolutional Neural Networks MOC - Deep Learning

title: Cross-Validation
text: Say it in 30s: A way to estimate generalization without wasting data on a fixed validation set. k-fold CV splits the data into k parts, trains on k−1 and validates on the held-out fold, rotates k times, and averages. You get a more stable performance estimate and a sense of its variance. Variants k-fold (k=5 or 10 typical): the default. Stratified k-fold : preserve class ratios per fold — use for imbalanced classification. Leave-one-out : k = n, low bias, high variance, expensive. Group k-fold : keep correlated rows (same user/patient) together to avoid leakage. Time-series split : train on past, validate on future — never shuffle time. Random k-fold leaks the future. Traps Do all preprocessing (scaling, feature selection) inside the fold, or you leak. CV tunes hyperparameters; still keep a final untouched test set. See depth: Model Evaluation Validation (§8), Time Series Stationarity (§9). Related: Generalization , Bias-Variance Tradeoff , Overfitting Underfitting .

title: Evaluation
text: The metrics round. Pick the right metric for the problem and defend it. # Chapters Model Evaluation Validation # Concept cards (owned here) Precision Recall ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC Cross-Validation # See also (from other areas) Bias-Variance Tradeoff — what validation curves diagnose (Foundations) Logistic Regression — usually well-calibrated probabilities (Models) # If asked what metric Tie the metric to the cost of errors: imbalanced → PR-AUC and recall/precision, ranking → NDCG/MAP/MRR, probabilities matter → calibration. Separate the offline ML metric from the online business metric.

title: Model Evaluation & Validation
heads: Ranking Metrics: NDCG vs MAP vs MRR
text: The Machine Learning Interview Bible Chapter 5 — Model Evaluation Validation Building a model is half the job; knowing whether it’s any good is the other half, and it’s where most candidates are thinnest. This chapter is about measuring honestly. We start from the confusion matrix that every classification metric is built on, untangle precision from recall and the threshold that trades them, separate ROC-AUC from PR-AUC, cover calibration and ranking metrics, then turn to regression metrics and — crucially — how to split data so your estimate isn’t a lie. The recurring theme: the metric is a modeling decision , and choosing the wrong one is how good models get shipped to do the wrong thing. What you’ll be able to say after this chapter Read a confusion matrix and derive precision, recall, and F1 from it cold. Explain the precision–recall tradeoff and how the threshold moves it. Say exactly when PR-AUC beats ROC-AUC (hint: heavy imbalance). Define calibration and why a well-ranked model can still be dishonest. Choose a cross-validation scheme that respects time and groups — no leakage. # The Confusion Matrix Every classification metric is an arithmetic combination of four counts, so the confusion matrix is the foundation you build everything else on. For a binary problem it cross-tabulates what actually happened against what the model predicted. Four cells, and every classification metric is just a ratio of them. Predicted Positive Predicted Negative Actually Positive True Positive (TP) False Negative (FN) — a miss Actually Negative False Positive (FP) — a false alarm True Negative (TN) The two error types are not interchangeable, and naming them correctly matters. A False Positive (Type I error) is a false alarm — you flagged something that was fine. A False Negative (Type II error) is a miss — you let something real slip through. Which one hurts more is entirely domain-dependent, and that asymmetry is what drives every metric choice in this chapter. Memory hook False Positive = “crying wolf” (Type I). False Negative = “missing the wolf” (Type II). Spam filter: a False Positive eats your real email; a False Negative just lets spam through — so you tune toward avoiding False Positives. Cancer screen: a False Negative is deadly — so you tune toward avoiding those. The cost asymmetry picks the metric. Interview angle Always ask, or state, which error is worse here . Candidates who optimize a model without distinguishing the cost of a miss from the cost of a false alarm signal they’ve never shipped anything. Tie it to the business: “in fraud, a missed fraud costs us the transaction; a false alarm costs a customer’s goodwill — those aren’t equal.” # Classification Metrics From those four cells come the metrics you’ll quote constantly. The danger metric is accuracy — (TP+TN)/total — because it collapses under imbalance: on a dataset that’s 99% negative, “always predict negative” scores 99% and is worthless. Precision and recall are the honest pair. Metric Formula Reads as Use when Accuracy T P + T N all \frac{TP+TN}{\text{all}} all T P + T N ​ Overall correctness Classes are balanced Precision T P T P + F P \frac{TP}{TP+FP} T P + F P T P ​ Of those I flagged, how many were right? False alarms are costly Recall (TPR) T P T P + F N \frac{TP}{TP+FN} T P + F N T P ​ Of the real positives, how many did I catch? Misses are costly F1 2 P R P + R \frac{2PR}{P+R} P + R 2 P R ​ Harmonic mean of P and R Imbalance, want one number Specificity (TNR) T N T N + F P \frac{TN}{TN+FP} T N + F P T N ​ Of the real negatives, how many did I clear? Care about the negative class Precision answers “when I say positive, am I right?” — it’s hurt by false alarms. Recall answers “did I find all the positives?” — it’s hurt by misses. F1 is their harmonic mean, not the arithmetic mean, deliberately: the harmonic mean stays low unless both are high, so a model can’t game F1 by maxing one and tanking the other. Memory hook Precision = “of my alarms, how many were real?” Recall = “of the real ones, how many did I sound an alarm for?” Precision polices false alarms; recall polices misses. F1 is the harmonic mean — it refuses to be fooled by one good number. Interview angle Expect “precision or recall for X?” Cancer screening → recall (never miss a case; false alarms get a follow-up test). Spam → precision (never trash a real email). Search results → precision (the top results must be relevant). Say the cost of each error type out loud and the answer falls out. # Threshold: Precision vs Recall Here’s the idea that ties the last section together: most classifiers output a probability , and you turn it into a label by picking a threshold (default 0.5, but that’s just a default). Precision and recall are not fixed properties of the model — they move as you slide the threshold , and they move in opposite directions. Slide the threshold high for precision, low for recall — you can’t max both at once. Raise the threshold and you only flag the cases you’re most sure about: precision climbs, recall falls (you miss the borderline positives). Lower it and you flag aggressively: recall climbs, precision falls (more false alarms). This is the precision–recall tradeoff , and the right threshold is a business decision , not a default — set it by the relative cost of a miss versus a false alarm. Memory hook The threshold is a dial, not a constant. Crank it up → cautious → high precision, low recall. Crank it down → trigger-happy → high recall, low precision. 0.5 is a default, not a law — set it by what an error costs. Interview angle “Your model’s recall is too low — what do you do?” First, cheap: lower the threshold (no retraining needed) and accept the precision hit. Then: resample/reweight for imbalance, add features, or change the model. Reaching for “lower the threshold” first shows you understand that precision and recall are threshold-dependent, not intrinsic. # ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC To judge a model across all thresholds at once, you use an area-under-curve summary. There are two, and knowing when each one lies is a classic senior question. The ROC curve plots True Positive Rate (recall) against False Positive Rate as the threshold sweeps. ROC-AUC is the area under it, interpretable as the probability the model ranks a random positive above a random negative. 0.5 is random, 1.0 is perfect. The PR curve plots Precision against Recall over the same sweep, and PR-AUC is its area. ROC can look great on imbalanced data; PR tells the truth because precision feels the flood of negatives. ROC-AUC PR-AUC Axes TPR vs FPR Precision vs Recall Baseline (random) 0.5 always The positive class prevalence Sensitive to imbalance? No — can look misleadingly good Yes — reflects rare-class difficulty Use when Classes roughly balanced; care about both classes Positive class is rare and is what you care about The key insight: FPR has the huge negative count in its denominator , so on imbalanced data a flood of false positives barely moves it — ROC-AUC stays optimistically high. Precision has the false positives in its denominator without the true negatives , so it feels every false alarm. When positives are rare and they’re what you care about (fraud, disease, click prediction), PR-AUC is the honest summary . Memory hook On a needle-in-a-haystack problem, ROC-AUC flatters and PR-AUC tells the truth. ROC dilutes false positives in a sea of true negatives; precision doesn’t get to hide them. Rare positive class → trust PR-AUC. Interview angle “You have 1% fraud and ROC-AUC is 0.95 — are you happy?” The trap is yes. Strong answer: ROC-AUC is inflated by the 99% negatives; check PR-AUC and the precision/recall at your operating threshold before celebrating. This single distinction is one of the most reliable senior-vs-junior separators in evaluation. # Calibration Ranking well and being honest about probabilities are different things, and the gap is calibration. A model is calibrated if, among all the times it says “0.7,” the event really happens about 70% of the time. AUC only cares about order ; calibration cares about whether the number means what it says . A calibrated model’s confidence matches reality; the diagonal is perfect. This matters whenever you act on the probability itself — expected-value decisions, pricing, risk thresholds, or feeding the score into downstream math. A model can have great AUC and terrible calibration: it ranks cases correctly but is systematically over- or under-confident. You diagnose it with a reliability diagram (predicted probability vs observed frequency) and fix it on held-out data with Platt scaling (fit a sigmoid) or isotonic regression (a flexible monotonic fit). Model Calibration out of the box Note Logistic regression Usually good Trained on log-loss; can drift if heavily regularized, reweighted or misspecified Naive Bayes Poor Independence assumption pushes probs to 0/1 SVM Uncalibrated scores (no probabilities) Needs Platt scaling Deep nets / boosted trees Deep nets: often overconfident; boosted trees/RF: often distorted (sigmoid-shaped, underconfident) Check a reliability diagram; calibrate if you act on the number Memory hook Calibration is honesty, not accuracy. “When I say 70%, does it happen 70% of the time?” AUC grades the ranking ; calibration grades the number . A model can ace one and flunk the other. Go deeper (optional) Don’t conflate calibration with discrimination (AUC). You can have perfect ranking and awful calibration (just squash all scores toward 0.5) or perfect calibration and poor ranking. If you only need to threshold or rank , calibration may not matter; if you multiply the probability into a decision , it’s essential. # Ranking Metrics: NDCG vs MAP vs MRR When the output is an ordered list — search, recommendations, retrieval — accuracy and AUC miss the point: what matters is whether the good items are near the top . Three metrics dominate, differing in what they reward. Metric Rewards Use when MRR (Mean Reciprocal Rank) The rank of the first relevant item One right answer (Q A, “I’m feeling lucky”) MAP (Mean Average Precision) Precision across all relevant items, binary relevance Multiple relevant items, relevant-or-not NDCG (Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain) Graded relevance, discounted by position Items have degrees of relevance (star ratings) All three share the position-discount instinct: a relevant result at rank 1 is worth more than the same result at rank 10. NDCG is the most general because it handles graded relevance (a 5-star match beats a 3-star match) and normalizes against the ideal ordering, so scores are comparable across queries. MRR is the simplest — just 1/(rank of the first hit) — and fits “single correct answer” tasks. Memory hook MRR cares only about the first good hit. MAP cares about all the good hits, present-or-absent. NDCG cares about all of them and how good each is , discounted by position. Increasing sophistication: first → all → all-and-graded. Interview angle “How would you evaluate a recommender?” Don’t say accuracy. Say a ranking metric and justify it: NDCG if you have graded feedback (ratings, watch time), MAP for binary relevance with several right answers, MRR if there’s essentially one. Then mention that offline ranking metrics are a proxy — the real test is an online A/B on engagement (Chapter 14). # Regression Metrics For continuous targets the question shifts to how far off, on average , and the choice among metrics is mostly about how you want to treat large errors and whether you want a unit-free score. Metric Behavior Use when MAE Mean absolute error; robust to outliers Outliers shouldn’t dominate; want error in original units MSE Mean squared error; punishes large errors hard Big misses are especially bad RMSE √MSE; same units as the target, still outlier-sensitive Want MSE’s penalty but readable units R² Fraction of variance explained (1 = perfect, 0 = mean-baseline) Want a unit-free “how much better than guessing the mean” The core tradeoff is MAE vs MSE/RMSE : squaring makes MSE punish big errors disproportionately, so it’s the right choice when a single large miss is unacceptable — but that same squaring makes it sensitive to outliers , which MAE shrugs off. R² rescales error against a “predict the mean” baseline, giving a unit-free score, but it can be misleadingly high on a strong trend and even go negative when the model is worse than the mean. (Adjusted R², which penalizes adding useless features, is covered in Chapter 3.) Memory hook MAE treats all errors fairly (robust). MSE/RMSE square the error, so it obsesses over the big misses (outlier-sensitive). R² answers “how much better than just guessing the average?” — unit-free, but can flatter you. Interview angle “MAE or RMSE?” Answer with the outlier story: RMSE if large errors are disproportionately costly and the data is clean; MAE if outliers exist and you don’t want a few of them to dictate the model. If asked why a model has R² of 0.0 — it’s no better than predicting the mean; negative R² means worse than the mean. # Cross-Validation: How to Split Data A single train/test split gives a noisy estimate — you got lucky or unlucky with which points landed in test. Cross-validation averages over several splits for a stabler estimate, but the way you split must respect the structure of your data, or you leak the future into the past and your metric becomes a fantasy. k-fold rotates the test fold; but time and groups demand special splits. Scheme How it works Use when k-fold Split into k folds; each takes a turn as test Standard i.i.d. tabular data Stratified k-fold k-fold preserving class proportions in each fold Classification, especially imbalanced Leave-One-Out k = n; each point is its own test fold Tiny datasets (expensive) Time-series split Always train on past, test on future Temporal data — never shuffle Group k-fold Keep each entity entirely in one fold Repeated users/patients/docs The two splits that prevent leakage are the ones interviewers probe. Time-series CV never shuffles — you train on the past and test on the future, because random shuffling would let the model “see tomorrow” to predict today. Group CV keeps all rows of one entity (a patient, a user) together, so the model can’t memorize an individual in training and get credit for “predicting” them in test. And the golden rule from Chapter 0 still binds: fit every preprocessing step (scaling, imputation) inside the training fold only , then apply it to the validation fold. Memory hook k-fold for ordinary data. Stratify when classes are imbalanced. Split by time for time series (never peek at the future). Split by group when the same entity repeats (never let it sit on both sides). The wrong split = silent leakage = a beautiful, lying score. Interview angle “How would you cross-validate a model that predicts next month’s sales?” The trap is plain k-fold. Right answer: a time-based split — train on earlier periods, validate on later ones, never shuffle — because shuffling leaks future information and inflates the score. Mention that preprocessing stats must be fit on the training fold only. Rapid Fire — Evaluation Validation Confusion matrix: TP/FP/FN/TN. False Positive = Type I (false alarm); False Negative = Type II (miss). Cost asymmetry picks the metric. - Accuracy lies under imbalance. Precision = of my alarms how many were real; Recall = of the real ones how many I caught; F1 = harmonic mean. - Threshold slides precision vs recall in opposite directions; 0.5 is a default, set it by error costs. - ROC-AUC flatters on imbalanced data (FPR hides false positives in true negatives); PR-AUC is honest when positives are rare. - Calibration = “when I say 70% it happens 70%.” AUC grades ranking, calibration grades the number; fix with Platt/isotonic. - Ranking: MRR (first hit) → MAP (all hits, binary) → NDCG (graded + position-discounted). - Regression: MAE robust; MSE/RMSE punish big errors and feel outliers; R² = variance explained vs the mean. - Cross-validation: stratify for imbalance, split by time for temporal data, split by group for repeated entities; fit preprocessing on the train fold only. # Which Metric When The chapter in one table — match the metric to the problem, because the metric is the objective you’re really optimizing. Problem Metric Balanced classification Accuracy (or AUC) Imbalanced classification PR-AUC, F1, precision/recall at threshold Cost of a miss ≫ false alarm Optimize recall Cost of a false alarm ≫ miss Optimize precision Acting on the probability value Calibration (reliability diagram + Platt/isotonic) Ranking / search / recommendation NDCG, MAP, or MRR Regression, clean data, punish big errors RMSE Regression with outliers MAE “How much better than the mean?” R² The closing principle ties the chapter to Chapter 0: separate the offline ML metric (what you compute on held-out data) from the online business metric (what you A/B test in production). A model that wins on offline AUC can still lose on revenue or engagement — so the metric you optimize must be a faithful proxy for the value you actually care about. Interview angle The unifying senior insight: choosing the metric is a modeling decision, made before you train. For any “how would you evaluate X?” answer in two layers — the offline metric tied to the error costs, and the online metric (A/B test on the business outcome) that’s the real arbiter. Saying “I’d pick the metric from what an error costs the business” is the line that lands. # One-Page Summary Concept The one thing to remember Confusion matrix TP/FP/FN/TN; FP = Type I (false alarm), FN = Type II (miss). Accuracy trap Useless under imbalance — “always negative” scores high and is worthless. Precision vs recall Precision = of my alarms how many real; recall = of the real ones how many caught. F1 Harmonic mean of precision and recall — both must be high. Threshold A dial that trades precision against recall; 0.5 is a default, set it by error cost. ROC vs PR AUC ROC-AUC flatters on imbalance; PR-AUC is honest when positives are rare. Calibration “When I say 70% it happens 70%” — AUC grades ranking, calibration grades the number. Ranking metrics MRR (first hit) → MAP (all hits) → NDCG (graded, position-discounted). Regression metrics MAE robust; RMSE punishes big errors / feels outliers; R² = variance explained. Cross-validation Stratify for imbalance, split by time for temporal, by group for repeats; fit preprocessing on train fold only. Which metric Match it to error costs; separate the offline metric from the online business metric. # Related Precision Recall ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC Cross-Validation Bias-Variance Tradeoff

title: Precision & Recall
text: Say it in 30s: Precision = of the things I flagged positive, how many were right (TP / (TP+FP)) — punishes false alarms. Recall = of the actual positives, how many did I catch (TP / (TP+FN)) — punishes misses. They trade off as you move the decision threshold. When to favor which Recall when missing a positive is costly: cancer screening, fraud, safety. Precision when a false alarm is costly: spam filters, recommending an expensive action. F1 = harmonic mean of the two, for a single number when you care about both. The threshold link Lower threshold → more positives → higher recall, lower precision. Raise it → the reverse. This is why you report the PR curve , not a single point, on imbalanced problems. Traps Accuracy is misleading under class imbalance (99% negatives → predict all-negative scores 99%). Precision/recall ignore true negatives by design — that s the point. See depth: Model Evaluation Validation (§2–3). Related: ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC , Logistic Regression , Bias-Variance Tradeoff .

title: ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC
text: Say it in 30s: Both summarize a classifier across all thresholds. ROC plots TPR vs FPR; its AUC is the probability a random positive is ranked above a random negative. PR plots precision vs recall. On imbalanced data, prefer PR-AUC — ROC-AUC looks deceptively good because the huge negative class makes FPR tiny. Key points ROC-AUC = 0.5 is random, 1.0 is perfect; threshold-independent and class-balance-insensitive (which is both a feature and a bug). PR-AUC baseline is the positive class prevalence, so it honestly reflects rarity. Use ROC-AUC to compare rankers in general; switch to PR-AUC when positives are rare and false positives matter (fraud, retrieval, medical). Trap: quoting a 0.95 ROC-AUC on a 1%-positive problem can hide poor precision at the operating point — show PR-AUC too. See depth: Model Evaluation Validation (§4). Related: Precision Recall , Logistic Regression .

title: Bias-Variance Tradeoff
text: Say it in 30s: For squared-error regression, expected test error decomposes exactly into bias² + variance + irreducible noise. Bias is error from wrong assumptions (too simple a model, underfits); variance is error from sensitivity to the training sample (too flexible a model, overfits). Lowering one usually raises the other, so the goal is the sweet spot, not zero of either. Key points More capacity (deeper tree, higher polynomial degree, less regularization) → lower bias, higher variance. More data lets you afford more capacity without paying as much variance. The dartboard picture: bias = is the cluster centered on the target; variance = how tight the cluster is. The U-curve: total test error falls then rises as complexity grows; minimum = optimal capacity. Modern asterisk: double descent — past the interpolation point, very overparameterized models can improve again. Common follow-ups / traps How do you reduce variance? → more data, regularization, simpler model, bagging/ensembling. How do you reduce bias? → richer model, better features, boosting. Don t confuse this with the bias/variance of an estimator in statistics (related, not identical framing). See depth: Fundamentals (§4). Related: Overfitting Underfitting , Regularization , Cross-Validation , Bagging vs Boosting .

title: Empirical Risk Minimization
text: Say it in 30s: We want to minimize true risk — expected loss over the real data distribution — but we can t see that distribution. So we minimize empirical risk , the average loss on our training sample, as a stand-in. ERM is pick the hypothesis with lowest average training loss. Why it works (and when it doesn t) Justified by the i.i.d. assumption : training and future data come from the same distribution, so empirical risk estimates true risk. Pure ERM overfits, so in practice we use regularized risk minimization : empirical loss + λ·penalty. When i.i.d. breaks (distribution shift, autocorrelated time series, sampling bias), empirical risk becomes an optimistic, misleading estimate. Trap: minimizing training loss is the means , not the goal. The goal is low true risk = generalization. See depth: Fundamentals (§2). Related: Generalization , Regularization , Maximum Likelihood Estimation .

title: Fundamentals
heads: Generalization: Why Held-Out Data Is Sacred
Regularization, Inductive Bias  No Free Lunch
Turning a vague problem into a crisp one: I-O-L-M
text: Foundations: the learning problem. Simplified illustrated edition. This is the bedrock the rest stands on. We answer four questions: what machine learning actually is , how supervised learning is set up as an optimization problem, why held-out data is sacred, and what the bias-variance tradeoff really means. Nail these and most fundamentals round questions become a handful of ideas you apply, not facts you memorize. What you ll be able to say after this chapter Define ML as function approximation under a generalization constraint . Name the five learning settings by their supervision signal . Explain why we minimize empirical risk but care about true risk. Diagnose underfitting vs overfitting from a learning curve. Turn any vague use ML for X prompt into a crisp problem with I-O-L-M . # What Machine Learning Is Classical software is rules in, answers out : a human writes the logic, the computer applies it. Machine learning flips the second half: answers in, rules out . You hand it worked examples and it reverse-engineers an approximate procedure. Classical code applies rules you wrote; ML infers the rules from examples. Why bother? For a huge class of problems nobody can write the rules by hand: telling a cat from a dog in pixels, predicting loan default, translating English to Japanese. The rules exist in human intuition but are too tangled to articulate. ML recovers an approximation of them from data. One subtlety to carry through: ML never learns the true rule. It learns a function that fits the data you showed it and, hopefully, behaves well on data you haven t. That gap between fits what I saw and works on what I haven t seen is the single most important theme in the field. Regularization, validation, and the bias-variance tradeoff are all machinery for managing it. Memory hook Classical programming = rules in, answers out . Machine learning = answers in, rules out . Interview angle What is machine learning? is a softball you can fumble. Weak: computers learning from data. Strong: we use data to pick a function from a hypothesis space, and we care about expected performance on unseen data, not training accuracy. Saying generalization in your first sentence signals seniority. # The five learning settings Learning problems are grouped by what kind of supervision signal the algorithm gets — how much, and what kind of, labeled feedback is available. The map of learning settings, organized by supervision signal. Setting Supervision signal Goal Examples Supervised Labeled ( x , y ) (x, y) ( x , y ) pairs Learn a mapping x → y x \to y x → y that generalizes Spam detection, credit scoring, demand forecasting Unsupervised Inputs only, no labels Find structure in the data Clustering, PCA/UMAP, density estimation Self-supervised Labels forged from the input itself Pretrain rich representations BERT (mask a word), GPT (next token), contrastive image learning Semi-supervised Few labels + lots of unlabeled data Spread few labels over data structure Pseudo-labeling, label propagation Reinforcement Reward from an environment Learn a policy maximizing cumulative reward AlphaGo, robotics, RLHF Memory hook Self-supervised learning is supervised learning that forges its own labels : hide a piece of the input, predict it, repeat a billion times. It s the engine behind foundation models. Interview angle A classic trap: is this supervised or unsupervised? for an ambiguous task. Don t name a box — name the supervision signal . Recommendation can be supervised (predict the rating), self-supervised (predict the next item), or RL (optimize long-term engagement). The signal is the discriminator. Go deeper (optional) The boundaries are porous. The dominant modern recipe — self-supervised pretraining then supervised fine-tuning — is neither purely one nor the other. Treat the taxonomy as vocabulary for describing the components of a system, not exclusive boxes. # Discriminative vs generative models A second axis, orthogonal to supervision, cuts across how a model represents the problem. People fumble this one constantly. Discriminative models draw the border; generative models learn each class s shape and derive the border. Discriminative Generative Learns p ( y ∣ x ) p(y \mid x) p ( y ∣ x ) — or just a decision boundary p ( x , y ) = p ( x ∣ y ) p ( y ) p(x, y) = p(x \mid y)\,p(y) p ( x , y ) = p ( x ∣ y ) p ( y ) — the full data story Answers Which side of the line is this? How is each class generated? then applies Bayes rule Can it sample? No Yes — can generate new x x x , detect outliers, handle missing features Examples Logistic regression, SVM, random forest, most NN classifiers Naive Bayes, GMM, HMM, VAE, diffusion, autoregressive LLMs Wins when You only need the label and have ample data Small data (assumptions hold), or you need to sample Memory hook Discriminative draws the border ; generative paints the countries . Generative knows enough to forge a new passport (sample data); discriminative only checks which side of the line you re on. Go deeper (optional) Ng Jordan s classic result: a generative model (Naive Bayes) has higher asymptotic error than its discriminative pair (logistic regression), but reaches that asymptote with far fewer samples. So generative can win in the small-data regime and lose in the large-data regime — they converge to different places at different speeds. Rapid fire — What ML is ML infers rules from examples; classical code applies hand-written rules. Reframe what is ML as function approximation under a generalization constraint . Five settings by supervision signal: supervised, unsupervised, self-supervised, semi-supervised, reinforcement. Self-supervised = supervised with manufactured labels; it powers foundation models. Discriminative models p ( y ∣ x ) p(y\mid x) p ( y ∣ x ) (border); generative models p ( x , y ) p(x,y) p ( x , y ) (countries, can sample). Generative wins small-data / sampling; discriminative wins large-data accuracy. # The Supervised Setup, Formally The formalism is exactly what separates a crisp answer from hand-waving. Supervised learning has six objects: Object What it is Example Input space X \mathcal{X} X The set of possible inputs Feature vectors, images, sentences Output space Y \mathcal{Y} Y The set of possible labels { 0 , 1 } \{0,1\} { 0 , 1 } for binary, R \mathbb{R} R for regression Distribution D \mathcal{D} D Unknown source of all data; we only see samples The real world we never observe directly Training set S S S n n n examples drawn i.i.d. from D \mathcal{D} D Your labeled dataset Hypothesis space H \mathcal{H} H Functions h : X → Y h : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y} h : X → Y you re willing to consider Linear models? Depth-3 trees? A given NN? Loss ℓ ( h ( x ) , y ) \ell(h(x), y) ℓ ( h ( x ) , y ) How wrong a single prediction is Squared loss, 0-1 loss, cross-entropy The goal: use S S S to pick an h h h that performs well on the whole distribution D \mathcal{D} D , not just on S S S . # True risk vs empirical risk What we actually care about is the true risk — the average loss over the entire distribution, R ( h ) = E [ ℓ ( h ( x ) , y ) ] R(h) = \mathbb{E}[\ell(h(x), y)] R ( h ) = E [ ℓ ( h ( x ) , y )] for a fresh example drawn from the real world. The problem is fatal: we cannot compute it , because we don t have D \mathcal{D} D , only the finite sample S S S . So we approximate it with the only data we have — the average loss on the training set. This is the empirical risk : R S ( h ) = 1 n ∑ i = 1 n ℓ ( h ( x i ) , y i ) R_S(h) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \ell(h(x_i), y_i) R S ​ ( h ) = n 1 ​ i = 1 ∑ n ​ ℓ ( h ( x i ​ ) , y i ​ ) By the law of large numbers, for a fixed h h h it converges to the true risk as n n n grows. It s the visible shadow cast by the invisible true risk. True risk R ( h ) R(h) R ( h ) Empirical risk R S ( h ) R_S(h) R S ​ ( h ) Defined over The whole distribution D \mathcal{D} D The finite training sample S S S Can we compute it? No — D \mathcal{D} D is unknown Yes — it s just an average Role What we want to minimize The proxy we actually minimize Catch Invisible Unbiased but noisy for a fixed h h h ; optimistically biased for the h h h picked by minimizing it # Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) Since we can t minimize the true risk directly, we minimize the empirical risk instead. That principle is Empirical Risk Minimization : pick the hypothesis with the smallest average error on your training data. Almost every model you ve trained does a version of this — linear regression minimizes squared loss, logistic regression minimizes log-loss, a neural net minimizes cross-entropy via SGD. ERM minimizes the wiggly empirical risk, but the minimum we actually want belongs to the smooth true risk. Here s the crucial gap: ERM minimizes R S R_S R S ​ , but we want to minimize R R R , and the minimizer of one isn t the minimizer of the other. When H \mathcal{H} H is rich and n n n is small, R S R_S R S ​ can hit zero (perfect training fit) while R R R stays large. That is overfitting , and it s why naive ERM on an unconstrained H \mathcal{H} H fails. Managing this gap is the entire game. Memory hook True risk is your score on the real exam; empirical risk is your score on the practice test. ERM means study to ace the practice test — it works only if the practice test resembles the real one and you didn t memorize the answer key. Interview angle What does training a model actually do? Senior answer: it performs regularized empirical risk minimization over a chosen hypothesis space, using the training sample as a proxy for the unknown distribution — and the whole challenge is that the proxy is imperfect, which is why we hold out data and regularize. Rapid fire — Supervised setup Objects: input space X \mathcal{X} X , output space Y \mathcal{Y} Y , distribution D \mathcal{D} D , i.i.d. sample S S S , hypothesis space H \mathcal{H} H , loss ℓ \ell ℓ . True risk R ( h ) = E [ ℓ ] R(h) = \mathbb{E}[\ell] R ( h ) = E [ ℓ ] is what we want but can t compute. Empirical risk R S ( h ) = 1 n ∑ ℓ R_S(h) = \frac{1}{n}\sum\ell R S ​ ( h ) = n 1 ​ ∑ ℓ is the computable proxy. ERM picks the hypothesis minimizing empirical risk; nearly all training is regularized ERM. The gap between R R R and R S R_S R S ​ is the source of overfitting and the reason for held-out data. # Generalization: Why Held-Out Data Is Sacred Generalization is performance on data the model wasn t trained on. It s the only thing that matters: a model that memorizes its training set and fails on everything else is worthless. This section is about measuring it honestly — mostly a matter of discipline. # The i.i.d. assumption The license to even hope for generalization is the assumption that training and future data are drawn i.i.d. from the same distribution D \mathcal{D} D . Identically distributed : test data looks statistically like training data. Independent : examples don t leak information about each other. When this breaks — the world shifts after you train, the test set comes from a different population, a time series is autocorrelated — generalization estimates turn optimistic and models silently degrade. Distribution shift is the number-one reason good offline models disappoint in production. Memory hook i.i.d. is the contract that says the future will be sampled from the same urn as the past. Every ML guarantee is voided the moment that contract breaks. # The train / validation / test split Because training error is an optimistically biased estimate of true risk, we estimate generalization on data the model never saw while fitting. Standard practice splits three ways. Three-way split (left) and the learning curve whose gap diagnoses bias vs variance (right). Split Typical % What it s for Training ~60–80% Fit the parameters (weights). The model directly minimizes loss here. Validation ~10–20% Tune hyperparameters and make model decisions: architecture, regularization, when to stop, which features. Test ~10–20% Used once , at the very end, for an honest unbiased estimate of real-world performance. Why do we need both validation and test? Every time you use the validation score to make a decision, you fit it a little. After trying a hundred configurations and keeping the best, the winner s validation score is optimistic — you ve partly overfit the validation set through selection. The untouched test set restores honesty. The golden rule Never touch the test set until the very end. Not to peek, not to just check, not to engineer features, not to pick a threshold. The moment a test observation influences any decision, the test set stops being an unbiased estimate and becomes just another training signal. Treat it as locked in a vault. Violating this is called data snooping (or leakage). It s insidious: it inflates your reported metrics while the model is secretly worse. The classic traps: Leakage type What goes wrong Fix Preprocessing on full data Normalization stats / imputation / feature ranks computed before the split leak test info into training Fit every transform on the training fold only , then apply Target leakage A feature is a proxy for or downstream of the label (e.g. account closed date for churn) Drop features unknown at prediction time Temporal leakage Random shuffling trains on the future to predict the past Always split by time for temporal problems Group leakage Same patient/user/doc in both train and test; model memorizes the entity Split by group Interview angle Your model scores 99% offline but tanks in production. What happened? Walk the checklist: distribution shift, target leakage, temporal/group leakage, normalization fit on full data, validation overfitting from too many trials. A systematic suspicion of suspiciously good numbers is the senior instinct interviewers screen for. # Reading a learning curve A learning curve plots error against training-set size (or epochs). It s a cheap diagnostic. As you add data, training error rises slightly and validation error falls; the two converge, and the vertical gap between them is the generalization gap . What you see What it means → the fix Big gap that doesn t close with more data High variance / overfitting → more data, more regularization, or a simpler model Both curves plateau high and sit close together High bias / underfitting → a more expressive model or better features (more data won t help) Rapid fire — Generalization Generalization = performance on unseen data; it s the only goal. i.i.d. (same distribution, independent samples) licenses generalization; distribution shift breaks it. Train fits parameters, validation tunes choices, test is the one-shot honest estimate. You need both val and test because repeated validation selection overfits the validation set. Golden rule: never touch the test set until the end. Leakage (preprocessing on full data, target/temporal/group) inflates offline metrics and kills production. Learning curve: persistent gap = variance; high converged floor = bias. # Overfitting, Underfitting the Bias-Variance Tradeoff Underfitting : the model is too simple to capture the pattern — high error on both train and test. Overfitting : the model is so flexible it captures noise as if it were signal — low train error, high test error. The art of ML is steering between the two. The same 18 noisy points fit by polynomials of degree 1, 4, and 14. Note the overfit model has the lowest training error and the worst test error. Model capacity (complexity) is the knob: polynomial degree, tree depth, number of NN parameters, the inverse of regularization strength. Low capacity → underfit; high capacity → overfit; the right spot depends on how much data you have (more data supports more capacity). Memory hook Underfitting is a student who didn t study (wrong on practice and exam). Overfitting is a student who memorized the practice answer key (perfect on practice, lost on the exam). You want the one who learned the concept . # The bias-variance decomposition For squared-error regression the tradeoff is exact. If data is y = f ( x ) + ε y = f(x) + \varepsilon y = f ( x ) + ε with zero-mean noise of variance σ 2 \sigma^2 σ 2 , then the expected error at a point, averaged over all training sets you might draw, splits cleanly: E [ ( y − f ^ ( x ) ) 2 ] = Bias 2 ⏟ too simple + Variance ⏟ too flexible + σ 2 ⏟ irreducible \mathbb{E}\big[(y - \hat{f}(x))^2\big] = \underbrace{\text{Bias}^2}_{\text{too simple}} + \underbrace{\text{Variance}}_{\text{too flexible}} + \underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{irreducible}} E [ ( y − f ^ ​ ( x ) ) 2 ] = too simple Bias 2 ​ ​ + too flexible Variance ​ ​ + irreducible σ 2 ​ ​ Term Plain English Signals Bias² How far the average prediction sits from the truth — systematic error in the same direction Model too simple Variance How much the prediction jumps around as you swap training sets Model too flexible, chasing noise σ 2 \sigma^2 σ 2 (noise) The floor — the label is partly random; no model beats it Irreducible The tension: simplifying lowers variance but raises bias ; enriching lowers bias but raises variance . You can t drive both to zero with finite data — push one down and the other comes up. Total error is their sum, so you minimize by trading off. Go deeper (optional) The clean additive split is special to squared loss . For 0-1 loss or cross-entropy the decomposition is messier and not additive the same way — a subtlety interviewers occasionally test. Don t claim bias-variance decomposes cleanly for classification accuracy: it doesn t. # The dartboard picture The most durable mental image: throwing darts at a target. The bullseye is the truth; each dart is a prediction from a model trained on one random dataset. Bias is aim (is the cluster centered?); variance is grouping (how tight is it?). Memory hook Bias = aim (is the cluster centered on the bullseye?). Variance = grouping (how tight is the cluster?). A sniper with a bent scope: low variance, high bias. A jittery shooter with good aim: low bias, high variance. # The U-curve Plot expected test error against complexity and you get the famous U. As complexity rises, bias² falls steeply but variance climbs; their sum plus the noise floor is U-shaped. The minimum is the optimal capacity for your data. Bias falls and variance rises with complexity; total error bottoms out at the sweet spot. Training error (not shown) keeps falling monotonically to the right — which is exactly why you can t pick complexity by training error . You pick it by validation error, which traces this U. Interview angle — which lever moves which term Expect how do you reduce variance without adding much bias? Knowing which lever moves which term is the actual test. To reduce VARIANCE (overfitting) To reduce BIAS (underfitting) More data A richer / more expressive model Bagging / ensembling (averages variance away) Boosting (fits the residual error) Regularization (trades a little bias for a lot of variance) Better features / less regularization # Double descent — the modern asterisk The clean U is the classical story, and mostly right. But in modern deep learning, as you grow a model past the point where it can perfectly fit (interpolate) the training data, test error often goes down again after a spike at the interpolation threshold . Double descent: error dips, spikes where the model exactly fits the data, then dips a second time. This is why a neural net with far more parameters than data points can still generalize beautifully. The leading explanation: among the many settings that perfectly fit the data, gradient descent has an implicit bias toward simple, low-norm solutions — so huge models effectively self-regularize. Go deeper (optional) Don t oversell this as overfitting isn t real. The classical U holds for a fixed effective complexity; double descent is a phenomenon of overparameterized interpolating models with optimizer-induced regularization. Both pictures are true in their regimes — saying so reads as well-calibrated rather than buzzword-chasing. Rapid fire — Bias, variance, capacity Underfit = high train AND test error (high bias). Overfit = low train, high test (high variance). Capacity (degree, depth, #params, 1/regularization) is the knob; more data supports more capacity. Squared error = = = Bias² + Variance + σ 2 \sigma^2 σ 2 (this clean split is special to squared loss). Bias = aim off-center; variance = loose grouping; noise = the floor you can t beat. U-curve: pick the minimum via validation error, never training error. Lower variance: more data, bagging, regularization. Lower bias: richer model, boosting, better features. Double descent: overparameterized nets can improve again past the interpolation threshold. # Regularization, Inductive Bias No Free Lunch Three tightly linked ideas explain why and how we deliberately constrain models. Idea What it means Regularization Any change to learning that reduces variance/overfitting, usually by penalizing complexity. Minimize R S ( h ) + λ Ω ( h ) R_S(h) + \lambda\,\Omega(h) R S ​ ( h ) + λ Ω ( h ) instead of R S ( h ) R_S(h) R S ​ ( h ) alone, where Ω \Omega Ω measures complexity ( ∥ w ∥ 2 \lVert w\rVert^2 ∥ w ∥ 2 ridge, ∥ w ∥ 1 \lVert w\rVert_1 ∥ w ∥ 1 ​ lasso) and λ \lambda λ sets the strength. It trades a little bias for a larger drop in variance — sliding you left toward the U-curve s sweet spot. Early stopping, dropout, weight decay, data augmentation, and ensembling are all regularizers in spirit. Inductive bias The assumptions a model uses to generalize beyond the data. Every model that generalizes has one. A linear model assumes linearity; a CNN assumes locality and translation invariance; an RNN/Transformer assumes sequence structure; a tree assumes axis-aligned splits. It s not a flaw — it s what lets a model prefer one of the infinitely many functions consistent with finite data. No Free Lunch Averaged over all possible problems, no learner beats any other. Any algorithm that excels on one class of problems must do correspondingly worse on another. There is no universally best model — so your job is to match the model s inductive bias to your problem s structure . Memory hook Inductive bias is the model s prejudice about what good functions look like before it sees data. Convolution s prejudice: a feature means the same thing wherever it appears. Pick a model whose prejudices fit your problem. Interview angle What s the best ML algorithm? The trap is naming one. Invoke No Free Lunch: there s no best algorithm in general; the right choice depends on the data s structure, size, and the inductive bias that fits — which is why we validate empirically rather than reason to a single winner. Deep nets crush vision/language because their biases (hierarchy, locality, compositionality) fit that data; on heterogeneous tabular data, gradient-boosted trees often win. Rapid fire — Regularization NFL Regularization = penalize complexity ( R S + λ Ω R_S + \lambda\Omega R S ​ + λ Ω ) to trade a little bias for a lot of variance reduction. Early stopping, dropout, weight decay, augmentation, ensembling are all variance-fighting regularizers. Inductive bias = built-in assumptions about plausible functions; it s what makes generalization possible. No Free Lunch: averaged over all problems, all learners tie — so match the model to the problem. There is no universally best algorithm; this is why we validate empirically. # Method Taxonomies to Speak Fluently A few orthogonal axes for classifying methods come up constantly. Speaking them fluently signals breadth. Axis Option A Option B Parametric vs nonparametric Parametric: fixed #params regardless of data size; can discard the data (linear/logistic regression, a fixed NN). Strong assumptions, fast, data-efficient, can underfit. Nonparametric: effective #params grows with data (kNN, kernels, trees, GPs). Flexible, fewer assumptions, data/compute hungry, can overfit. ( ≠ \ne  = zero parameters.) Batch vs online Batch/offline: train on all data at once, deploy a fixed model. Mini-batch SGD is still batch — an optimization detail, not online. Online: update incrementally per example/mini-batch. Suits streaming and non-stationary data; adapts to drift but can be unstable. Problem framing Classification (discrete label; accuracy, AUC), Regression (continuous; MSE, MAE, R 2 R^2 R 2 ) Ranking (relative order; NDCG, MAP, MRR), Generation (structured output; perplexity, human eval) Memory hook Parametric pours the data into a fixed-size mold and discards it. Nonparametric keeps the data and grows with it — kNN is the extreme: the model is literally the training set. The same business problem can often be framed multiple ways, and choosing the framing is itself a modeling decision . Recommend items can be classification (click / no-click), regression (predict rating), or ranking — and the ranking framing usually matches the real objective best. Axis Option A Option B Pick A when… Params Parametric (linreg, fixed NN) Nonparametric (kNN, trees, GP) Limited data, a structural prior, need speed/small footprint Training Batch / offline Online / incremental Data is static, fits in memory, no drift (B for streaming) Output Classification / Regression Ranking / Generation Answer is one discrete/continuous target (ranking when order is the goal) Model Discriminative Generative You only need the label and have ample data (generative to sample / small data) Rapid fire — Method taxonomies Parametric = fixed #params, can discard data; nonparametric = #params grow with data. Nonparametric ≠ \ne  = zero params. Parametric: efficient, strong assumptions, may underfit. Nonparametric: flexible, hungry, may overfit. Batch trains on all data at once; online updates per example. Mini-batch SGD is still batch. Output type sets the loss + metric: classification, regression, ranking, generation. Framing the business problem (classification vs regression vs ranking) is itself a key modeling decision. # The End-to-End ML Workflow Interviews increasingly test whether you can operate , not just recite algorithms. The lifecycle is the same everywhere, and narrating it crisply is its own skill. The ML lifecycle. The amateur sprints to Iterate ; the pro invests in Frame and Data. Stage What happens (and where people slip) 1. Frame Turn a vague business goal into a precise ML problem. Highest-leverage and most-skipped step. 2. Data Collect, clean, label, understand; build features; set up the split (respecting time/groups). Most time goes here; most failures originate here. 3. Baseline Build the dumbest reasonable model first (majority class, a linear model, a heuristic). It calibrates expectations and exposes leakage. Skipping it is a classic junior mistake. 4. Iterate Improve via features, models, tuning — one change at a time. Use the validation set. Diagnose with learning curves to know which lever to pull. 5. Evaluate Measure against the business-aligned metric on held-out data, with error analysis by slice. Touch the test set once , here. 6. Deploy monitor Ship it, then watch for distribution shift, drift, latency, degradation. Production is where i.i.d. assumptions go to die. Plan retraining. Memory hook Frame → Data → Baseline → Iterate → Evaluate → Deploy. Amateurs sprint to the fun modeling; pros invest in Frame and Data, build a Baseline before anything fancy, and treat Deploy/monitor as half the job. # Turning a vague problem into a crisp one: I-O-L-M This separates levels in interviews. We want to reduce customer churn — how would you use ML? The wrong move is naming algorithms. The right move is defining the ML problem by pinning down four things. Question to answer Churn example I — Input What features exist at prediction time ? (A feature known only after the event is leakage.) Usage frequency, tenure, support tickets, plan type, recent activity trend O — Output What exactly are you predicting, in what form, over what horizon? Probability an active subscriber cancels within the next 30 days → calibrated classification L — Label source Where does ground truth come from? Is it reliable, available, unbiased? Did this customer cancel in the 30-day window? — from historical billing logs M — Metric How is success measured, tied to business value? Precision/recall or AUC offline; retained revenue from interventions online Nail those four and the modeling almost chooses itself. Get them wrong and the fanciest model is solving the wrong problem. Note that accuracy is misleading for rare events — churn is rare, so nobody churns scores high and is useless — so always separate the offline ML metric from the online business metric you ll A/B test. Memory hook To crispen any vague ML ask, answer I-O-L-M: Input (known at prediction time?), Output (what exactly, with what horizon?), Label (where s the ground truth?), Metric (success tied to business value?). Interview angle For any how would you build X with ML? question, spend your first 90 seconds on framing — input, precise output with horizon, label source, business-tied metric — then mention a baseline, then talk models. Candidates who jump straight to I d use XGBoost signal they ve never owned a problem end to end. Rapid fire — Workflow framing Lifecycle: Frame → Data → Baseline → Iterate → Evaluate → Deploy/monitor. Most time goes to Data. Always build a dumb baseline first: it calibrates expectations and surfaces leakage. Iterate on validation; touch the test set once at Evaluate. Deployment isn t the end: monitor for drift and plan retraining. Crispen any vague problem with I-O-L-M, tied to business value. Separate the offline ML metric from the online business metric. # One-Page Summary Concept The one thing to remember What ML is Inferring rules from examples; the real goal is generalization , not training fit. Five settings By supervision signal: supervised, unsupervised, self-supervised, semi-supervised, reinforcement. Disc vs gen Discriminative draws the border p ( y ∣ x ) p(y\mid x) p ( y ∣ x ) ; generative paints the countries p ( x , y ) p(x,y) p ( x , y ) and can sample. Supervised setup X \mathcal{X} X , Y \mathcal{Y} Y , distribution D \mathcal{D} D , i.i.d. sample S S S , hypothesis space H \mathcal{H} H , loss ℓ \ell ℓ . Risk True risk R ( h ) R(h) R ( h ) is wanted but unknowable; empirical risk R S ( h ) R_S(h) R S ​ ( h ) is the proxy ERM minimizes. i.i.d. Same distribution + independent samples licenses generalization; distribution shift breaks it. Split Train fits parameters, validation tunes choices, test is the one-shot honest estimate. Golden rule Never touch the test set until the end. Watch for data leakage. Over/underfit Underfit = high train+test (bias). Overfit = low train, high test (variance). Bias-variance Squared error = = = Bias² + Variance + σ 2 \sigma^2 σ 2 . Bias = aim, variance = grouping. Pick the U-curve min via validation. Double descent Overparameterized nets can improve again past the interpolation threshold. Reg / bias / NFL Regularization trades bias for less variance; inductive bias enables generalization; no universally best learner. Taxonomies Parametric vs nonparametric; batch vs online; classification/regression/ranking/generation. Workflow + framing Frame → Data → Baseline → Iterate → Evaluate → Deploy. Crispen with I-O-L-M, frame before you model. # Related Bias-Variance Tradeoff Overfitting Underfitting Empirical Risk Minimization Generalization Regularization Generative vs Discriminative

title: Generalization
text: Say it in 30s: A model generalizes if it performs well on data it never saw during training. The whole point of ML is low error on the true distribution, not low error on the training set. Held-out data is how we estimate it. Key points The i.i.d. assumption is the license to even hope for generalization: test data is statistically like training data. Train / validation / test split : train fits parameters, validation tunes hyperparameters and model choice, test is touched once for an unbiased final estimate. Distribution shift is the #1 reason good offline models disappoint in production — the i.i.d. assumption quietly fails. The generalization gap = test error − training error; large gap signals overfitting. Trap: any decision made by looking at the test set leaks information and inflates your estimate. Guard the test set. See depth: Fundamentals (§3). Related: Empirical Risk Minimization , Overfitting Underfitting , Cross-Validation , Bias-Variance Tradeoff .

title: Overfitting & Underfitting
text: Say it in 30s: Underfitting = the model is too simple to capture the signal (high training error AND high test error). Overfitting = the model memorizes the training sample including its noise (low training error, high test error). You diagnose which one you have from the gap between training and validation curves. Reading the learning curve Big gap that doesn t close with more data → high variance / overfitting → more data, regularization, simpler model. Both curves plateau high and sit close together → high bias / underfitting → richer model or better features (more data won t help). Fixes Overfitting: regularization, dropout, early stopping, data augmentation, more data, ensembling. Underfitting: more capacity, better/more features, train longer, reduce regularization. Trap: a low training error alone tells you nothing. Always quote the validation gap. See depth: Fundamentals (§3–4). Related: Bias-Variance Tradeoff , Regularization , Cross-Validation , Generalization .

title: Regularization
text: Say it in 30s: Anything that constrains a model to reduce variance at the cost of a little bias. Most often an added penalty on model complexity: minimize (empirical loss + λ·penalty). λ trades fit against simplicity. L1 vs L2 (the classic question) L2 / Ridge (penalize Σwᵢ²): shrinks weights smoothly toward zero, never exactly zero. Handles correlated features by sharing weight. Has a closed form. L1 / Lasso (penalize Σ|wᵢ|): drives some weights exactly to zero → built-in feature selection / sparsity. The corner of the diamond constraint is why. No closed form (subgradient / soft-thresholding at zero). Elastic Net : L1 + L2, gets sparsity plus stability with correlated features. Beyond penalties: early stopping, dropout, data augmentation, weight decay, ensembling are all variance-fighting regularizers. Trap: larger λ = more regularization = more bias, less variance. Tune λ on validation, not test. See depth: Loss Functions (§2.5–2.6), Regression Methods (§3.3), Fundamentals (§5). Related: Bias-Variance Tradeoff , Overfitting Underfitting .
