Pin down: Business goal and who the user is Scale — DAU, # items, QPS Latency budget (e.g. ~100ms for ranking) Freshness requirements What good actually means Open with: First I ll align on the goal and success metric, then scale and latency, then ask what data we have. # 2. ML task metrics What does the model predict ? Framing: ranking vs classification vs retrieval. Offline metrics (AUC, NDCG, recall@k) AND online metrics (CTR, watch time, revenue) AND guardrails. The key move: the proxy you optimize ≠ the thing you actually care about. Tune proxy weights against an online north-star (e.g. D7/D30 retention) via A/B tests. # 3. Data features Sources, labels (explicit vs implicit), leakage, cold start. Feature families: user · item · user×item cross · context. The cross features are where ranking earns its keep. Implicit-feedback bias — name all three: Exposure / selection bias (feedback loop — you only see labels for what you showed) Position bias (rank drives clicks regardless of quality) Noisy negatives (a skip ≠ a confirmed dislike) Fixes: negative sampling, inverse propensity weighting / position-as-feature (zeroed at serving), exploration traffic to break the loop. # 4. Model Start with a baseline , then justify complexity. For large scale: multistage — retrieval → ranking → re-ranking. Discuss tradeoffs , not just the fanciest option. # 5. Serving scale Retrieval: two-tower model + ANN index (HNSW / ScaNN / FAISS). Item embeddings precomputed offline indexed; user tower runs once per request → single ANN lookup. The decoupling is the serving win. Multiple retrieval sources unioned (personalized + trending + social + fresh-exploration). Feature store, online vs batch inference, caching. # 6. Evaluation iteration Offline: ranking metric (NDCG), check calibration if probs feed downstream. Online: A/B test vs north-star (retention) + guardrail metrics (reports, diversity, creator health). Post-launch: monitor feature prediction drift , watch online metrics decay, retrain regularly (daily/continuous for fast domains). Continuous retraining on biased logs amplifies bias → exploration matters long-term. # Two-stage architecture cheat Stage Catalog → out Job Model Retrieval billions → thousands recall, cheap two-tower + ANN Ranking thousands → hundreds precision heavy multi-task (MMoE) Re-rank hundreds → ~10 diversity, policy rules + light model # Cold start Item: content embeddings at upload → retrievable immediately (also = freshness story). User: onboarding preferences + popular/trending prior, let real interactions take over. # Common ways people fail Jump straight to the model. Never define metrics properly (or don t connect offline ↔ online). Ignore data/serving reality. Circle instead of committing — state the structured answer up front. Use generic language instead of canonical component names. MOC - System Design ·

title: ML in Production & Monitoring
heads: Detecting data drift: PSI and KS
text: System Design: what happens after the offline metric looks good, and how a model stays good once real traffic reaches it. A trained model is a small part of a production ML system. The surrounding pieces (data pipelines, serving, rollout, monitoring, retraining, governance) determine whether the offline gain survives contact with reality. This chapter complements ML System Design Framework , which covers how to scope and structure a design answer, by covering the operational half: how predictions are served, how rollouts are made safe, what to monitor, and what to do when something breaks. What you ll be able to say after this chapter Choose between batch, online, and streaming serving from latency, freshness, and cost requirements. Explain training-serving skew, its common causes, and how feature stores and shared code reduce it. Name the main latency and throughput levers and the tradeoff each one buys. Sequence a safe rollout: offline checks, shadow, canary, A/B, with a rollback trigger. Distinguish covariate shift, label shift, and concept drift, and say which monitors detect which (and which cannot). Compute PSI and explain why KS and PSI alerts need judgment. Define a retraining policy and the reproducibility artifacts that support it. # Serving Patterns Pattern How predictions are produced Latency Freshness Typical fit Batch Score all (or all relevant) entities on a schedule; write results to a table or cache Reads are instant; staleness equals the schedule interval Hours to days Nightly churn scores, email targeting, candidate generation that tolerates staleness Online (request-response) Model called synchronously per request with fresh features Tens to hundreds of milliseconds budget Seconds or less Fraud checks at payment time, search ranking, personalization Streaming (near-real-time) Events processed continuously; features and/or scores updated as events arrive Sub-second to seconds from event to updated score Seconds Rolling behavioral features, anomaly detection on event streams, session-based recommendations Edge / on-device Model runs on the client No network round trip Updated with app or model releases Privacy-sensitive, offline, or ultra-low-latency use cases Many systems are hybrids : expensive user or item representations are computed in batch, cheap fresh signals are joined online, and a lightweight model combines them at request time. This is the common structure of multi-stage retrieval-and-ranking designs. Selection logic: If the decision does not depend on information newer than the batch interval, batch is generally the cheapest and simplest option, with the added benefit that outputs can be inspected before use. If the input exists only at request time (the current query, cart, or transaction), online scoring is required for at least part of the model. Streaming adds operational complexity (ordering, late events, state, exactly-once semantics), so it is justified when freshness measurably changes the outcome. Interview angle Anchor the choice in numbers: the latency budget , the QPS , the feature freshness the metric actually needs , and the cost per prediction . A common strong move is to ask what is the accuracy lost per hour of staleness? because that converts a vague freshness debate into a measurable tradeoff. # Training-Serving Skew Training-serving skew is a difference between the data or computation a model saw in training and what it receives in production. It is a leading cause of the offline-online gap, and unlike drift it is present from day one. Cause Example Mitigation Different code paths Features computed with SQL in training and re-implemented in a service for serving, with different handling of nulls or rounding One shared transformation library or definition used by both paths Different data sources or freshness Training reads a warehouse snapshot that is later corrected; serving reads a live store with late or missing values Log the features exactly as served and train on those logged values Time-travel errors Training features computed using data that would not have existed at that moment (see Data Preprocessing Feature Engineering ) Point-in-time correct joins, a documented prediction timestamp per feature Preprocessing state mismatch Scaler, vocabulary, or encoder refit or version-mismatched at serving Package the fitted preprocessing together with the model as a single artifact Default and missing-value handling A timeout returns zeros at serving, while training had null Explicit missing-value contract and monitoring of the missing rate per feature Population mismatch Training on exposed or approved cases only, serving on everyone Include exploration traffic; reweight or model the selection process Detection. Log the served feature vector and prediction for a sample of traffic. Compare per-feature distributions between the logged serving features and the training set, and, more decisively, recompute the features offline for the same entities and timestamps and diff them against the logged values. The diff measures skew directly. # Feature stores A feature store is a system that defines features once and serves them for both training and inference. Component Role Feature definitions (registry) Named, versioned transformations with ownership and documentation Offline store Historical feature values (a warehouse-style table), used to build training sets with point-in-time joins Online store Low-latency key-value lookups of the latest values for serving Materialization / sync Pipelines that compute features and write them to both stores consistently What it buys: consistency between training and serving, reuse across teams, and point-in-time correctness. What it costs: an additional system to run, schema and versioning discipline, and freshness limits tied to the materialization schedule. For a small system with a few features, a shared library and logged-feature training data may offer most of the benefit with less machinery. # Latency and Throughput Levers Latency is the time for one request; throughput is requests per unit time. Tail latency (p95, p99) is usually the binding constraint because user experience and downstream timeouts are set by the slow requests, not the average. Lever What it does Tradeoff Quantization Store weights (and possibly activations) in lower precision, such as 8-bit integers in place of 32-bit floats Smaller memory and faster arithmetic on supporting hardware; some accuracy loss that varies by model and method, so it must be measured on the target task Pruning / sparsity Remove low-importance weights or structures Speedups depend on hardware and structure; unstructured sparsity often gives memory savings without wall-clock gains Distillation Train a smaller student to match a larger teacher s outputs (often soft probabilities) A cheaper model with accuracy near the teacher s in many cases; requires a training run and representative data Caching Store results for repeated inputs or precomputed embeddings Large savings when the request distribution is skewed; adds staleness and invalidation concerns Batching Group requests so one forward pass serves several Better hardware utilization and throughput; adds queueing delay, so dynamic batching with a maximum wait time balances the two Model cascade / early exit A cheap model handles easy cases, an expensive one handles the rest Reduces average cost; adds routing logic and a threshold to calibrate Feature pruning and cheap features Drop costly features with low marginal gain Feature fetches (network calls) often dominate latency more than the model itself Compiled / optimized runtimes Graph optimization, operator fusion, hardware-specific kernels Engineering effort; behavior can differ slightly from the training framework and should be verified Horizontal scaling and autoscaling More replicas behind a load balancer Raises throughput, not single-request latency; cold starts and cost Approximate retrieval Approximate nearest-neighbor search in place of exact Large speedups; recall falls slightly and should be monitored Interview angle Before optimizing the model, profile the request: network calls to feature stores, serialization, and preprocessing often account for more of the budget than the forward pass. Then state the lever together with the metric it risks (quantization risks accuracy; batching risks tail latency; caching risks staleness). Go deeper (optional) Rough capacity planning: with average per-request service time s s s seconds and c c c parallel workers, maximum sustainable throughput is about c / s c/s c / s requests per second. Queueing theory also says that latency rises sharply as utilization approaches 100%, so targets such as 50-70% utilization at peak leave headroom for tails and bursts. These are rules of thumb that depend on the arrival pattern. # Deployment Strategies Offline metrics do not guarantee online performance because of skew, feedback effects, and population differences, so rollouts proceed in stages that reveal different problems. Stage What happens What it catches Limit Offline validation Holdout metrics, slice metrics, regression tests against a fixed evaluation set, latency benchmarks Obvious quality regressions, resource violations Cannot reveal serving bugs or user response Shadow mode New model receives live traffic and logs predictions; users see the old model s output Serving errors, latency, skew, distribution of outputs vs the incumbent No user impact measured, and no feedback effects Canary release New model serves a small slice (for example 1-5%) with automatic health checks Crashes, latency regressions, gross metric drops on real traffic Small slice gives low statistical power for subtle effects A/B test Randomized split with a pre-registered primary metric, guardrails, and sample size Causal effect on business metrics Needs adequate duration and sample size; interference and novelty effects can bias results Gradual ramp Increase traffic share in steps while monitoring Scale-dependent issues Slower; needs defined gates between steps Interleaving (ranking) Mix results from two rankers within one list and attribute clicks High sensitivity for ranking comparisons with fewer users Measures preference, not every business metric Bandit rollout Adaptively shift traffic toward the better variant Lower cost of exploring a worse arm Harder inference on the final effect size Rollback. Define the rollback trigger before launch: which metrics, which thresholds, which window. Keep the previous model version deployed and addressable so that rollback is a configuration switch rather than a rebuild. Use feature flags or a routing layer so traffic can be shifted in seconds. When the model s outputs feed stateful consumers (caches, downstream features), rollback may also require invalidating or recomputing those outputs. Design considerations for A/B tests of ML models: randomize by the right unit (user, rather than request, when experience is persistent); pre-specify guardrails (latency, error rate, fairness slices, revenue); account for multiple comparisons when many metrics are checked; and watch for network or marketplace interference , where treatment and control compete for the same resource, which can bias the measured effect. # Monitoring Monitoring needs three layers: system health (latency, errors, throughput, resource use), data quality and drift (inputs and outputs), and model quality (accuracy against outcomes, when available). # Types of shift Let x x x be the inputs and y y y the label. The distinctions below define what changed and what monitors can see. Shift What changes What stays fixed Example Consequence Covariate shift (data drift) p ( x ) p(x) p ( x ) p ( y ∣ x ) p(y \mid x) p ( y ∣ x ) New user demographic enters the app Model may be extrapolating; accuracy falls where it is out of its training support, and may not fall if the model is correct there Label shift (prior shift) p ( y ) p(y) p ( y ) p ( x ∣ y ) p(x \mid y) p ( x ∣ y ) Disease prevalence rises during a season Posterior probabilities become miscalibrated; ranking can remain fine; thresholds need adjusting Concept drift p ( y ∣ x ) p(y \mid x) p ( y ∣ x ) (anything may change) Fraudsters change tactics; user preferences change The learned mapping is wrong; retraining on fresh labels is needed Upstream / pipeline change The meaning, units, or availability of a feature Underlying world A source column changes units or starts returning nulls Often abrupt; resembles drift in monitors but is a bug Drift in p ( x ) p(x) p ( x ) is not by itself evidence of lower accuracy , and absence of drift in p ( x ) p(x) p ( x ) does not rule out concept drift, because p ( y ∣ x ) p(y\mid x) p ( y ∣ x ) can change while p ( x ) p(x) p ( x ) is stable. Input monitors are early-warning signals that need to be connected to outcomes. Under label shift, the target prior can be estimated without target labels by solving for new class proportions using the confusion matrix of the existing classifier on held-out data: with confusion matrix C C C (entries P ( y ^ = i , y = j ) P(\hat y = i, y = j) P ( y ^ ​ = i , y = j ) ) and the model s predicted-label distribution μ \mu μ on new data, the new class prior ratio weights solve w = C − 1 μ w = C^{-1}\mu w = C − 1 μ . This assumes label shift holds and C C C is invertible; it is one of the few label-free corrections with a clean derivation. # Detecting data drift: PSI and KS Population Stability Index (PSI) compares binned distributions of a feature (or score) between a reference sample and a current sample. With B B B bins, expected (reference) proportions e i e_i e i ​ and actual (current) proportions a i a_i a i ​ : P S I = ∑ i = 1 B ( a i − e i ) ln ⁡ a i e i \mathrm{PSI} = \sum_{i=1}^{B} (a_i - e_i)\,\ln\frac{a_i}{e_i} PSI = i = 1 ∑ B ​ ( a i ​ − e i ​ ) ln e i ​ a i ​ ​ This is the symmetrized KL divergence between the two binned distributions. Common rules of thumb (below about 0.1 small, 0.1 to 0.25 moderate, above 0.25 large) are conventions from credit-scoring practice rather than statistical thresholds. Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) two-sample test uses the maximum gap between the two empirical CDFs, D = sup ⁡ x ∣ F r e f ( x ) − F c u r ( x ) ∣ D = \sup_x |F_{ref}(x) - F_{cur}(x)| D = sup x ​ ∣ F r e f ​ ( x ) − F c u r ​ ( x ) ∣ , for continuous features. It is distribution-free for continuous data. Issue Why it matters Sample-size sensitivity With very large samples, KS p p p -values flag tiny, practically irrelevant differences; with small samples, real shifts go undetected. Report effect size ( D D D , PSI) alongside any p p p -value Binning sensitivity (PSI) Results depend on the number and placement of bins; bins are usually set from reference quantiles, and empty bins need smoothing to avoid ln ⁡ 0 \ln 0 ln 0 Univariate only Both examine one feature at a time and miss changes in correlations or joint structure; multivariate options include a domain classifier (train a model to separate reference from current rows; AUC near 0.5 means indistinguishable), or distances on embeddings Categorical features KS does not apply directly; use PSI, chi-squared, or Jensen-Shannon distance on category frequencies Multiple testing Monitoring hundreds of features at a 5% level yields many false alarms; correct the thresholds, rank by effect size, or alert on the top features by importance Seasonality Weekly or annual cycles look like drift if the reference window is mismatched; compare to the same phase of the cycle Drift is not impact A feature that the model barely uses can drift without consequence; weigh by feature importance or by the change in prediction distribution Also monitor the model output distribution (score histogram, positive prediction rate), missing-value rate per feature , out-of-range or new-category rate , and schema and freshness of upstream tables. Output and null-rate monitors are cheap, need no labels, and catch many pipeline failures. # Delayed and missing labels Ground truth often arrives late (loan default after months), arrives partially, or arrives biased (only reviewed cases are labeled). Options: Situation Approach Labels delayed but eventually complete Track metrics on matured cohorts, and report the lag; evaluate on recent cohorts when their labels close Labels partial or selectively observed Sample a small random audit set for unbiased labels; weight by inverse sampling probability Labels very slow or absent Use proxy metrics : early engagement signals, user reports, complaint rates, or agreement with a slower, more accurate model Feedback loops Hold out exploration traffic, since a model that only observes outcomes for items it chose gets a biased picture of the rest Proxy metrics are useful when they are validated: periodically check the proxy s correlation with the true outcome on matured data, because a proxy can drift away from the quantity it was meant to track. Interview angle A well-rounded monitoring answer has three tiers: (1) label-free signals available immediately (input drift, output distribution, null rates, latency), (2) proxy metrics available in hours or days, (3) true performance on matured labels. Then add that alerts are tied to a runbook and an owner, and that thresholds are tuned to limit alert fatigue. # Slices Aggregate metrics can mask regressions in subpopulations (region, device, new users, protected groups). Track key metrics per slice, with confidence intervals, since small slices produce noisy estimates. # Retraining Policies Policy Trigger Strengths Limits Scheduled Fixed cadence (daily, weekly, monthly) Simple, predictable May retrain needlessly, or too slowly after sudden change Triggered Drift or performance alert passes a threshold Responds to need, saves compute Needs well-tuned alerts; labels may lag Continuous / online learning Update on each event or mini-batch Fast adaptation Risk of instability, poisoning, and feedback loops; harder to audit and reproduce Manual Human decision Controlled Slow and inconsistent Choosing cadence: estimate how fast the world changes (the half-life of model accuracy, measured by evaluating older models on newer data), compare against the cost of retraining and the risk each release carries. A common compromise is scheduled retraining with performance-based gates and drift triggers for exceptional events. Retraining decisions: Window. Training on all history gives more data; a sliding window favors recency. When behavior changes, sample weights that decay with age are a middle path. Warm start vs from scratch. Warm starting is cheaper; retraining from scratch avoids accumulating past quirks and is easier to reproduce. Promotion gate. A retrained model replaces the incumbent only if it passes automated checks: holdout metrics at least as good on recent data and on key slices, calibration within tolerance, latency and size within budget, and no regression on a fixed regression-test set. Then it follows the staged rollout above. Label quality. Retraining on labels generated by the model s own decisions can reinforce its biases; include randomized exploration or independent labels where feasible. # Model Registry, Versioning, Reproducibility A model registry is a catalog of trained model artifacts with their metadata and lifecycle stage (for instance: experimental, staging, production, archived). Item to record Why Code version (commit hash) and environment (library versions, container image) Reconstruct the training run Data version / snapshot and query Same data must be recoverable; includes label definitions and time ranges Feature definitions and preprocessing artifacts Prevent skew; the fitted scaler/encoder is part of the model Hyperparameters and random seeds Replication and comparison Evaluation results , including slice metrics and the evaluation dataset version Justify promotion; baseline for future comparison Lineage (parent model, upstream tables) Impact analysis when a source changes Approvals and stage transitions Auditability and governance Serving signature (input schema, output schema) Detect contract violations at inference Reproducibility caveats: exact bitwise reproduction can fail even with fixed seeds because of nondeterministic GPU kernels, parallel reduction order, and library differences, so the practical target is statistically equivalent results, with seeds and determinism flags used where they are available. Version data as carefully as code, since a model without its data snapshot is not reproducible. Further practices: automate training as a pipeline (rather than a notebook) so that each run is a tracked, parameterized artifact; keep a fixed golden evaluation set and a small suite of regression tests (known inputs with expected output ranges); and validate input schemas at the serving boundary. # Failure Modes and Incident Response Failure mode Typical signal Common root cause First response Silent feature break Null rate or constant-value spike; score distribution shifts abruptly Upstream schema change, a failed job, unit change Roll back or fall back to defaults; fix the pipeline; backfill Training-serving skew Offline-online gap from launch; logged vs recomputed features disagree Duplicate feature logic, time-travel in training data Diff logged and recomputed features; unify code paths Gradual concept drift Slow decay of matured-label metrics Behavior or environment changes Retrain, with updated window and features Feedback loop Narrowing diversity; self-confirming labels Model decisions determine which labels are seen Add exploration, independent labels, diversity constraints Latency regression p99 climbs; timeouts Heavier model, slow feature fetch, cold starts, traffic growth Scale out, cache, fall back to a lighter model Cascading dependency failure Many systems degrade at once An upstream model s change alters this model s inputs Version contracts between models; staged rollouts with downstream checks Data poisoning / adversarial input Targeted shifts; attacks on thresholds Open data intake, adversaries adapting Rate-limit, validate inputs, monitor for abnormal clusters, review training-data intake Bad rollout Canary or A/B guardrail breach Insufficient offline coverage Automated rollback to the previous version Incident process , in rough order: detect (alert or user report), triage severity and blast radius, mitigate first (roll back, switch to a fallback model or rule-based default, disable the feature), diagnose root cause with logged inputs and versions, fix and validate, then run a blameless post-mortem that produces concrete follow-ups (a new monitor, a new test, a clearer data contract). Prefer mitigation over diagnosis during the incident, since restoring service limits harm while the investigation continues. Fallbacks and graceful degradation should exist before they are needed: a simpler model, cached last-known-good predictions, or a rules-based default when the model service times out or the inputs fail validation. The fallback behavior itself should be tested and monitored. Warning Alerts that fire too often get ignored, and alerts that never fire hide real failures. Treat thresholds as hypotheses: review them after incidents, and attach each one to an owner and a runbook. # Responsible-AI Basics Operational ML comes with obligations around fairness, privacy, and transparency. The material below is the minimal toolkit usually expected in design discussions. # Fairness metrics at a glance Let Y ^ \hat Y Y ^ be the decision, Y Y Y the true outcome, and A A A a protected attribute (group). The common group criteria are: Criterion Condition Intuition Demographic (statistical) parity P ( Y ^ = 1 ∣ A = a ) P(\hat Y=1 \mid A=a) P ( Y ^ = 1 ∣ A = a ) equal across groups Same positive rate per group, regardless of outcome base rates Equal opportunity P ( Y ^ = 1 ∣ Y = 1 , A = a ) P(\hat Y=1 \mid Y=1, A=a) P ( Y ^ = 1 ∣ Y = 1 , A = a ) equal (equal true positive rates) Qualified people are accepted at equal rates Equalized odds Equal true positive and false positive rates across groups Error rates match across groups Predictive parity P ( Y = 1 ∣ Y ^ = 1 , A = a ) P(Y=1 \mid \hat Y=1, A=a) P ( Y = 1 ∣ Y ^ = 1 , A = a ) equal (equal precision) A positive decision means the same thing for each group Calibration within groups P ( Y = 1 ∣ score = s , A = a ) P(Y=1 \mid \text{score}=s, A=a) P ( Y = 1 ∣ score = s , A = a ) equal for each s s s Scores carry the same probabilistic meaning in each group These criteria generally cannot all hold at once . When group base rates P ( Y = 1 ∣ A = a ) P(Y=1\mid A=a) P ( Y = 1 ∣ A = a ) differ and the classifier is imperfect, calibration within groups and equal false positive and false negative rates are mutually incompatible, apart from degenerate cases. Choosing a criterion is therefore a policy decision tied to the harm of each error type, to be made with stakeholders and documented. Practical points: compute metrics per group with confidence intervals; examine whether protected attributes are available at evaluation time (they may be excluded from the model but still needed for auditing); note that dropping the protected feature does not remove its influence when proxies (zip code, name patterns) are present; and consider mitigation at three stages: pre-processing (reweighting, data repair), in-training (constraints or penalties), or post-processing (group-specific thresholds), each with its own accuracy-fairness tradeoff and legal considerations that depend on jurisdiction. # Privacy Concept Key point Data minimization and retention limits Collect and keep only what the task needs; delete on schedule PII handling Pseudonymize or tokenize identifiers; restrict access; avoid placing raw identifiers in feature stores and logs Anonymization limits Removing direct identifiers does not guarantee anonymity, since combinations of quasi-identifiers can re-identify individuals (the motivation for k-anonymity and its extensions) Model leakage Models can memorize training examples; membership inference and extraction attacks exploit this, with risk higher for overfit models and rare records Differential privacy A formal guarantee: a mechanism M M M is ( ε , δ ) (\varepsilon,\delta) ( ε , δ ) -DP if for datasets differing in one individual, P ( M ( D ) ∈ S ) ≤ e ε P ( M ( D ′ ) ∈ S ) + δ P(M(D)\in S) \le e^{\varepsilon}P(M(D )\in S)+\delta P ( M ( D ) ∈ S ) ≤ e ε P ( M ( D ′ ) ∈ S ) + δ . Training with DP-SGD (per-example gradient clipping plus noise) provides it, at a cost in accuracy that grows as ε \varepsilon ε shrinks Federated learning Training happens on-device and only updates are shared; this reduces raw data movement but does not by itself guarantee privacy, as updates can leak information without additional protections Also in scope: transparency (model cards and datasheets that record intended use, data, metrics by slice, and limits), explainability suited to the audience, human oversight for high-stakes decisions, and monitoring for harm after launch , because fairness and privacy properties can degrade as the data drifts. Interview angle When asked about fairness, name at least two criteria, state that they conflict when base rates differ, and tie the choice to the cost of each error type in the application. That demonstrates that a metric choice is a product decision with tradeoffs, in addition to a formula. # One-Page Summary Topic Key idea Serving Batch (cheap, stale), online (fresh, latency-bound), streaming (fresh features, complex); hybrids are common. Decide from latency, freshness value, QPS, cost. Skew Training-serving skew exists from day one: duplicate feature code, time-travel, preprocessing mismatch. Detect by logging served features and recomputing offline. Feature store One definition, offline and online stores, point-in-time joins; costs an extra system. Latency Profile first (feature fetches often dominate). Quantization, distillation, caching, batching, cascades, each with a named tradeoff; watch p99. Rollout Offline checks, shadow, canary, A/B or ramp, with predefined rollback triggers and the old version kept ready. Shift types Covariate: p ( x ) p(x) p ( x ) changes. Label: p ( y ) p(y) p ( y ) changes. Concept: p ( y ∣ x ) p(y\mid x) p ( y ∣ x ) changes. Input drift is not proof of accuracy loss. Drift tests P S I = ∑ ( a i − e i ) ln ⁡ ( a i / e i ) \mathrm{PSI}=\sum (a_i-e_i)\ln(a_i/e_i) PSI = ∑ ( a i ​ − e i ​ ) ln ( a i ​ / e i ​ ) ; KS gap between CDFs. Limits: sample-size sensitivity, univariate, binning, multiple testing, seasonality. Labels Delayed or biased labels: matured cohorts, audit samples, validated proxies. Retraining Scheduled, triggered, or continuous; gate promotion on recent-data and slice metrics, then roll out in stages. Reproducibility Version code, data, features, preprocessing, seeds, and eval results in a registry; aim for statistical rather than bitwise reproducibility. Incidents Mitigate first (rollback, fallback), then diagnose, fix, and run a blameless post-mortem. Responsible AI Fairness criteria conflict when base rates differ; privacy needs minimization, leakage awareness, and optionally differential privacy. # Related ML System Design Framework for scoping and the end-to-end design spine Data Preprocessing Feature Engineering for leakage and feature definitions Model Evaluation Validation for offline metrics and calibration MOC - System Design

title: System Design
text: The open-ended round. You re handed a vague product prompt and graded on how you scope, structure, and trade off — not on naming the fanciest model. # Chapters ML System Design Framework — the repeatable 6-step spine Recommender Systems — CF, MF, two-tower, ranking losses, biases, evaluation Bandits Reinforcement Learning Basics — MDPs, Q-learning, bandits, off-policy evaluation ML in Production Monitoring — serving, skew, rollout, drift monitoring, retraining, responsible AI # See also (from other areas) ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC — offline metric selection (Evaluation) Precision Recall — ranking/retrieval tradeoffs (Evaluation) Cross-Entropy Loss — multi-task heads (Losses) Data Preprocessing Feature Engineering — leakage and feature pipelines (Data Features) # The one-liner Scope before you build. Spend the first third on objective + metrics + constraints, drive a multistage architecture, name the canonical components, and always tie the offline proxy back to an online north-star metric with guardrails.

title: Recommender Systems
text: System Design: the modeling methods behind recommendation. The architecture view lives elsewhere; this chapter is the ML-methods angle. For the end-to-end shape (candidate generation, ranking, re-ranking, serving, feature stores) use ML System Design Framework and ML System Design Interview Prep . This chapter covers what those pages assume you can explain: how the models work, how they are trained, how they fail, and how they are evaluated. What you ll be able to say after this chapter Contrast user-based/item-based collaborative filtering with matrix factorization, and explain ALS and implicit feedback. Describe a two-tower retriever, in-batch negatives, and why logQ correction is needed. Choose between pointwise, pairwise and listwise ranking losses. Design a multi-task ranker and combine its heads into one score. Name the biases in logged data (position, selection, exposure) and the standard mitigations. Pick and compute the right offline metric, and say why offline gains may not transfer online. # The Problem Setup A user-item interaction matrix R ∈ R ∣ U ∣ × ∣ I ∣ R \in \mathbb{R}^{|U|\times|I|} R ∈ R ∣ U ∣ × ∣ I ∣ is extremely sparse (commonly well under 1% observed). The task is to score unobserved pairs and return a short ordered list. Two features of the data shape everything: Feedback is mostly implicit : clicks, watch time, purchases, skips. Absence of an interaction is ambiguous: not seen, seen and ignored, or disliked. Feedback is biased by the system that produced it : users only interact with what was shown, and in the position it was shown. Stage Goal Typical model Scale of candidates Retrieval (candidate generation) High recall, cheap Two-tower + approximate nearest neighbor, CF, co-occurrence Millions to billions down to hundreds or thousands Ranking Precise ordering with rich features Deep ranker with cross-features, multi-task Hundreds to thousands down to tens Re-ranking Business rules, diversity, fairness, calibration Slate-level heuristics or models Tens # Collaborative Filtering Collaborative filtering (CF) uses only the interaction pattern: users who behaved alike in the past will probably behave alike again. Memory-based (neighborhood) methods User-based : predict r ^ u i = r ˉ u + ∑ v ∈ N ( u ) s ( u , v ) ( r v i − r ˉ v ) ∑ v ∈ N ( u ) ∣ s ( u , v ) ∣ \hat r_{ui} = \bar r_u + \frac{\sum_{v\in N(u)} s(u,v)(r_{vi}-\bar r_v)}{\sum_{v\in N(u)}|s(u,v)|} r ^ u i ​ = r ˉ u ​ + ∑ v ∈ N ( u ) ​ ∣ s ( u , v ) ∣ ∑ v ∈ N ( u ) ​ s ( u , v ) ( r v i ​ − r ˉ v ​ ) ​ with similarity s s s (cosine, Pearson). Item-based : use similarity between items computed from co-engagement. Items are typically more stable and numerous users per item give better statistics, so item-based is often preferred when users greatly outnumber items. Strengths: simple, interpretable, strong baseline. Weaknesses: poor on sparse data, expensive at scale without approximation, no handling of cold start. Model-based methods learn compact representations, the most important family being matrix factorization. # Matrix Factorization Represent each user and item by a k k k -dimensional vector ( k k k typically tens to a few hundred) and predict by inner product plus biases: r ^ u i = μ + b u + b i + p u ⊤ q i \hat r_{ui} = \mu + b_u + b_i + p_u^\top q_i r ^ u i ​ = μ + b u ​ + b i ​ + p u ⊤ ​ q i ​ For explicit ratings, minimize over observed pairs Ω \Omega Ω : min ⁡ P , Q , b ∑ ( u , i ) ∈ Ω ( r u i − r ^ u i ) 2 + λ ( ∥ p u ∥ 2 + ∥ q i ∥ 2 + b u 2 + b i 2 ) \min_{P,Q,b}\ \sum_{(u,i)\in\Omega}\big(r_{ui}-\hat r_{ui}\big)^2 + \lambda\big(\|p_u\|^2+\|q_i\|^2+b_u^2+b_i^2\big) P , Q , b min ​ ( u , i ) ∈ Ω ∑ ​ ( r u i ​ − r ^ u i ​ ) 2 + λ ( ∥ p u ​ ∥ 2 + ∥ q i ​ ∥ 2 + b u 2 ​ + b i 2 ​ ) Two standard solvers: Solver Update Properties SGD For each observed ( u , i ) (u,i) ( u , i ) with error e u i e_{ui} e u i ​ : p u ← p u + η ( e u i q i − λ p u ) p_u \leftarrow p_u + \eta(e_{ui}q_i - \lambda p_u) p u ​ ← p u ​ + η ( e u i ​ q i ​ − λ p u ​ ) , and symmetrically for q i q_i q i ​ Simple, streams data, scales with observed entries; needs a learning rate and is hard to parallelize cleanly ALS (alternating least squares) Fix Q Q Q , solve for each p u p_u p u ​ in closed form as a ridge regression; fix P P P , solve for each q i q_i q i ​ ; alternate Each subproblem is convex with an exact solution; users (or items) update independently, so it parallelizes well; handles dense implicit objectives efficiently The objective is non-convex jointly in ( P , Q ) (P,Q) ( P , Q ) but convex in each block, which is why alternation works. # Implicit feedback With clicks or plays there are no true negatives. The common formulation (weighted matrix factorization for implicit data) defines a preference p u i = 1 [ interaction ] p_{ui}=\mathbb{1}[\text{interaction}] p u i ​ = 1 [ interaction ] and a confidence c u i = 1 + α r u i c_{ui}=1+\alpha\, r_{ui} c u i ​ = 1 + α r u i ​ (for example from interaction count), then minimizes over all pairs: min ⁡ ∑ u , i c u i ( p u i − x u ⊤ y i ) 2 + λ ( ∑ u ∥ x u ∥ 2 + ∑ i ∥ y i ∥ 2 ) \min\ \sum_{u,i} c_{ui}\big(p_{ui}-x_u^\top y_i\big)^2 + \lambda\big(\sum_u\|x_u\|^2+\sum_i\|y_i\|^2\big) min u , i ∑ ​ c u i ​ ( p u i ​ − x u ⊤ ​ y i ​ ) 2 + λ ( u ∑ ​ ∥ x u ​ ∥ 2 + i ∑ ​ ∥ y i ​ ∥ 2 ) Summing over all pairs looks quadratic in cost, but ALS algebra reuses Y ⊤ Y Y^\top Y Y ⊤ Y so the per-user solve costs scale with the user s number of observed items rather than the whole catalog. Alternatives treat unobserved items as sampled negatives and optimize a ranking objective such as Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR), described below. Interview angle A common probe: why not treat missing entries as zeros and fit squared error? The answer: they are not negatives, they are unknown, and fitting zeros pulls scores of unseen but good items down. Implicit-feedback MF handles it with confidence weighting (observed entries high confidence, unobserved low) or with negative sampling and a ranking loss. Go deeper MF with dot product is a special case of a two-tower model with linear towers and one-hot IDs as inputs. Neural models generalize it by replacing each tower with a network that can take side features; this is what lets them score new items and users through content features. # Two-Tower Retrieval A two-tower (dual encoder) model computes a user embedding u = f θ ( user, context ) u = f_\theta(\text{user, context}) u = f θ ​ ( user, context ) and an item embedding v = g ϕ ( item ) v = g_\phi(\text{item}) v = g ϕ ​ ( item ) , scores by a dot product or cosine, and trains so that matched pairs score higher than unmatched ones. Because item embeddings do not depend on the user, they are computed offline and indexed in an approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) structure; serving is one user-tower forward pass plus an ANN lookup. The price of this factorization is expressiveness: the interaction between user and item features is restricted to a single inner product, so fine-grained cross-features are left to the ranker. # Training with sampled softmax Treat retrieval as extreme classification over the catalog. With a positive item i i i and scores s ( u , j ) = u ⊤ v j s(u,j)=u^\top v_j s ( u , j ) = u ⊤ v j ​ , the full softmax loss is L = − log ⁡ exp ⁡ ( s ( u , i ) / τ ) ∑ j ∈ I exp ⁡ ( s ( u , j ) / τ ) \mathcal{L} = -\log\frac{\exp(s(u,i)/\tau)}{\sum_{j\in I}\exp(s(u,j)/\tau)} L = − lo g ∑ j ∈ I ​ exp ( s ( u , j ) / τ ) exp ( s ( u , i ) / τ ) ​ which is too expensive for large catalogs, so the denominator is approximated using a sampled set of negatives. A temperature τ \tau τ controls how sharply hard negatives are emphasized. # Negative sampling Scheme How Strength Risk Random negatives Uniform over catalog Cheap, unbiased view of the catalog Mostly easy negatives; weak learning signal In-batch negatives Other positives in the same batch serve as negatives for each example Free (reuses computed embeddings), scales batch-wise Sampling is proportional to item popularity, biasing the model against popular items; false negatives when the same item appears twice Hard negatives Items ranked highly by the current model but not interacted with; or ANN-mined Sharper decision boundary Can include unlabeled true positives (false negatives); too-hard negatives destabilize training Impression negatives Shown but not clicked Matches the serving distribution Biased by the previous ranker; position bias Mixed Combination (for example in-batch plus random plus a small share of hard) Balanced More hyperparameters # Why logQ correction With in-batch negatives, an item j j j appears as a negative with probability proportional to its frequency q j q_j q j ​ in the training data (items that are popular are frequent in batches). The model then sees popular items as negatives far more often than they would appear under uniform sampling, so it learns to push them down, and the retrieval ends up under-recommending popular items relative to the true objective. The standard fix subtracts the log of the sampling probability from each logit, estimating the full-softmax objective from a non-uniform sample: s c ( u , j ) = s ( u , j ) − log ⁡ q j s^{c}(u,j) = s(u,j) - \log q_j s c ( u , j ) = s ( u , j ) − lo g q j ​ so the training denominator becomes ∑ j exp ⁡ ( s ( u , j ) − log ⁡ q j ) \sum_j \exp(s(u,j)-\log q_j) ∑ j ​ exp ( s ( u , j ) − lo g q j ​ ) . Intuitively, a negative that was oversampled by factor q j q_j q j ​ is downweighted by 1 / q j 1/q_j 1/ q j ​ (importance correction). q j q_j q j ​ is estimated from streaming item counts. At serving time the uncorrected score s ( u , j ) s(u,j) s ( u , j ) is used. The correction reduces a systematic bias but can increase variance for rare items, and the estimate of q j q_j q j ​ must track drift. Common pitfalls Mixing up train and serve distributions (training only on clicked impressions while serving over the whole catalog), forgetting L2-normalization when using cosine with a temperature, and evaluating retrieval with a model whose ANN index is stale relative to the item tower. # Ranking Models The ranker takes a few hundred candidates and uses rich user, item, context and cross features, typically a deep network (feature crosses via factorization machines, cross networks, or attention over the user history) with an output layer per objective. # Learning-to-rank losses Family Training signal Example losses Pros Cons Pointwise Each (user, item) independently Log loss for click, regression for watch time Simple, calibrated probabilities, easy to combine with business logic Ignores relative order; optimizes a proxy of ranking quality Pairwise Pairs where one item should beat another BPR: − log ⁡ σ ( s i − s j ) -\log\sigma(s_i - s_j) − lo g σ ( s i ​ − s j ​ ) ; hinge; RankNet Directly targets ordering Pair construction and bias; O ( n 2 ) O(n^2) O ( n 2 ) pairs; calibration lost Listwise A whole ranked list ListNet (softmax cross-entropy over the list), LambdaRank / LambdaMART (gradients weighted by the metric change from swapping two items) Can align with metrics like NDCG More complex; needs list-level data; calibration lost Notes on choosing: Pointwise logistic loss gives probabilities usable downstream (for example in expected-value formulas or ads auctions). Pairwise and listwise losses give only scores good for ordering; calibrate separately if probabilities are needed. LambdaRank-style weights multiply the pairwise gradient by ∣ Δ NDCG ∣ |\Delta \text{NDCG}| ∣Δ NDCG ∣ of swapping the two items, which concentrates effort on the top of the list. This is a heuristic gradient rather than the gradient of a smooth loss, though it is observed to improve NDCG in many settings. All three can be hybridized: for example a pointwise head plus a pairwise auxiliary loss. # Multi-task and multi-objective ranking A single click probability rewards clickbait. Production rankers typically predict several outcomes: click, long watch, like, share, comment, hide/dislike, purchase. Architecture options Design Idea Trade-off Shared-bottom One shared trunk, one head per task Efficient, but conflicting tasks can hurt each other (negative transfer) Mixture-of-experts (MMoE-style) Several expert networks; a per-task gate mixes experts More flexible for tasks with different relatedness; costlier, gates can collapse Separate models Independent model per task No interference; higher cost, no sharing for sparse tasks Combining heads into one ranking score is usually a product-defined formula, for example a weighted sum of predicted probabilities, score = ∑ k w k p ^ k \text{score} = \sum_k w_k\,\hat p_k score = ∑ k ​ w k ​ p ^ ​ k ​ , or a multiplicative form such as p ^ click a p ^ like b \hat p_{\text{click}}^{a}\,\hat p_{\text{like}}^{b} p ^ ​ click a ​ p ^ ​ like b ​ minus penalties for negative signals. Weights encode business priorities and are tuned with online experiments, because an offline metric cannot tell which weighting improves long-term satisfaction. Negative feedback (hide, report) is often given a large negative weight because it is rare but costly. Training considerations : tasks with very different label frequencies need loss weighting or separate sampling; delayed labels (purchases) cause label-lag bias; and calibration per head matters when the combination formula assumes comparable probabilities. Interview angle When asked what do you optimize? , avoid a single click metric. A strong answer states the ranking score is a function of several predicted outcomes, justifies each (engagement, satisfaction, negative feedback), and explains the weights are product decisions validated by A/B tests with guardrail metrics. # Cold Start Case Approach New item Content-based features (text, image, category, creator) fed to the item tower; exploration quota or boost for new items; use creator-level priors; fast embedding updates as interactions arrive New user Onboarding questions or imported signals; start from popular or demographic/contextual priors (location, device, time); exploit the first few interactions with a session-based model New system Heuristics and popularity, then simple CF as data accumulates ID-based embeddings have no signal for unseen IDs, so hybrid models combine ID embeddings with content features and fall back to content features when the ID is new (for example with ID dropout during training so the model learns to rely on content when the ID is uninformative). # Exploration A system that only shows its top predictions never learns about items it currently underrates; the logged data then reinforces its own beliefs. Exploration deliberately gathers information at some short-term cost. Practical forms: Randomization within a small traffic slice, or random insertion into low-stakes slots. Bandit-style selection for new or uncertain items: see Bandits Reinforcement Learning Basics for epsilon-greedy, UCB and Thompson sampling. Uncertainty-aware scoring (for example ensembles or dropout-based variance used as an optimism bonus). Logging the propensity (probability with which each item was shown) so the data can later be used for unbiased off-policy learning and evaluation. # Biases in Logged Data Bias What happens Mitigations Position bias Higher slots get more clicks regardless of relevance Feature the position in training and set it to a default at serving; inverse propensity weighting by examination probability; a separate position tower trained jointly and dropped at inference; randomized-position experiments to estimate propensities Selection / exposure bias Only shown items receive labels; the unlabeled items are not negatives Train on impressions with propensity correction; exploration traffic; treat missing as unknown Popularity bias Popular items dominate positives, then dominate recommendations logQ correction, popularity-aware negative sampling, re-ranking for exposure Conformity / presentation bias Thumbnails, titles and context change clicks Include presentation features, use deeper engagement signals Survivorship / feedback bias Only active users generate data Weight by user inclusion probability, track cohorts that left Inverse propensity scoring (IPS) reweights each logged example by 1 / π i 1/\pi_i 1/ π i ​ where π i \pi_i π i ​ is the probability that the item was exposed or examined. The estimator is unbiased when propensities are correct and positive wherever relevance is non-zero, but variance explodes for small propensities, so weights are typically clipped. Go deeper The joint position-bias tower works because during training the model can attribute some of the click to position and the rest to relevance; dropping it at serving yields a score meant to reflect relevance only. It relies on position being sufficiently randomized or otherwise identifiable from the features; if the ranker s own scores determine position, the two effects are confounded and the decomposition is not identified. # Offline metrics Let the ranked list for a user be i 1 , … , i K i_1,\ldots,i_K i 1 ​ , … , i K ​ and rel k ∈ { 0 , 1 } \text{rel}_k\in\{0,1\} rel k ​ ∈ { 0 , 1 } (or graded) the relevance at rank k k k ; R u R_u R u ​ is the user s relevant set. Metric Definition Use Recall@K ∣ { relevant in top K } ∣ ∣ R u ∣ \dfrac{|\{\text{relevant in top }K\}|}{|R_u|} ∣ R u ​ ∣ ∣ { relevant in top K } ∣ ​ Retrieval: did the candidate set contain the good items Precision@K ∣ { relevant in top K } ∣ K \dfrac{|\{\text{relevant in top }K\}|}{K} K ∣ { relevant in top K } ∣ ​ Quality of the shown list MRR 1 ∣ U ∣ ∑ u 1 rank of first relevant \dfrac{1}{|U|}\sum_u \dfrac{1}{\text{rank of first relevant}} ∣ U ∣ 1 ​ ∑ u ​ rank of first relevant 1 ​ One right answer, such as navigation or next item MAP Mean over users of AP = 1 ∣ R u ∣ ∑ k P @ k ⋅ rel k \text{AP}=\dfrac{1}{|R_u|}\sum_k P@k\cdot\text{rel}_k AP = ∣ R u ​ ∣ 1 ​ ∑ k ​ P @ k ⋅ rel k ​ Binary relevance, all relevant items matter NDCG@K DCG@K IDCG@K \dfrac{\text{DCG@K}}{\text{IDCG@K}} IDCG@K DCG@K ​ , with DCG@K = ∑ k = 1 K 2 rel k − 1 log ⁡ 2 ( k + 1 ) \text{DCG@K}=\sum_{k=1}^K \dfrac{2^{\text{rel}_k}-1}{\log_2(k+1)} DCG@K = ∑ k = 1 K ​ lo g 2 ​ ( k + 1 ) 2 rel k ​ − 1 ​ Graded relevance and position-discounted gain AUC / log loss Pointwise discrimination / calibration Ranker heads; see ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC Interpreting them: MRR focuses on the first hit only; MAP rewards placing all relevant items early; NDCG handles graded labels and the logarithmic discount; recall@K is rank-insensitive within the top K K K . See Precision Recall for the underlying tradeoff. Evaluation pitfalls Random splits leak the future: use time-based splits (train on the past, test on later interactions), since random splitting lets the model see a user s later behavior when predicting earlier behavior. Evaluating against logged clicks measures agreement with the old policy, not true relevance. Sampled metrics (ranking the positive against a few hundred random negatives instead of the whole catalog) can order models differently from full-catalog metrics. Also check per-segment performance (new users, tail items) because an average can hide regressions. # Online evaluation Offline metrics are proxies. The decision metric comes from A/B tests (or interleaving for faster sensitivity in ranking comparisons) on engagement and retention, with guardrails such as latency, negative feedback rate, creator-side health and diversity. Offline-online gaps arise from feedback loops, position bias in logged labels, novelty effects, and objectives that the offline metric does not capture. Long-term effects (retention, satisfaction) often need holdouts running for weeks. # Diversity, Fairness and Feedback Loops Diversity and novelty. Ranking by predicted relevance alone tends to produce near-duplicate lists. Re-ranking methods trade relevance against redundancy: Maximal Marginal Relevance picks the next item maximizing λ rel ( i ) − ( 1 − λ ) max ⁡ j ∈ S sim ( i , j ) \lambda\,\text{rel}(i) - (1-\lambda)\max_{j\in S}\text{sim}(i,j) λ rel ( i ) − ( 1 − λ ) max j ∈ S ​ sim ( i , j ) ; determinantal point processes model set-level diversity; simple rules cap items per creator or category. Diversity is measured by intra-list distance, coverage, or category entropy, and it is justified by user value (variety, satisfaction) rather than assumed free. Fairness. Several stakeholders exist: users (quality across groups), item providers (exposure), and the platform. Provider-side fairness often targets exposure proportional to merit under some definition, which is a policy choice with trade-offs, not a single formula. Common tools: auditing metrics per group, constrained re-ranking for exposure, reducing popularity bias, and avoiding proxies for protected attributes in features. The correct definition depends on the product and legal context. Feedback loops. The model s recommendations determine what users see, which determines the next training data, which updates the model. Effects include popularity concentration, filter bubbles, and drift toward what is easy to engage with. Mitigations: logged propensities and exploration, counterfactual or off-policy corrections, holdout traffic served by a randomized or older policy for unbiased evaluation, diversity constraints, and monitoring distribution shift in exposure and in item and user cohorts. # One-Page Summary Topic Key facts Data Sparse and implicit; missing means unknown, not negative; logged under a prior policy CF Neighborhood methods are simple; MF learns embeddings via SGD or ALS; r ^ = μ + b u + b i + p u ⊤ q i \hat r = \mu + b_u + b_i + p_u^\top q_i r ^ = μ + b u ​ + b i ​ + p u ⊤ ​ q i ​ Implicit MF Confidence-weighted squared loss over all pairs (ALS) or BPR with sampled negatives Two-tower Independent user/item encoders, dot product, offline item index plus ANN; no cross-features Negatives Random (easy), in-batch (free, popularity-biased), hard (sharp, false-negative risk) logQ Subtract log ⁡ q j \log q_j lo g q j ​ from in-batch logits to correct popularity-proportional sampling; serve uncorrected scores Ranking losses Pointwise (calibrated), pairwise (BPR, RankNet), listwise (ListNet, LambdaRank for NDCG) Multi-task Shared-bottom vs MMoE vs separate; combine head outputs with product-tuned weights; heavy penalty for negative feedback Cold start Content features, ID dropout, exploration quota, onboarding signals Biases Position (tower or IPS), selection/exposure, popularity; log propensities Metrics Recall@K for retrieval; NDCG for graded ranking; MAP for binary all-relevant; MRR for first hit; time-based splits Online A/B with guardrails and holdouts; interleaving for sensitivity Beyond accuracy Diversity via MMR/DPP/caps; fairness is a stated policy; manage feedback loops with exploration and holdouts # Related ML System Design Framework ML System Design Interview Prep Bandits Reinforcement Learning Basics Precision Recall ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC Cross-Entropy Loss MOC - System Design

title: Time Series
text: Forecasting and why time breaks the i.i.d. assumption. # Chapters Time Series Stationarity # See also (from other areas) Cross-Validation — time-series split, never shuffle (Evaluation) # If asked to forecast Check stationarity (and difference if needed), read ACF/PACF for order, baseline with ARIMA/ETS before ML, and validate with a forward-chaining split so you never train on the future.

title: Time Series Stationarity
heads: The four components of a series
ACF and PACF — reading the order of a model
text: Time-series forecasting — the one corner of ML where the i.i.d. assumption is dead on arrival: order is the signal, and the past leaks into the future. After this chapter You can say why time series breaks ordinary ML; decompose a series and test it for stationarity; read ACF/PACF to pick model orders; write down the AR, MA, ARIMA, and exponential-smoothing equations; choose between classical and ML approaches; and validate with the right backtest and metric. # Why time series is different In standard supervised learning the examples are exchangeable — shuffle the rows and nothing changes. A time series is the opposite: each observation y t y_t y t ​ is indexed by time, and order is the signal . Observations are autocorrelated ( y t y_t y t ​ depends on its own past), so you can never shuffle or do random train/test splits — doing so trains on the future to predict the past, the most fatal leak in forecasting. And the process itself often changes over time, so the distribution is moving. The mindset: a forecast is a conditional expectation y ^ t + h = E [ y t + h ∣ information up to t ] \hat{y}_{t+h} = \mathbb{E}[y_{t+h} \mid \text{information up to } t] y ^ ​ t + h ​ = E [ y t + h ​ ∣ information up to t ] . # The four components of a series The classical lens decomposes a series into four parts; most models target one explicitly. Additive decomposition: the observed series is the sum of trend, seasonal, and residual parts. Component What it is Example Trend ( T T T ) Long-run direction A product s user base growing over years Seasonality ( S S S ) Fixed, known-period cycle Retail spiking every December; traffic by hour Cyclical ( C C C ) Long swings, no fixed period Business cycles — harder to model Residual ( R R R ) What s left after structure Irregular, ideally unpredictable The distinction interviewers like: seasonality has a fixed period (12 months, 7 days) while a cycle does not — that s why seasonality is easy to encode and cycles are not. # Additive vs multiplicative How the components combine is a modeling choice. The additive model assumes they add: y t = T t + S t + R t y_t = T_t + S_t + R_t y t ​ = T t ​ + S t ​ + R t ​ Use it when the seasonal swing is a roughly constant size regardless of level. The multiplicative model assumes they multiply: y t = T t × S t × R t y_t = T_t \times S_t \times R_t y t ​ = T t ​ × S t ​ × R t ​ Use it when the swing scales with the level (December is always +30%). A key trick: logs turn multiplicative into additive, since log ⁡ ( T ⋅ S ⋅ R ) = log ⁡ T + log ⁡ S + log ⁡ R \log(T\cdot S\cdot R) = \log T + \log S + \log R lo g ( T ⋅ S ⋅ R ) = lo g T + lo g S + lo g R — which is why log-transforming is the standard first move when variance grows with the level. # Stationarity Most classical models assume the series is stationary : statistical properties don t change over time. Weak (covariance) stationarity requires a constant mean, constant variance, and an autocovariance Cov ⁡ ( y t , y t + k ) \operatorname{Cov}(y_t, y_{t+k}) Cov ( y t ​ , y t + k ​ ) that depends only on the lag k k k , not absolute time. A stationary series has stable structure, so a fixed set of coefficients can capture it. Differencing turns a trending (non-stationary) series into one with a stable mean. The usual fix is differencing — model the change, ∇ y t = y t − y t − 1 \nabla y_t = y_t - y_{t-1} ∇ y t ​ = y t ​ − y t − 1 ​ — which removes a linear trend; seasonal differencing y t − y t − m y_t - y_{t-m} y t ​ − y t − m ​ removes a season of length m m m . The number of differences needed is the d d d in ARIMA. Confirm with a unit-root test (Augmented Dickey–Fuller), whose null is non-stationary ; a small p-value means you can treat it as stationary. Use the minimum d d d — over-differencing injects artificial autocorrelation. # ACF and PACF — reading the order of a model Two plots tell you which classical model to use. The ACF at lag k k k is the correlation between y t y_t y t ​ and y t − k y_{t-k} y t − k ​ , including indirect effects through intermediate lags. The PACF at lag k k k is the same correlation after removing all shorter lags — the direct effect only. AR(2) signature: the PACF cuts off at the AR order while the ACF decays. MA is the mirror image. Plot pattern Implies PACF cuts off after lag p p p ; ACF tails off AR( p p p ) — read p p p from the PACF ACF cuts off after lag q q q ; PACF tails off MA( q q q ) — read q q q from the ACF Both tail off gradually ARMA( p , q p, q p , q ) — pick via AIC/BIC # Classical models: the ARIMA family ARIMA is built from two atoms. An autoregressive AR( p p p ) model says today is a linear function of its own recent past plus noise: y t = c + ϕ 1 y t − 1 + ϕ 2 y t − 2 + ⋯ + ϕ p y t − p + ε t y_t = c + \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \phi_2 y_{t-2} + \dots + \phi_p y_{t-p} + \varepsilon_t y t ​ = c + ϕ 1 ​ y t − 1 ​ + ϕ 2 ​ y t − 2 ​ + ⋯ + ϕ p ​ y t − p ​ + ε t ​ A moving-average MA( q q q ) model says today is a function of recent shocks (past forecast errors): y t = μ + ε t + θ 1 ε t − 1 + θ 2 ε t − 2 + ⋯ + θ q ε t − q y_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t + \theta_1 \varepsilon_{t-1} + \theta_2 \varepsilon_{t-2} + \dots + \theta_q \varepsilon_{t-q} y t ​ = μ + ε t ​ + θ 1 ​ ε t − 1 ​ + θ 2 ​ ε t − 2 ​ + ⋯ + θ q ​ ε t − q ​ Combine them for ARMA( p , q p, q p , q ) ; apply it to a series differenced d d d times and you get ARIMA( p , d , q p, d, q p , d , q ) — difference until stationary, then explain it with p p p autoregressive and q q q moving-average terms. SARIMA adds a seasonal set of terms at lag m m m ; ARIMAX/SARIMAX add exogenous regressors (promotions, holidays, price). Orders come from ACF/PACF plus minimizing AIC/BIC; auto_arima automates the search. Interview cue Difference between AR and MA? AR regresses on past observed values; MA regresses on past errors/shocks. AR has long memory (a shock propagates through the recursion); a pure MA( q q q ) remembers exactly q q q steps. # Exponential smoothing (ETS) The other classical family forecasts with a weighted average of past observations whose weights decay exponentially — recent data matters most. Simple Exponential Smoothing (SES) tracks just the level: ℓ t = α y t + ( 1 − α ) ℓ t − 1 , y ^ t + h = ℓ t \ell_t = \alpha\, y_t + (1 - \alpha)\,\ell_{t-1}, \qquad \hat{y}_{t+h} = \ell_t ℓ t ​ = α y t ​ + ( 1 − α ) ℓ t − 1 ​ , y ^ ​ t + h ​ = ℓ t ​ α ∈ ( 0 , 1 ] \alpha \in (0,1] α ∈ ( 0 , 1 ] sets how fast old data is forgotten. SES has no trend or seasonality, so it forecasts a flat line. Holt adds a trend equation (sloped forecast); Holt–Winters adds a seasonal one. Modern libraries frame these as the ETS (Error, Trend, Seasonal) state-space family with likelihood fitting and prediction intervals. Useful fact: SES ≡ \equiv ≡ ARIMA(0,1,1) and Holt ≡ \equiv ≡ ARIMA(0,2,2) — two languages for an overlapping set of processes. Model Captures Forecast shape SES Level only Flat Holt Level + trend Sloped line Holt–Winters Level + trend + seasonality Sloped line with repeating season # Modern / ML approaches With many related series, long histories, rich covariates, or nonlinearities, ML methods take over. Approach Idea Shines when Lags + gradient boosting Engineer lag/rolling/calendar features, fit XGBoost/LightGBM Tabular forecasting with strong covariates Prophet Trend + Fourier seasonality + holidays, fit Bayesian Business series, holidays, gaps; interpretable DeepAR Autoregressive RNN across many series, outputs a distribution Thousands of related series; needs uncertainty N-BEATS / N-HiTS Deep fully-connected basis expansion, no recurrence Strong pure-DL univariate accuracy Temporal Fusion Transformer Attention over mixed covariates; quantiles Multi-horizon with mixed covariate types Two ideas matter more than any architecture. The shift from local models (one ARIMA per series) to global models (one network across all series) lets a sparse series borrow strength from similar ones — a main reason global models (e.g. LightGBM in M5, the ES-RNN hybrid in M4) won recent M-competitions. And probabilistic forecasting — outputting quantiles or a full distribution — matters because inventory and staffing decisions live in the tails. Note that well-tuned classical models and gradient boosting remain hard to beat on a single short series; deep learning earns its keep at scale. # Validation done right You cannot use random K-fold — it leaks the future. The correct procedure respects time: train up to time t t t , forecast the next h h h steps, score, then roll the cutoff forward and repeat. Time-series cross-validation: train on the past, test on the next block, roll forward. An expanding window keeps all history; a sliding window keeps a fixed recent window (better under drift). Three details separate a correct backtest from a broken one: forecast at the same horizon h h h you care about in production; insert a gap if features look ahead; and build every feature from information available at prediction time. Always compare against a naive baseline ( tomorrow = today, this December = last December ) — a model that can t beat the last value isn t worth shipping. # Forecasting metrics Metric Idea Watch out for MAE mean ∣ y − y ^ ∣ \text{mean}\,\lvert y - \hat{y}\rvert mean ∣ y − y ^ ​ ∣ Robust; same units; linear in error RMSE mean ( y − y ^ ) 2 \sqrt{\text{mean}\,(y - \hat{y})^2} mean ( y − y ^ ​ ) 2 ​ Penalizes big misses; outlier-sensitive MAPE mean ∣ y − y ^ ∣ / ∣ y ∣ \text{mean}\,\lvert y - \hat{y}\rvert / \lvert y\rvert mean ∣ y − y ^ ​ ∣ / ∣ y ∣ Explodes near zero; asymmetric MASE MAE ÷ naive model’s MAE \text{MAE} \div \text{naive model s MAE} MAE ÷ naive model’s MAE Cleanest: 1 1 1 beats naive; scale-free WAPE ∑ ∣ y − y ^ ∣ / ∑ ∣ y ∣ \sum\lvert y - \hat{y}\rvert / \sum\lvert y\rvert ∑ ∣ y − y ^ ​ ∣ / ∑ ∣ y ∣ Volume-weighted; popular in retail Pinball loss asymmetric per-quantile loss For probabilistic forecasts; pair with coverage Choose by the decision: RMSE when big misses are costly, MAE/WAPE when cost is linear, MASE for scale-free comparison across series, and pinball loss + coverage for distributions. Avoid MAPE for series that approach zero. Interview cue Why not MAPE? Undefined at zero, blows up for small actuals, and asymmetric — so it quietly rewards under-forecasting. Reach for MASE (scale-free, naive-anchored) or WAPE. # One-page summary Topic The one thing to remember Why it s different Order is the signal; data is autocorrelated; never shuffle or random-split. Components Trend + seasonality (fixed period) + cycle (no fixed period) + noise (in practice the cycle is folded into trend or residual). Additive vs multiplicative Constant swing → additive; swing scales with level → multiplicative (log makes it additive). Stationarity Constant mean/variance/autocovariance. Difference to remove trend; ADF to confirm; minimum d d d . ACF / PACF PACF cuts at p p p → AR( p p p ); ACF cuts at q q q → MA( q q q ); both tail → ARMA. ARIMA family AR = past values; MA = past errors; I = differencing. SARIMA adds seasonality; X adds covariates. Exponential smoothing Exponentially decaying weights. SES (level) → Holt (+trend) → Holt–Winters (+season). Modern ML Lags + boosting; Prophet; DeepAR/TFT/N-BEATS. Global local at scale; forecast distributions. Validation Rolling/expanding backtest at the production horizon; beat a naive baseline. Metrics RMSE (big misses), MAE/WAPE (linear), MASE (scale-free), pinball+coverage (probabilistic). Avoid MAPE near zero. # Related Cross-Validation

title: Anomaly Detection
heads: Drift, concept change, and feedback loops
text:
Finding the rare, the unusual, and the broken, usually with few or no labels. An anomaly is an observation that deviates from what the data-generating process normally produces. Practical uses include fraud, equipment faults, intrusion, data-quality problems, and rare disease signals. Three features make the problem hard and interview-worthy: anomalies are rare (extreme class imbalance), they are heterogeneous (there is no single anomalous distribution to learn), and labels are scarce and biased. Most of the craft is in framing the problem and in evaluating honestly, not in the choice of algorithm. What you ll be able to say after this chapter Distinguish outlier detection from novelty detection, and supervised from unsupervised framings. Explain the statistical, distance, density (LOF), isolation, one-class SVM, and reconstruction approaches, with the condition under which each fails. Derive the Isolation Forest score and say why short paths mean anomalous. Evaluate a detector with scarce labels using PR-AUC and precision@k, and set a threshold from an alert budget. Describe how drift and feedback loops degrade detectors in production. # Outlier detection versus novelty detection Outlier detection Novelty detection Training data Contains a (usually small) unknown fraction of anomalies Assumed clean: only normal examples Goal Flag the abnormal points in the dataset itself Decide whether a new point is unlike the training data Typical fit Robust methods (isolation forest, LOF, robust covariance) One-class models trained on normal-only data Risk Anomalies distort the model of normal Clean data is rarely clean; contamination biases the boundary # Supervised, semi-supervised, unsupervised Framing Labels needed Works when Weakness Supervised (a classifier on labeled anomaly vs normal) Many labeled anomalies Anomaly types are known, stable, and well represented Misses novel types; labels lag behind new attacks or faults Semi-supervised (model normal, perhaps tune with a few labels) Normal examples; a few anomalies for tuning Normal behavior is well sampled Needs clean-ish data Unsupervised (score everything; no labels) None Anomalies are rare and differ from the bulk Hard to evaluate; the notion of unusual is a modeling choice A pragmatic rule: with enough labeled examples of the failure types you care about, a supervised classifier (gradient boosting with class weights or resampling; see Decision Trees and Gradient Boosting ) usually outperforms unsupervised scores on those known types. Unsupervised scores are most valuable for unknown unknowns , as a feature into the supervised model, and for bootstrapping labels. Hybrid systems commonly use both: a supervised model for known patterns and an unsupervised detector as a safety net, whose top alerts feed review and then become new labels. Interview angle Start by asking: what is an anomaly here, what does a miss cost versus a false alarm, how many alerts can people review per day, and are there any labels (and how were they obtained)? These answers choose the framing, the metric, and the threshold before any algorithm is mentioned. # Statistical methods Parametric univariate. Under approximate normality, flag ∣ z ∣ = ∣ x − x ˉ ∣ / s |z|=|x- ar x|/s ∣ z ∣ = ∣ x − x ˉ ∣/ s above a cutoff (3 is a common convention, not a law). The mean and standard deviation are themselves distorted by the outliers they are meant to detect (the masking effect), so robust versions are preferable: the modified z-score M = 0.6745 ( x − median ) / MAD M=0.6745\,(x-	ext{median})/	ext{MAD} M = 0.6745 ( x − median ) / MAD (with MAD = median ∣ x − median ∣ 	ext{MAD}=	ext{median}|x-	ext{median}| MAD = median ∣ x − median ∣ ; a cutoff of about 3.5 is a common rule of thumb), or the IQR fences [ Q 1 − 1.5 IQR , Q 3 + 1.5 IQR ] [Q_1-1.5\,	ext{IQR},\,Q_3+1.5\,	ext{IQR}] [ Q 1 ​ − 1.5 IQR , Q 3 ​ + 1.5 IQR ] . These assume roughly unimodal data and are one-dimensional. Multivariate Mahalanobis distance. d M 2 ( x ) = ( x − μ ) T Σ − 1 ( x − μ ) . d_M^2(x)=(x-\mu)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu). d M 2 ​ ( x ) = ( x − μ ) T Σ − 1 ( x − μ ) . If x ∼ N p ( μ , Σ ) x\sim\mathcal{N}_p(\mu,\Sigma) x ∼ N p ​ ( μ , Σ ) , then d M 2 ∼ χ p 2 d_M^2\sim\chi^2_p d M 2 ​ ∼ χ p 2 ​ , which gives a principled threshold (for example the 99.9th percentile of χ p 2 \chi^2_p χ p 2 ​ ). Mahalanobis accounts for correlations: a point can be unremarkable on each feature and still be anomalous because it violates the correlation structure. Conditions and cautions: it assumes an elliptical, roughly Gaussian bulk; estimating μ , Σ \mu,\Sigma μ , Σ from contaminated data inflates Σ \Sigma Σ and masks outliers, so use a robust estimator such as the minimum covariance determinant (MCD) ; Σ \Sigma Σ must be invertible and well conditioned (shrinkage or PCA first when p p p is large relative to n n n ). Density models. Fit a density p ^ ( x ) \hat p(x) p ^ ​ ( x ) (a GMM, kernel density estimate, or normalizing flow) and flag low p ^ ( x ) \hat p(x) p ^ ​ ( x ) . The framing is principled, but density estimation in high dimensions is hard, and low density is not always anomalous in a useful sense (a high-dimensional Gaussian puts most of its mass away from the mode). Time series. For temporal data, remove trend and seasonality first (otherwise every Monday morning is anomalous ), then score residuals; see Time Series Stationarity . Contextual anomalies, where a value is normal in one context and abnormal in another (a high load at 3 a.m.), need context in the model. # Distance-based methods k-nearest-neighbor score. Score each point by its distance to its k k k -th nearest neighbor (or the mean distance to its k k k nearest neighbors). Isolated points have large scores. It is simple and nonparametric, but costs O ( n 2 ) O(n^2) O ( n 2 ) naively (indexes help in low dimensions), needs scaled features, degrades in high dimensions as distances concentrate, and uses one global notion of far , which is a problem when normal regions differ in density. That last limitation motivates LOF. # Density-based: Local Outlier Factor (LOF) LOF compares a point s local density with the densities of its neighbors, so it can flag a point that is unusual relative to its own neighborhood even when it would be unremarkable in a sparser region elsewhere. For a point a a a , let k -dist ( b ) k	ext{-dist}(b) k -dist ( b ) be the distance from b b b to its k k k -th neighbor and N k ( a ) N_k(a) N k ​ ( a ) its k k k -neighborhood. Reachability distance: reach-dist k ( a , b ) = max ⁡ { k -dist ( b ) , d ( a , b ) } 	ext{reach-dist}_k(a,b)=\max\{k	ext{-dist}(b),\,d(a,b)\} reach-dist k ​ ( a , b ) = max { k -dist ( b ) , d ( a , b )} . This smooths statistical fluctuation by flooring the distance at the neighbor s own scale. Local reachability density: lrd k ( a ) = ( 1 ∣ N k ( a ) ∣ ∑ b ∈ N k ( a ) reach-dist k ( a , b ) ) − 1 	ext{lrd}_k(a)=\Big( rac{1}{|N_k(a)|}\sum_{b\in N_k(a)}	ext{reach-dist}_k(a,b)\Big)^{-1} lrd k ​ ( a ) = ( ∣ N k ​ ( a ) ∣ 1 ​ ∑ b ∈ N k ​ ( a ) ​ reach-dist k ​ ( a , b ) ) − 1 . Score: LOF k ( a ) = 1 ∣ N k ( a ) ∣ ∑ b ∈ N k ( a ) lrd k ( b ) lrd k ( a ) . 	ext{LOF}_k(a)= rac{1}{|N_k(a)|}\sum_{b\in N_k(a)} rac{	ext{lrd}_k(b)}{	ext{lrd}_k(a)} . LOF k ​ ( a ) = ∣ N k ​ ( a ) ∣ 1 ​ b ∈ N k ​ ( a ) ∑ ​ lrd k ​ ( a ) lrd k ​ ( b ) ​ . Interpretation: LOF ≈ 1 	ext{LOF}\approx1 LOF ≈ 1 means a a a is about as dense as its neighbors; LOF ≫ 1 	ext{LOF}\gg1 LOF ≫ 1 means a a a sits in a region much sparser than the points around it. Choosing k k k matters: too small is noisy, too large blurs local structure (a common heuristic is to try a range and aggregate). Like other distance methods it needs scaling and suffers in high dimensions, and the score has no absolute scale across datasets. In the novelty-detection setting, fit on normal data and score new points. # Isolation Forest Idea. Anomalies are few and different , so they are easier to isolate with random cuts. Build many random trees: at each node, pick a feature at random and a split value uniformly between that feature s min and max within the node s data; recurse until a point is alone (or a depth limit is reached). Anomalies end up isolated after fewer splits; normal points in dense regions need many. Score. Let h ( x ) h(x) h ( x ) be the path length (number of edges) to isolate x x x in one tree and E [ h ( x ) ] E[h(x)] E [ h ( x )] its average over the forest. Normalize by the average path length of an unsuccessful search in a binary search tree on ψ \psi ψ points: c ( ψ ) = 2 H ( ψ − 1 ) − 2 ( ψ − 1 ) ψ , H ( i ) ≈ ln ⁡ i + 0.5772 ( Euler’s constant ) , c(\psi)=2H(\psi-1)- rac{2(\psi-1)}{\psi},\qquad H(i)\approx\ln i+0.5772\ (	ext{Euler s constant}), c ( ψ ) = 2 H ( ψ − 1 ) − ψ 2 ( ψ − 1 ) ​ , H ( i ) ≈ ln i + 0.5772 ( Euler’s constant ) , s ( x , ψ ) = 2 − E [ h ( x ) ] / c ( ψ ) . s(x,\psi)=2^{-E[h(x)]/c(\psi)} . s ( x , ψ ) = 2 − E [ h ( x )] / c ( ψ ) . Reading s s s : E [ h ] → 0 E[h]	o0 E [ h ] → 0 gives s → 1 s	o1 s → 1 (anomalous); E [ h ] = c ( ψ ) E[h]=c(\psi) E [ h ] = c ( ψ ) gives s = 0.5 s=0.5 s = 0.5 (typical); E [ h ] ≫ c ( ψ ) E[h]\gg c(\psi) E [ h ] ≫ c ( ψ ) gives s → 0 s	o0 s → 0 (clearly normal). If all points score close to 0.5 0.5 0.5 , the data contain no distinct anomalies. Why it scales. Each tree is built on a small subsample (the original paper uses ψ = 256 \psi=256 ψ = 256 and about 100 trees), with trees capped at depth about ⌈ log ⁡ 2 ψ ⌉ \lceil\log_2\psiceil ⌈ lo g 2 ​ ψ ⌉ . Subsampling reduces swamping (normal points near anomalies being mislabeled) and masking (clusters of anomalies hiding one another) and makes training roughly linear in n n n with low memory. No distance computation is needed. Limits. Splits are axis-parallel, so anomalies that are unusual only through a combination of correlated features along a diagonal may get artifacts in score maps (the Extended Isolation Forest uses random hyperplanes to address this). Irrelevant features dilute the random splits; remove noise features or use feature selection. Local anomalies hidden inside dense regions of another cluster can be missed, since isolation is global rather than relative to local density (LOF handles this better). The contamination parameter only sets the threshold (a quantile of scores), not the model; if it is wrong, the cutoff is wrong. Categorical features need encoding, and the encoding affects splits. # One-class SVM A one-class SVM learns a boundary around normal data in a kernel feature space. In the ν 
u ν -formulation (Schölkopf et al.) it separates the data from the origin with maximum margin: min ⁡ w , ρ , ξ 1 2 ∥ w ∥ 2 + 1 ν n ∑ i ξ i − ρ s.t. w ⋅ ϕ ( x i ) ≥ ρ − ξ i , ξ i ≥ 0 , \min_{w,ho,\xi}\ 	frac12\lVert wVert^2+ rac{1}{
u n}\sum_i\xi_i-ho\quad	ext{s.t.}\ \ w\cdot\phi(x_i)\geho-\xi_i,\ \xi_i\ge0, w , ρ , ξ min ​ 2 1 ​ ∥ w ∥ 2 + ν n 1 ​ i ∑ ​ ξ i ​ − ρ s.t. w ⋅ ϕ ( x i ​ ) ≥ ρ − ξ i ​ , ξ i ​ ≥ 0 , and the decision function is f ( x ) = sign ( w ⋅ ϕ ( x ) − ρ ) f(x)=	ext{sign}(w\cdot\phi(x)-ho) f ( x ) = sign ( w ⋅ ϕ ( x ) − ρ ) . The parameter ν ∈ ( 0 , 1 ] 
u\in(0,1] ν ∈ ( 0 , 1 ] is an upper bound on the fraction of training points treated as outliers and a lower bound on the fraction of support vectors, which makes it interpretable.
