With an RBF kernel the boundary can wrap flexible shapes. Conditions and cautions: training is roughly between quadratic and cubic in n n n , which limits it to moderate datasets; results are sensitive to the kernel width γ \gamma γ and to feature scaling; it assumes mostly normal training data (it is a novelty-detection tool) and degrades when contaminated; and it offers little guidance for high-dimensional or heterogeneous data. See Support Vector Machines for the margin and kernel background. # Reconstruction-based: autoencoders and PCA Train a model to reconstruct normal data through a bottleneck; at test time, large reconstruction error ∥ x − x ^ ∥ \lVert x-\hat xVert ∥ x − x ^ ∥ suggests that x x x does not follow the learned structure. PCA reconstruction error (distance to the principal subspace) is the linear baseline and often competitive; see Eigenvectors, PCA and SVD . An autoencoder generalizes this to nonlinear manifolds (see Clustering Dimensionality Reduction ). Conditions and cautions: The premise is that the model reconstructs normal data well and anomalies poorly. An over-capacity autoencoder can learn an approximate identity and reconstruct anomalies too, especially if the training data are contaminated. Control capacity, use denoising or regularization, and monitor reconstruction on a validation set. Error is dominated by feature scale and by inherently noisy features; scale inputs and consider per-feature normalization of the error. Reconstruction error can be small for anomalies that lie close to the learned manifold (an anomaly that is simple ) and large for normal but hard examples; it measures complexity as well as abnormality. Variants: VAEs (use the ELBO or reconstruction probability), sequence autoencoders for time series, and forecasting-residual models. # Choosing a method Method Core signal Good when Fails when Z-score / MAD / IQR Distance from center One variable, unimodal Multimodal, multivariate structure Mahalanobis (robust) Distance under covariance Roughly elliptical bulk, correlated features Non-Gaussian bulk, p ≫ n p\gg n p ≫ n without shrinkage kNN distance Isolation in space Moderate d d d , homogeneous density Varying density, high d d d LOF Local density ratio Regions of different density High d d d , poor k k k , large n n n Isolation forest Ease of random isolation Large n n n , mixed scales, global anomalies Diagonal structure, many noise features, local anomalies One-class SVM Kernel boundary of normal Small/moderate clean data Large n n n , contaminated data, untuned γ \gamma γ Autoencoder / PCA residual Reconstruction error High-dimensional structured data (images, sensors) Over-capacity net, anomalies near the manifold Supervised classifier Learned decision boundary Plenty of labeled anomalies, stable types Novel anomaly types An effective baseline order for tabular data: robust statistical rules for sanity, isolation forest as the first multivariate detector, LOF or a robust Mahalanobis check as a complement, and a supervised model once labels accrue. # Why accuracy and ROC-AUC mislead If 0.1 % 0.1\% 0.1% of points are anomalous, predicting normal gets 99.9 % 99.9\% 99.9% accuracy. ROC-AUC uses the false positive rate , whose denominator is the huge number of negatives, so a detector can show a high ROC-AUC while most of its alerts are false (see ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC ). Precision is what the reviewing human experiences. Metric Use Note PR-AUC (average precision) Threshold-free ranking quality with rare positives Baseline equals the prevalence, so compare against it, not against 0.5 0.5 0.5 Precision@k , recall@k Quality of the top k k k alerts, where k k k is the review budget Directly maps to operations; depends on k k k Recall at fixed precision (or precision at fixed recall) Business operating point Needs enough labels to estimate stably Cost-weighted loss c F N ⋅ F N + c F P ⋅ F P c_{FN}\cdot FN+c_{FP}\cdot FP c F N ​ ⋅ F N + c F P ​ ⋅ F P Costs must be estimated; see Precision Recall Alert rate / time to detect Operational health For streaming systems, include detection delay # Label problems Selection bias. If only flagged cases are investigated, the labeled set reflects what the current system flags; anomalies the system misses are labeled normal or never labeled. Estimates of recall are therefore optimistic. Mitigations: audit a random sample of unflagged cases, and keep a small randomized exploration channel. Label noise and delay. Fraud labels can arrive weeks late; normal is often just not yet reported . Evaluate on data old enough to be labeled, and expect recent performance to be underestimated. Synthetic anomalies. Injecting artificial outliers is useful for smoke tests but measures how well the detector finds the type you injected ; the number is not a forecast of real performance. Few positives mean wide uncertainty. With tens of positives, PR-AUC and precision@k have large variance; report bootstrap intervals and avoid over-tuning on them. Time-aware splits. Validate with forward-chaining splits, since anomalies and normal behavior shift over time (see Cross-Validation ). When no labels exist, use proxies: manual review of the top- k k k with a rubric, stability of the top set across seeds and subsamples, agreement among detectors, and sensitivity to injected known anomalies. # Thresholding An anomaly score is a ranking; an action needs a threshold. Options: Approach How Condition and caveat Alert budget Flag the top q q q percent or top k k k per day Fits human review capacity; ignores whether the day is truly more anomalous Contamination quantile Choose the cutoff at the expected anomaly fraction Depends on a prevalence estimate that is usually uncertain Statistical χ 2 \chi^2 χ 2 quantile for Mahalanobis; ± 3 \pm3 ± 3 MAD-based Valid only if distributional assumptions hold Extreme value theory Fit a generalized Pareto distribution to the score tail (peaks-over-threshold) to set a tail-probability cutoff Needs enough tail data; assumes tail stationarity Cost-based Pick the threshold minimizing expected cost on validation data Needs labels and cost estimates Segmented thresholds Separate thresholds per segment (device type, region, hour) Prevents a heterogeneous population from being dominated by its noisiest segment; needs enough data per segment Consider two-stage designs: a cheap detector with a loose threshold produces candidates, and a stronger model or human review makes the final call. Always report how threshold choice changes alert volume, because that is what determines whether the system is usable. # Drift, concept change, and feedback loops Normal changes. Seasonality, product launches, and infrastructure changes shift the baseline; a detector trained on old data flags the new normal en masse (a false-alarm flood) or, if it adapts silently, absorbs a genuine fault into normal . Use rolling or recent training windows, seasonality-aware features, and scheduled retraining; compare adaptation speed with the speed of the faults you must catch. Monitor the detector itself. Track the score distribution, alert rate, and input feature distributions; a sudden shift in alert rate is a drift signal as often as an incident signal. Pair the detector with data-quality checks so that a broken upstream feed is not mistaken for an anomaly (or vice versa). Adversarial adaptation. In fraud and security, actors react to detection; the anomaly distribution is non-stationary by design, and a fixed model decays. Rotate features, keep unsupervised coverage, and refresh labels quickly. Feedback loops. Acting on alerts changes the data (blocked transactions never get completed, so they never get confirmed labels). Keep a holdout of un-actioned cases where safe, and treat the labeled set as biased. Concept versus covariate shift. If p ( x ) p(x) p ( x ) shifts but the notion of anomalous stays the same, recalibrate thresholds; if the notion itself changes, labels and the objective need revisiting. Distinguish them before retraining blindly. Interview angle The strongest answers on this topic spend as much time on evaluation, thresholds, and monitoring as on algorithms. A good summary: pick the metric from the review budget (precision@k and PR-AUC against the prevalence baseline), audit a random slice of unflagged cases to estimate recall, and monitor alert rate and score drift after launch. Common pitfalls Tuning hyperparameters (like the contamination fraction) on the same few labeled anomalies used to report performance; reporting ROC-AUC alone on a heavily imbalanced set; training a novelty detector on data that was never checked for contamination; ignoring seasonality so that scheduled behavior triggers alarms. # One-Page Summary Concept Key point Outlier vs novelty Outlier: anomalies in the training data. Novelty: training data assumed clean; score new points. Supervised vs unsupervised Supervised wins for known, well-labeled types; unsupervised covers unknown types and bootstraps labels; hybrids are common. Z-score / MAD Mean and SD are corrupted by outliers (masking); use median and MAD or IQR fences. Mahalanobis d M 2 ∼ χ p 2 d_M^2\sim\chi_p^2 d M 2 ​ ∼ χ p 2 ​ under Gaussian; use robust covariance (MCD) for contaminated data. kNN distance Large distance to the k k k -th neighbor; global notion of far fails with varying density. LOF Ratio of neighbors local density to own density; ≈ 1 \approx1 ≈ 1 inlier, ≫ 1 \gg1 ≫ 1 outlier. Isolation forest Random splits isolate anomalies in short paths; s = 2 − E [ h ] / c ( ψ ) s=2^{-E[h]/c(\psi)} s = 2 − E [ h ] / c ( ψ ) ; subsample ψ ≈ 256 \psi\approx256 ψ ≈ 256 . One-class SVM Kernel boundary around normal data; ν 
u ν bounds outlier fraction; sensitive to γ \gamma γ ; moderate n n n . Reconstruction High error flags anomalies; PCA residual is the linear baseline; over-capacity nets can reconstruct anomalies. Metrics PR-AUC (baseline = prevalence), precision@k, recall at fixed precision; ROC-AUC is optimistic when negatives dominate. Label issues Selection bias, delayed labels, few positives; audit a random slice and use time-aware splits. Thresholds Alert budget, contamination quantile, EVT, cost-based, per-segment; two-stage designs. Production Drift changes normal; monitor score and alert rate; adversaries adapt; feedback loops bias labels. # Related Clustering Dimensionality Reduction Decision Trees and Gradient Boosting Support Vector Machines ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC Precision Recall Time Series Stationarity MOC - Unsupervised

title: Clustering & Dimensionality Reduction
heads: Setting the scene: what structure can mean
Dimensionality reduction for visualization: t-SNE and UMAP
What you may and may not read from the plot
text: Unsupervised learning: finding structure when there is no label to check against. Unsupervised methods answer questions of the form what is the shape of this data? rather than what is y y y ? . Two families dominate interviews: clustering (group similar points) and dimensionality reduction / embedding (represent points with fewer coordinates). Both share one uncomfortable property: there is no ground truth, so every method embeds an assumption about what structure means, and a good answer names that assumption and the condition under which it fails. What you ll be able to say after this chapter Write the k-means objective, explain why Lloyd s algorithm converges, and say why k-means++ helps. Derive the E and M steps of a Gaussian mixture model and state its exact relation to k-means. Pick between k-means, GMM, hierarchical, DBSCAN/HDBSCAN from the shape and density of the data. Evaluate a clustering without labels, and say what silhouette cannot tell you. Explain what t-SNE and UMAP preserve, and what you must not read off their plots. # Setting the scene: what structure can mean Notion of structure Method family Assumption it bakes in Compact, roughly spherical blobs k-means Euclidean distance to a centroid defines membership Overlapping ellipsoidal blobs Gaussian mixture Data are generated from a mixture of Gaussians Nested groups at several scales Hierarchical A tree of merges is meaningful Dense regions separated by sparse ones DBSCAN / HDBSCAN Clusters are connected high-density regions Low-dimensional manifold PCA, t-SNE, UMAP, autoencoder Data lie near a lower-dimensional surface Two preprocessing facts apply to nearly everything below. First, almost all of these methods use a distance, so feature scaling changes the answer ; standardize (or choose a deliberate weighting) before clustering. Second, in high dimensions pairwise distances concentrate (the ratio of nearest to farthest distance tends toward 1 for many distributions), so distance-based clustering usually works better after reducing dimension, for example with PCA (see Eigenvectors, PCA and SVD ). # Objective Given n n n points x i ∈ R d x_i \in \mathbb{R}^d x i ​ ∈ R d and a chosen k k k , k-means seeks centroids μ 1 , … , μ k \mu_1,\dots,\mu_k μ 1 ​ , … , μ k ​ and assignments c ( i ) ∈ { 1 , … , k } c(i)\in\{1,\dots,k\} c ( i ) ∈ { 1 , … , k } minimizing the within-cluster sum of squares (also called inertia or distortion): J ( c , μ ) = ∑ i = 1 n ∥ x i − μ c ( i ) ∥ 2 . J(c,\mu) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lVert x_i - \mu_{c(i)} \rVert^2 . J ( c , μ ) = i = 1 ∑ n ​ ∥ x i ​ − μ c ( i ) ​ ∥ 2 . Finding the global minimum is NP-hard in general, so in practice a local-search heuristic is used. # Lloyd s algorithm Alternate two steps, each of which cannot increase J J J : Assignment. With centroids fixed, assign each point to its nearest centroid: c ( i ) = arg ⁡ min ⁡ k ∥ x i − μ k ∥ 2 c(i)=\arg\min_k \lVert x_i-\mu_k\rVert^2 c ( i ) = ar g min k ​ ∥ x i ​ − μ k ​ ∥ 2 . This minimizes J J J over c c c for fixed μ \mu μ . Update. With assignments fixed, set each centroid to the mean of its points: μ k = 1 ∣ C k ∣ ∑ i ∈ C k x i \mu_k = \frac{1}{|C_k|}\sum_{i\in C_k} x_i μ k ​ = ∣ C k ​ ∣ 1 ​ ∑ i ∈ C k ​ ​ x i ​ . The mean is the minimizer of the sum of squared distances to a set of points, so this minimizes J J J over μ \mu μ for fixed c c c . This is coordinate descent on J J J . Because J J J is bounded below by zero and never increases, and there are finitely many partitions, the algorithm terminates at a local minimum (or fixed point). Each iteration costs O ( n k d ) O(nkd) O ( nk d ) . Different initializations can give different local minima, so the standard practice is several restarts and keeping the lowest J J J . # Initialization: k-means++ Random initialization can place several centroids in one dense blob and leave other blobs uncovered. k-means++ seeds sequentially: choose the first centroid uniformly at random; then choose each subsequent centroid from the data with probability proportional to D ( x ) 2 D(x)^2 D ( x ) 2 , the squared distance to the nearest centroid already chosen. Far-away points are more likely to be picked, which spreads the seeds. In expectation the seeding alone is O ( log ⁡ k ) O(\log k) O ( lo g k ) -competitive with the optimal objective, and in practice it usually needs fewer Lloyd iterations and gives lower J J J than uniform seeding. # Choosing k k k J J J decreases monotonically in k k k (more centroids can only fit better, reaching 0 0 0 at k = n k=n k = n ), so J J J alone cannot choose k k k . Method Idea Weakness Elbow Plot J J J against k k k and look for the bend where gains diminish The bend is often absent or subjective Silhouette Pick k k k maximizing the mean silhouette (defined below) Favors convex, well-separated clusters; can prefer k = 2 k=2 k = 2 Gap statistic Compare log ⁡ J \log J lo g J with its value under a reference (e.g. uniform) null Costly; depends on the null distribution Stability Cluster bootstrap or subsample resamples; choose k k k whose partitions agree Stable does not imply meaningful Downstream use Choose the k k k that serves the task (segments the business can act on) Task-specific Interview angle When asked how do you choose k k k ? , do not stop at the elbow. Say: the elbow and silhouette are heuristics that can disagree; there may be no true k k k ; so combine an internal criterion, a stability check, and whether the segments are actionable. Acknowledging that the right k k k can be a modeling decision rather than a fact about the data is a mark of seniority. # Limits and failure modes Voronoi geometry. Assignment to the nearest centroid means cluster boundaries are straight (hyperplanes). Non-convex shapes (rings, crescents) are split incorrectly. Equal-variance, equal-size bias. Because only the mean matters, k-means tends to cut large or wide clusters to balance variance, and cannot represent clusters with different spreads or correlated features. Unequal cluster sizes can lead to a big cluster being split. Scale and outliers. Squared error amplifies outliers; a few extreme points can claim a centroid. k k k -medians or k k k -medoids (PAM) are more robust, at higher cost. Hard assignment. A point on a boundary gets the same label as a point at a centroid; no uncertainty is reported. Euclidean only. The mean minimizing squared error is tied to Euclidean distance; other distances need other algorithms (k-medoids, spectral clustering, or cosine/spherical k-means with normalized vectors). Scalability levers. Mini-batch k-means updates centroids with small random batches, trading a little objective for large speedups on big data. A common mistake Running k-means on raw features of different units (income in dollars, age in years). The largest-scale feature dominates the distance, so clusters reflect that feature alone. Standardize first, and for categorical data use k-modes or a mixed-type distance rather than one-hot features treated as continuous. # The model A Gaussian mixture model (GMM) assumes each point is generated by first drawing a latent component z ∼ Categorical ( π ) z\sim\text{Categorical}(\pi) z ∼ Categorical ( π ) and then x ∣ z = k ∼ N ( μ k , Σ k ) x\mid z=k\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_k,\Sigma_k) x ∣ z = k ∼ N ( μ k ​ , Σ k ​ ) . The density is p ( x ) = ∑ k = 1 K π k N ( x ∣ μ k , Σ k ) , π k ≥ 0 , ∑ k π k = 1. p(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_k\,\mathcal{N}(x\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k),\qquad \pi_k\ge0,\ \sum_k\pi_k=1 . p ( x ) = k = 1 ∑ K ​ π k ​ N ( x ∣ μ k ​ , Σ k ​ ) , π k ​ ≥ 0 , k ∑ ​ π k ​ = 1. It is a generative model (see Generative vs Discriminative ): it defines p ( x ) p(x) p ( x ) , can sample, and can score new points. Maximum likelihood is ℓ ( θ ) = ∑ i = 1 n log ⁡ ∑ k = 1 K π k N ( x i ∣ μ k , Σ k ) . \ell(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_k\,\mathcal{N}(x_i\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k). ℓ ( θ ) = i = 1 ∑ n ​ lo g k = 1 ∑ K ​ π k ​ N ( x i ​ ∣ μ k ​ , Σ k ​ ) . The logarithm of a sum does not split into per-component terms, so there is no closed-form maximizer. If the z i z_i z i ​ were observed, the log-likelihood would be ∑ i log ⁡ π z i N ( x i ∣ μ z i , Σ z i ) \sum_i \log \pi_{z_i}\mathcal{N}(x_i\mid\mu_{z_i},\Sigma_{z_i}) ∑ i ​ lo g π z i ​ ​ N ( x i ​ ∣ μ z i ​ ​ , Σ z i ​ ​ ) , which is trivially maximized by per-group sample statistics. EM exploits this by guessing the missing z i z_i z i ​ softly. # EM: the two steps E-step. With current parameters θ ( t ) \theta^{(t)} θ ( t ) , compute the responsibility of component k k k for point i i i , which is the posterior probability of the latent assignment (Bayes rule): γ i k = p ( z i = k ∣ x i , θ ( t ) ) = π k N ( x i ∣ μ k , Σ k ) ∑ j π j N ( x i ∣ μ j , Σ j ) . \gamma_{ik}=p(z_i=k\mid x_i,\theta^{(t)})=\frac{\pi_k\,\mathcal{N}(x_i\mid\mu_k,\Sigma_k)}{\sum_{j}\pi_j\,\mathcal{N}(x_i\mid\mu_j,\Sigma_j)} . γ ik ​ = p ( z i ​ = k ∣ x i ​ , θ ( t ) ) = ∑ j ​ π j ​ N ( x i ​ ∣ μ j ​ , Σ j ​ ) π k ​ N ( x i ​ ∣ μ k ​ , Σ k ​ ) ​ . M-step. Maximize the expected complete-data log-likelihood with responsibilities as soft counts. With N k = ∑ i γ i k N_k=\sum_i\gamma_{ik} N k ​ = ∑ i ​ γ ik ​ : π k = N k n , μ k = 1 N k ∑ i γ i k x i , Σ k = 1 N k ∑ i γ i k ( x i − μ k ) ( x i − μ k ) T . \pi_k=\frac{N_k}{n},\qquad \mu_k=\frac{1}{N_k}\sum_i\gamma_{ik}\,x_i,\qquad \Sigma_k=\frac{1}{N_k}\sum_i\gamma_{ik}(x_i-\mu_k)(x_i-\mu_k)^{\mathsf T}. π k ​ = n N k ​ ​ , μ k ​ = N k ​ 1 ​ i ∑ ​ γ ik ​ x i ​ , Σ k ​ = N k ​ 1 ​ i ∑ ​ γ ik ​ ( x i ​ − μ k ​ ) ( x i ​ − μ k ​ ) T . These are weighted versions of the usual sample proportion, mean, and covariance. # Why EM works (conceptually) For any distribution q i ( k ) q_i(k) q i ​ ( k ) over the latent variable, Jensen s inequality gives a lower bound (the evidence lower bound , ELBO): log ⁡ p ( X ∣ θ ) ≥ ∑ i ∑ k q i ( k ) log ⁡ p ( x i , z i = k ∣ θ ) q i ( k ) . \log p(X\mid\theta)\ \ge\ \sum_i\sum_k q_i(k)\log\frac{p(x_i,z_i=k\mid\theta)}{q_i(k)} . lo g p ( X ∣ θ ) ≥ i ∑ ​ k ∑ ​ q i ​ ( k ) lo g q i ​ ( k ) p ( x i ​ , z i ​ = k ∣ θ ) ​ . The bound is tight exactly when q i ( k ) q_i(k) q i ​ ( k ) equals the posterior p ( z i = k ∣ x i , θ ) p(z_i=k\mid x_i,\theta) p ( z i ​ = k ∣ x i ​ , θ ) . So the E-step sets q q q to the posterior, making the bound touch the log-likelihood at the current θ \theta θ ; the M-step then raises the bound over θ \theta θ . Since the bound sits below the likelihood and touches it at the old θ \theta θ , the likelihood cannot decrease. EM therefore monotonically increases the likelihood and converges to a stationary point, generally a local maximum, so initialization and restarts matter (k-means is commonly used to initialize). # Relation to k-means k-means is a limiting special case of GMM-EM: take equal mixing weights, shared spherical covariance Σ k = σ 2 I \Sigma_k=\sigma^2 I Σ k ​ = σ 2 I , and let σ 2 → 0 \sigma^2\to0 σ 2 → 0 . The responsibilities then collapse to hard 0/1 assignments to the nearest centroid (the E-step becomes the assignment step), and the M-step reduces to the mean update. Conversely, a GMM adds three things: soft assignments, per-cluster covariance and weight, and a proper probabilistic model. k-means GMM (EM) Assignment Hard Soft (responsibilities) Cluster shape Spherical, equal size Ellipsoidal via Σ k \Sigma_k Σ k ​ ; unequal weights Objective Within-cluster SSE Log-likelihood Parameters per cluster d d d (mean) d + d ( d + 1 ) / 2 + 1 d + d(d+1)/2 + 1 d + d ( d + 1 ) /2 + 1 for full covariance Choose K K K Elbow, silhouette Likelihood with penalty: BIC or AIC Pitfalls Local minima Local maxima, singular covariances Practical points. Singularities. If one component centers on a single point and its covariance shrinks to zero, the density there diverges and the likelihood is unbounded. Guard with a covariance floor (add ϵ I \epsilon I ϵ I , reg_covar ) or a prior. Covariance structure. Full, diagonal, tied, and spherical covariances trade flexibility against the parameter count; with limited data and high d d d , diagonal or tied is often more stable than full. Choosing K K K . Because GMM has a likelihood, BIC = − 2 ℓ + p ln ⁡ n =-2\ell+p\ln n = − 2 ℓ + p ln n ( p p p free parameters) penalizes complexity; minimum BIC across a grid of K K K and covariance types is a common recipe. This presumes the Gaussian assumption is roughly right; with non-Gaussian clusters BIC may add components just to approximate a skewed shape. Mixtures are also density estimators. A GMM can be used directly for anomaly scoring through low p ( x ) p(x) p ( x ) (see Anomaly Detection ). Go deeper (optional) EM is a general recipe for latent-variable models with tractable posteriors (HMMs, factor analysis, mixtures of experts). When the posterior is intractable, one optimizes the ELBO with an approximate q q q , which is the road from EM to variational inference and VAEs. # Hierarchical clustering Agglomerative clustering starts with each point as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the closest pair of clusters until one remains, recording the merges in a dendrogram . Cutting the dendrogram at a height gives a flat clustering; no k k k needs to be fixed in advance, and one tree supports many resolutions. (Divisive clustering goes top-down and is less common.) What closest pair means is the linkage : Linkage Distance between clusters A , B A,B A , B Behavior Single min ⁡ a ∈ A , b ∈ B d ( a , b ) \min_{a\in A,b\in B}d(a,b) min a ∈ A , b ∈ B ​ d ( a , b ) Follows thin chains; chaining merges distinct clusters joined by a bridge of points; good for elongated shapes, sensitive to noise Complete max ⁡ a , b d ( a , b ) \max_{a,b}d(a,b) max a , b ​ d ( a , b ) Prefers compact clusters of similar diameter; sensitive to outliers Average (UPGMA) mean of d ( a , b ) d(a,b) d ( a , b ) Compromise between the two Ward Merge that minimizes the increase in total within-cluster SSE Behaves like a hierarchical k-means; tends to equal-sized compact clusters; defined for Euclidean distance Cost: a naive implementation needs the O ( n 2 ) O(n^2) O ( n 2 ) distance matrix in memory and roughly O ( n 2 log ⁡ n ) O(n^2\log n) O ( n 2 lo g n ) to O ( n 3 ) O(n^3) O ( n 3 ) time depending on the algorithm, so it does not scale to very large n n n without approximations. Merges are greedy and irreversible: an early bad merge is never undone. The cophenetic correlation (correlation between original distances and the dendrogram s merge heights) measures how faithfully the tree represents the data. Hierarchical methods accept any dissimilarity, which makes them handy for non-Euclidean data (edit distance, correlation distance) when the matrix is small enough. # DBSCAN DBSCAN defines clusters as connected regions of high density. It has two parameters: a radius ε \varepsilon ε and a count minPts . A core point has at least minPts points (itself included) within ε \varepsilon ε . A border point lies within ε \varepsilon ε of a core point but is not itself core. Everything else is noise . Clusters are formed by chaining core points that lie within ε \varepsilon ε of one another, plus their border points. Strengths: no k k k needed, arbitrary cluster shapes, an explicit noise label, and good behavior with outliers. Weaknesses: A single global ε \varepsilon ε cannot fit clusters of very different density: a value that separates dense clusters will label a sparse cluster as noise, while one that keeps the sparse cluster together merges the dense ones. High dimensions. Distance concentration makes ε \varepsilon ε hard to set; run it after dimensionality reduction. Parameter sensitivity. A k k k -distance plot (sorted distance to the minPts \text{minPts} minPts -th neighbor) helps choose ε \varepsilon ε at its knee. Heuristics: minPts at least d + 1 d+1 d + 1 , often about 2 d 2d 2 d , larger for noisy data. Border points can be assigned order-dependently when reachable from two clusters. With a spatial index in low dimensions it is roughly O ( n log ⁡ n ) O(n\log n) O ( n lo g n ) ; the worst case is O ( n 2 ) O(n^2) O ( n 2 ) . # HDBSCAN HDBSCAN removes the global ε \varepsilon ε . It transforms distances into a mutual reachability distance (inflating distances in sparse regions using each point s core distance), builds a minimum spanning tree and the resulting single-linkage hierarchy, condenses the tree by discarding splits that shed fewer than min_cluster_size points, and then extracts the clusters that persist longest (maximum stability ). It can therefore find clusters of varying density, labels low-density points as noise, and is much less sensitive to parameters, with min_cluster_size being the main one. It is generally the preferred density method when density varies, at higher compute cost than k-means; it still struggles in raw high-dimensional space. Interview angle Your clusters are crescents and there are outliers. What now? Answer: k-means will fail (convex Voronoi cells, outlier-sensitive). Use DBSCAN or HDBSCAN, after scaling and possibly PCA; use HDBSCAN if densities differ; check the noise fraction; and validate with stability or with a task-specific check rather than silhouette, which assumes convexity. # Evaluating clusters without ground truth If labels exist for a held-out subset, external indices apply: the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI, chance-corrected agreement between two partitions) and Normalized Mutual Information (NMI). Treat them as sanity checks: labels may encode a different notion of grouping than the data s dominant structure. Without labels, use internal indices and stability. Silhouette. For point i i i let a ( i ) a(i) a ( i ) be its mean distance to the other points in its own cluster and b ( i ) b(i) b ( i ) the smallest mean distance to the points of any other cluster. Then s ( i ) = b ( i ) − a ( i ) max ⁡ { a ( i ) , b ( i ) } ∈ [ − 1 , 1 ] . s(i)=\frac{b(i)-a(i)}{\max\{a(i),b(i)\}}\in[-1,1]. s ( i ) = max { a ( i ) , b ( i )} b ( i ) − a ( i ) ​ ∈ [ − 1 , 1 ] . Values near 1 1 1 mean well inside the cluster; near 0 0 0 means on a boundary; negative suggests a likely mislabel. Average silhouette across points scores the whole partition. Cost is O ( n 2 ) O(n^2) O ( n 2 ) unless subsampled. Index Better is What it rewards Caveat Silhouette Higher Cohesion and separation Biased toward convex clusters; misleads for density-based results Davies-Bouldin Lower Small within-cluster scatter relative to between-centroid distance Centroid-based; assumes roughly spherical clusters Calinski-Harabasz Higher Ratio of between- to within-cluster dispersion Tends to favor spherical, similar-sized clusters; rises with k k k in some data Stability Higher agreement Reproducibility under resampling Reproducible clusters can still be arbitrary Stability assessment. Draw many bootstrap or subsample resamples, cluster each, and compare partitions on shared points (for example with ARI). High agreement suggests the structure is a property of the data rather than of the sample or initialization. Also compare across algorithms and random seeds. Internal indices are not truth Internal indices measure whether a clustering matches the geometric assumption that index encodes. A method that optimizes the same geometry (k-means and silhouette) will score well by construction. Say so, and add a task-based check: do the segments differ on a metric you care about, are they interpretable, are they stable over time? # Dimensionality reduction for visualization: t-SNE and UMAP PCA (linear, global variance; see Eigenvectors, PCA and SVD ) is the first tool for compression and denoising. For visualizing nonlinear structure in 2D or 3D, neighbor-embedding methods are the usual choice. Both build a neighborhood graph in the original space and find low-dimensional coordinates that reproduce it. # t-SNE In the original space, for each point i i i define a Gaussian neighbor distribution p j ∣ i ∝ exp ⁡ ( − ∥ x i − x j ∥ 2 / 2 σ i 2 ) p_{j\mid i}\propto\exp(-\lVert x_i-x_j\rVert^2/2\sigma_i^2) p j ∣ i ​ ∝ exp ( − ∥ x i ​ − x j ​ ∥ 2 /2 σ i 2 ​ ) , with σ i \sigma_i σ i ​ found by binary search so that the entropy of P i P_i P i ​ matches the chosen perplexity , Perp = 2 H ( P i ) \text{Perp}=2^{H(P_i)} Perp = 2 H ( P i ​ ) . Perplexity acts as a soft effective number of neighbors . Symmetrize: p i j = ( p j ∣ i + p i ∣ j ) / 2 n p_{ij}=(p_{j\mid i}+p_{i\mid j})/2n p ij ​ = ( p j ∣ i ​ + p i ∣ j ​ ) /2 n . In the embedding, use a Student- t t t kernel with one degree of freedom (heavy tails): q i j ∝ ( 1 + ∥ y i − y j ∥ 2 ) − 1 q_{ij}\propto(1+\lVert y_i-y_j\rVert^2)^{-1} q ij ​ ∝ ( 1 + ∥ y i ​ − y j ​ ∥ 2 ) − 1 , normalized over all pairs. Minimize K L ( P ∥ Q ) = ∑ i ≠ j p i j log ⁡ p i j q i j \mathrm{KL}(P\Vert Q)=\sum_{i\ne j}p_{ij}\log\frac{p_{ij}}{q_{ij}} KL ( P ∥ Q ) = ∑ i  = j ​ p ij ​ lo g q ij ​ p ij ​ ​ over the y i y_i y i ​ by gradient descent. Why this design: K L ( P ∥ Q ) \mathrm{KL}(P\Vert Q) KL ( P ∥ Q ) is asymmetric. Placing two near points far apart (large p p p , small q q q ) is penalized heavily, while placing two far points near each other (small p p p , large q q q ) costs little. So local neighborhoods are preserved well; global arrangement is not guaranteed . The heavy-tailed kernel lets moderately dissimilar points sit farther apart in 2D than a Gaussian would, relieving the crowding problem (in 2D there is not enough room for all the moderately distant neighbors that exist in high dimensions). Practical facts: the objective is non-convex, so runs differ by initialization and seed; results depend on perplexity (commonly 5 to 50, smaller than n n n ; try several) and on enough iterations and an adequate learning rate; the Barnes-Hut and FFT-based approximations give about O ( n log ⁡ n ) O(n\log n) O ( n lo g n ) or better; and classic t-SNE has no out-of-sample mapping for new points. # UMAP UMAP builds a weighted ( k k k -nearest-neighbor) graph in the original space, interpreted as a fuzzy topological representation, then optimizes an embedding whose fuzzy graph matches it by minimizing a cross-entropy between edge weights, using attractive forces along edges and repulsive forces from sampled non-edges. Its two main hyperparameters are n_neighbors (local versus global emphasis: larger values capture broader structure) and min_dist (how tightly points may pack in the embedding; smaller values give tighter clumps). Compared with t-SNE, UMAP is typically faster, can embed new points via a fitted transform, supports supervised and other-metric variants, and often (not always) retains more of the large-scale layout, partly owing to its spectral initialization rather than purely the objective. # What you may and may not read from the plot Read with care Reason Distances between clusters Not preserved; far apart on the plot does not mean far apart in the data Cluster sizes and densities t-SNE s per-point bandwidth σ i \sigma_i σ i ​ equalizes local density; UMAP s min_dist rescales it, so a tight blob can be a diffuse one Apparent clusters Low perplexity or small n_neighbors can split a continuum into islands; random noise can look clustered Absence of structure One run with poor settings can hide real structure Axes Arbitrary; carry no meaning Good practice: run several seeds and hyperparameter settings; confirm clusters with a method on the original (or PCA-reduced) space; and do not feed raw 2D t-SNE coordinates to a downstream model as if they were faithful features. A common pipeline is PCA to roughly 30 to 100 dimensions to denoise and speed up, then t-SNE or UMAP. Interview angle Two clusters look far apart in the t-SNE plot; are they more different than two that look close? Answer: not necessarily; t-SNE preserves local neighborhoods, not global distances or cluster sizes. Use it to generate hypotheses, then verify in the original space. # Autoencoders (briefly) An autoencoder learns an encoder z = f ϕ ( x ) z=f_\phi(x) z = f ϕ ​ ( x ) to a low-dimensional code and a decoder x ^ = g θ ( z ) \hat x=g_\theta(z) x ^ = g θ ​ ( z ) , minimizing a reconstruction loss such as ∥ x − x ^ ∥ 2 \lVert x-\hat x\rVert^2 ∥ x − x ^ ∥ 2 . The bottleneck forces compression. A single-hidden-layer linear autoencoder with squared error recovers the same subspace as PCA (though not necessarily the individual principal axes); nonlinear activations and depth allow curved manifolds. Variants: denoising (reconstruct clean x x x from a corrupted input, discouraging the identity map), sparse (penalty on activations), contractive , and variational (VAE: a probabilistic latent space regularized toward a prior, enabling sampling). Uses: learned embeddings for downstream models, denoising, and reconstruction-based anomaly detection ( Anomaly Detection ). Cautions: an over-capacity network can learn near-identity and reconstruct everything; the code is not guaranteed to be interpretable or to preserve distances; and results depend on architecture and training stability. # Choosing among methods Situation First choice Why Watch out for Large n n n , compact blobs, need speed k-means (mini-batch if huge) O ( n k d ) O(nkd) O ( nk d ) , simple Scaling; outliers; choice of k k k Overlapping or elliptical clusters, want probabilities GMM Soft, per-cluster covariance Local optima; singularities; d d d large Want a tree or multiple resolutions; small n n n Hierarchical (Ward or average) One tree, any linkage/distance O ( n 2 ) O(n^2) O ( n 2 ) memory; irreversible merges Arbitrary shapes, noise, similar densities DBSCAN No k k k ; noise label One global ε \varepsilon ε ; high d d d Arbitrary shapes, varying density HDBSCAN Robust to density change Compute; still weak in raw high d d d Compression, denoising, preprocessing PCA Linear, deterministic, invertible Only linear structure 2D picture of nonlinear structure UMAP or t-SNE Preserve neighborhoods Not for distances or cluster sizes Learned nonlinear features or reconstruction scoring Autoencoder Flexible Training cost; near-identity solutions A default workflow when the data are tabular and high-dimensional: standardize, reduce with PCA, try k-means and a GMM across a range of k k k , check silhouette/BIC and stability, inspect the clusters by profiling feature means, then visualize with UMAP or t-SNE for communication only. # One-Page Summary Concept Key point k-means objective Minimize within-cluster SSE ∑ i ∥ x i − μ c ( i ) ∥ 2 \sum_i\lVert x_i-\mu_{c(i)}\rVert^2 ∑ i ​ ∥ x i ​ − μ c ( i ) ​ ∥ 2 ; NP-hard globally, Lloyd finds a local minimum. Lloyd Alternate nearest-centroid assignment and mean update; J J J never increases; O ( n k d ) O(nkd) O ( nk d ) per iteration. k-means++ Seed proportional to D ( x ) 2 D(x)^2 D ( x ) 2 ; O ( log ⁡ k ) O(\log k) O ( lo g k ) -competitive in expectation; fewer bad local minima. Choosing k k k Elbow, silhouette, gap, stability, usefulness; none is definitive. k-means limits Convex, equal-variance bias; outlier and scale sensitive; hard labels. GMM p ( x ) = ∑ k π k N ( μ k , Σ k ) p(x)=\sum_k\pi_k\mathcal{N}(\mu_k,\Sigma_k) p ( x ) = ∑ k ​ π k ​ N ( μ k ​ , Σ k ​ ) ; EM maximizes likelihood. E-step / M-step Responsibilities γ i k \gamma_{ik} γ ik ​ by Bayes rule; weighted proportion, mean, covariance. EM guarantee Likelihood non-decreasing (ELBO touches at the E-step); local maximum only. k-means vs GMM k-means = GMM with equal weights, σ 2 I \sigma^2 I σ 2 I , σ 2 → 0 \sigma^2\to0 σ 2 → 0 . Hierarchical Dendrogram; single chains, complete compact, average in between, Ward minimizes SSE increase. DBSCAN Core/border/noise via ε \varepsilon ε and minPts; arbitrary shapes; struggles with varying density. HDBSCAN Mutual reachability + stability extraction; varying density; main knob min_cluster_size . Evaluation Silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, Calinski-Harabasz are geometry-biased; add stability and task checks. t-SNE Matches neighbor distributions via K L ( P ∥ Q ) \mathrm{KL}(P\Vert Q) KL ( P ∥ Q ) with Student- t t t ; perplexity sets neighborhood size. UMAP Fuzzy neighbor graph and cross-entropy; faster, has transform; neighbors and min_dist knobs. Plot caveats Do not read inter-cluster distance, cluster size, or axes. Autoencoder Bottleneck reconstruction; linear case spans PCA subspace. # Related Eigenvectors, PCA and SVD Anomaly Detection Generative vs Discriminative Classification Methods MOC - Unsupervised

title: Unsupervised
text: Finding structure and rare events without labels, and judging the result when there is no ground truth. # Chapters Clustering Dimensionality Reduction Anomaly Detection # See also (from other areas) Eigenvectors, PCA and SVD — PCA and SVD derivations (Math Optimization) Generative vs Discriminative — GMM as a generative model (Classical Models) Decision Trees and Gradient Boosting — the supervised alternative when anomaly labels exist (Classical Models) ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC — why PR-AUC for rare events (Evaluation) Precision Recall — precision@k and alert budgets (Evaluation) Time Series Stationarity — detrending before scoring temporal anomalies (Time Series) # If asked about unsupervised problems Name the structure you are assuming (blobs, density, manifold, rare and different ), standardize and reduce dimension first, pick the method whose assumption fits, and evaluate with stability and a task-specific check since internal indices share the method s geometry. For anomalies, set the metric (PR-AUC, precision@k) and threshold from the review budget, and plan for drift.

title: ML System Design Interview Prep
text: # Stage 1: Business Objective Goal: Understand WHY this system exists before touching anything technical. Interviewers want to see you think before building. Questions to ask: What is the core business goal? (revenue, safety, engagement, retention?) What is the scale? (DAU, QPS, catalog size) What latency is acceptable? ( 100ms real-time, 1s near-real-time, batch OK?) What data freshness is needed? (model needs to reflect events from 5 min ago or 5 days ago?) Are there hard constraints? (regulatory, fairness, GDPR, COPPA, geographic) Which is worse: false positives or false negatives? Is there an existing system? What s broken about it? Business metrics to know: CTR, CVR (conversion rate), GMV DAU/MAU, retention, session length Map FP/FN cost to business: fraud FN = money lost, fraud FP = user friction # Stage 2: ML Objective Goal: Translate business goal → concrete ML problem. Task types: Binary classification — spam, fraud, click prediction Multi-class — intent detection, category tagging Ranking / LTR — search, feed, recommendations Regression — price, ETA, bid value Multi-task — predict CTR + CVR jointly Generative — query rewriting, summarization Business metric → ML proxy: Business Metric ML Proxy CTR AUC-ROC, log loss Revenue CVR, predicted value Relevance NDCG, MRR, MAP Safety Recall @ high precision Engagement Predicted watch time Loss functions: Problem Loss Binary classification Binary cross-entropy (log loss) Multi-class Categorical cross-entropy Imbalanced classification Focal loss Regression MSE / MAE / Huber Ranking (pairwise) BPR loss, hinge loss Ranking (listwise) LambdaRank, ApproxNDCG Embeddings / contrastive Triplet loss, NT-Xent (SimCLR) Distillation KL divergence + task loss Key framing decisions: Point-wise vs. pairwise vs. listwise ranking Single-task vs. multi-task (shared bottom, mixture of experts) Do you need calibrated probabilities or just a good ranking? # Stage 3: High-Level Design Goal: Sketch the end-to-end pipeline. Get the boxes and arrows right before going deep. Standard pipeline: Data sources → Feature engineering → Feature store ↓ Training pipeline → Model registry ↓ Serving layer → Prediction store / cache ↓ Logging → Feedback loop Common architecture patterns: Two-tower (retrieval) User tower + Item tower → dot product → ANN index Item embeddings precomputed offline Used by: YouTube, Pinterest, TikTok for candidate generation Cascade / Funnel (retrieval → ranking → re-ranking) Retrieval (ANN, BM25, CF) → Ranking (GBDT, DNN) → Re-ranking (business rules, diversity) Used in: search, feed ranking, ads Sequence model (temporal) LSTM / Transformer over user history → next-item prediction Used in: Netflix, Spotify, TikTok Real-time + batch hybrid Batch features (stable, cheap) + real-time features (fresh, expensive) merged at serving # Stage 4: Data Feature Engineering Goal: Where does data come from, how do you label it, what features do you extract. Data sources: User interaction logs (clicks, watches, purchases, skips, dwell time) Item/entity metadata (title, category, price, content embeddings) Context (time of day, device, location, session position) Social graph (follows, co-views, shares) External signals (weather, trending topics) Labeling strategies: Explicit: ratings, thumbs up/down — sparse, high quality Implicit: clicks, watches, purchases — dense, noisy (click ≠ satisfaction) Proxy labels: watched 50% of video as engagement positive Human annotation: content quality, safety, NLP tasks Label leakage gotchas: Features computed after the event (e.g., final view count when predicting CTR) Future data leaking into training window Feature types: User: demographics, long-term interests, embedding of ID Item: category, price, recency, popularity, content embedding User-item cross: past CTR on this category, historical spend Context: time, device, session position, query Feature engineering techniques: Normalization / standardization — for neural nets Log transform — heavy-tailed distributions (price, counts) Bucketization — continuous → categorical Target encoding — replace category with mean label (watch for leakage) Embeddings — for high-cardinality IDs (users, items, queries) Hashing trick — very high cardinality, reduces memory Feature crosses — jointly encode two features (A × B) Sequence aggregation — mean/sum/attention pooling over user history Feature store: Offline store: Hive, BigQuery, Spark — batch features, used in training Online store: Redis, DynamoDB (managed by Feast / Tecton) — low-latency features at serve time Point-in-time correctness: training features must reflect what was known AT prediction time Class imbalance: Downsample negatives (very common in click prediction — 1:100 or worse) Calibration correction after downsampling negatives at keep-rate w: p = p_s / (p_s + (1-p_s)/w), equivalent to adding log(w) to the logit Weighted loss Focal loss # Stage 5: Model Goal: Choose and justify your model. Know the tradeoffs. Model cheat sheet: Need Model Fast baseline Logistic regression Tabular data, ranking LightGBM / XGBoost Large-scale retrieval Two-tower + FAISS ANN Dense ranking DNN / DCN (Deep Cross Network) Sequential / session Transformer (SASRec, BERT4Rec) Social graph GNN (GraphSAGE, PinSage) Multimodal (text + image) CLIP-style dual encoder Model tradeoffs: Logistic Regression Pros: fast, interpretable, calibrated, easy to debug Cons: low capacity, needs manual feature engineering When: baseline, very high QPS, features already good GBDT (XGBoost, LightGBM) Pros: handles tabular data extremely well, no normalization needed, built-in feature importance Cons: doesn t handle embeddings, hard to do online learning When: ranking, fraud, structured tabular data DNN / MLP Pros: learns feature interactions, handles embeddings end-to-end Cons: more data needed, harder to debug, slower than GBDT When: ranking with many features, multi-task setups Two-Tower Pros: item tower precomputed offline → fast retrieval Cons: no user-item interaction at inference time (shallow) When: retrieval at massive scale Transformer Pros: captures sequential context, state of the art for NLP Cons: expensive to train and serve, needs lots of data When: session modeling, NLP tasks, query understanding GNN Pros: captures social / graph structure natively Cons: complex to build and serve When: social feed ranking, fraud on transaction graphs Training considerations: Learning rate schedule: warmup + cosine decay Regularization: L1/L2, dropout, early stopping Positional bias: items shown first get more clicks — debias during training Exposure bias: model only sees items that were previously shown # Stage 6: Inference Serving Goal: Get predictions to users at scale, efficiently. Batch vs. Real-time vs. Near-real-time: Mode Latency Freshness Use case Batch 0ms (precomputed) Stale (hours/days) Email recs, item embeddings Near-real-time Seconds/minutes Fresh Trending, fraud streaming Real-time 100ms Very fresh Feed ranking, search Serving architectures: Precomputed / lookup: store embeddings or scores in Redis, retrieve at serve time Online inference: feature retrieval → model scoring → post-processing in budget Cascade / multi-stage: cheap model for retrieval → expensive model on small candidate set Latency optimization: Quantization: FP32 → FP16 or INT8 (2-4x speedup, small accuracy loss) Distillation: train small student from large teacher Pruning: remove low-importance weights Caching: cache predictions for popular user/item pairs ANN for retrieval: FAISS, ScaNN, HNSW (millisecond-scale over billions of vectors) Batching: group requests on GPU to maximize throughput Scalability: Horizontal scaling: replica-based, load balanced GPU serving: large batches / transformers CPU serving: low-latency tabular / small models Feature lookup budget: Redis P99 ~1ms, DB can be 10-100ms — budget carefully Deployment strategies: Shadow mode: run new model in parallel, no user impact, compare offline Canary: 1-5% traffic, monitor metrics A/B test: randomized experiment, measure business metric Interleaving: blend two ranked lists, measure clicks — faster signal than A/B Multi-armed bandit: explore/exploit, useful when A/B is too slow # Stage 7: Deep Dives Improvements Goal: Show depth by proactively naming hard problems and how you d solve them. Cold Start New user: popular items, context features (device, referral), demographic priors New item: content embeddings (image, text, metadata), zero-shot via pretrained model Exploration: epsilon-greedy, Thompson sampling, UCB Data Freshness / Training Latency How fast does the model react to new events? Options: real-time feature updates, online learning (SGD on stream), continuous training Tradeoff: freshness vs. stability Model Monitoring Drift Data drift: input distributions shift (COVID changed all user behavior overnight) Concept drift: feature-label relationship changes Detection: KL divergence, PSI (Population Stability Index), shadow scoring Response: automated retraining triggers, alerting Bias Fairness Selection bias: model trained on biased exposure (only seen items) Popularity bias: popular items get over-recommended, feedback loop amplifies Demographic fairness: disparate impact across groups Debiasing: inverse propensity scoring (IPS), adversarial debiasing, constrained optimization Feedback Loops / Echo Chambers Model recommends what it predicts users like → users only see those items → model gets reinforced Mitigations: exploration budgets, diversity constraints, counterfactual evaluation Multi-Objective Optimization Competing objectives: engagement vs. revenue vs. safety vs. diversity Approaches: weighted sum of losses, Pareto optimization, constrained (maximize revenue s.t. engagement ≥ threshold), mixture of experts per objective Reranking After ranking: diversity (no 3 consecutive same artist), freshness boost, sponsored insertion, safety filtering Privacy Differential privacy: calibrated noise on gradients or outputs Federated learning: train on-device, aggregate updates ID hashing = pseudonymization only; not a formal privacy guarantee # Loss Functions Problem Loss Binary classification Binary cross-entropy Multi-class Categorical cross-entropy Imbalanced Focal loss Regression (outlier sensitive) MSE Regression (robust) MAE / Huber Ranking pairwise BPR, hinge Ranking listwise LambdaRank, ApproxNDCG Embeddings Triplet loss, NT-Xent Distillation KL divergence # Models Need Model Baseline Logistic regression Tabular / ranking LightGBM / XGBoost Retrieval at scale Two-tower + FAISS Dense ranking DNN / DCN Session / sequential SASRec / BERT4Rec Graph signals GNN (GraphSAGE, PinSage) Multimodal CLIP-style dual encoder # Inference Need Approach Sub-10ms Precomputed + Redis lookup ~100ms budget Online inference, light model Stale OK Batch + feature store Real-time events Kafka + Flink streaming Large model, throughput matters Quantization + GPU batching Billion-scale retrieval ANN (FAISS, ScaNN, HNSW) # Business Metric → ML Metric Business ML CTR AUC-ROC, log loss Revenue CVR, predicted bid value Relevance NDCG, MRR, MAP Safety Recall @ fixed high precision Engagement Predicted watch time

title: Models and Loss Functions Reference
heads: Deep  Cross Network — DCN (Google, 2017) → DCN v2 (2020)
text: # Problem Type → Baseline → Advanced Model Problem Type Baseline Advanced Binary classification (tabular) Logistic regression LightGBM / XGBoost → DNN Click prediction / ads ranking Logistic regression Wide Deep → DCN v2 Candidate retrieval (rec sys) Matrix factorization (ALS) Two-tower DNN + FAISS ANN Feed / search ranking LightGBM DCN v2, DLRM, MMoE (multi-task) Session-based recs Popularity baseline SASRec / BERT4Rec (Transformer) NLP: classification TF-IDF + LR Fine-tuned BERT / RoBERTa NLP: ranking / retrieval BM25 Bi-encoder (two-tower) → Cross-encoder Fraud detection LightGBM LightGBM + GNN (transaction graph) Image classification Linear on features ResNet → ViT Multimodal (text + image) Separate models, concat features CLIP-style dual encoder Time series / forecasting ARIMA, moving average LSTM → Temporal Fusion Transformer Graph problems (social, fraud) Node degree features + LR GraphSAGE, PinSage, GNN # Wide Deep (Google, 2016) Wide side : linear model on manually specified feature crosses (you write user_app × search_query ) Deep side : embedding + MLP for generalization Limitation : the cross features on the wide side must be hand-engineered When to use : you have strong domain knowledge about which specific interactions matter # Deep Cross Network — DCN (Google, 2017) → DCN v2 (2020) Replaces the wide side with a cross network that automatically learns bounded-degree feature interactions DCN v2 uses a matrix-based cross layer (more expressive than the original vector-based one) Reduces (not eliminates) manual cross engineering A strong upgrade over Wide Deep when you don t know which crosses matter When to use : large feature spaces, ranking problems where you don t know which crosses matter; a strong, common default for ranking, alongside DLRM/DeepFM # Summary Wide Deep → DCN → DCN v2 (manual crosses) (auto crosses, vector) (auto crosses, matrix — best) # Classification Binary Cross-Entropy (Log Loss) L = -[y·log(p) + (1-y)·log(1-p)] Use: click prediction, fraud, any binary label Output: sigmoid → probability Default choice for binary problems Categorical Cross-Entropy (Softmax Loss) L = -Σ y_i · log(p_i) Use: multi-class (mutually exclusive), intent detection, NLP classification Output: softmax → probability distribution Focal Loss L = -α_t (1-p_t)^γ · log(p_t) (p_t = probability assigned to the true class) Use: severe class imbalance (fraud, safety, object detection) The (1-p_t)^γ term downweights easy examples (of either class), focuses training on hard examples γ=2 is typical; originated in RetinaNet Often helps when easy negatives dominate; probabilities need recalibration # Regression MSE (Mean Squared Error) L = (y - ŷ)² Penalizes large errors heavily (squared) Sensitive to outliers Use: when large errors are disproportionately bad MAE (Mean Absolute Error) L = |y - ŷ| More robust to outliers than MSE Use: when outliers are common and you don t want them to dominate Huber Loss L = 0.5(y-ŷ)² if |y-ŷ| ≤ δ L = δ·|y-ŷ| - 0.5δ² otherwise Best of both: MSE for small errors, MAE for large ones Use: default regression loss when you re unsure (bid prediction, ETA) # Ranking BPR Loss (Bayesian Personalized Ranking) — pairwise L = -log(σ(ŷ_pos - ŷ_neg)) Pushes score of positive item above negative item Use: implicit feedback (clicks, watches) where you have user-item pairs Common in recommendation systems Hinge Loss — pairwise L = max(0, margin - (ŷ_pos - ŷ_neg)) Similar to BPR but with a hard margin Use: ranking when you want a minimum score gap LambdaRank / LambdaMART — listwise Pairwise gradients weighted by the NDCG change from swapping the pair (a listwise-aware heuristic); LambdaMART is the GBDT version Used inside LightGBM/XGBoost for ranking ( objective=lambdarank ) Use: when you care about the full ranked list quality, not just pairwise order ApproxNDCG / SoftNDCG — listwise Differentiable approximation of NDCG Used in neural ranking models Use: training neural rankers end-to-end # Embedding / Contrastive Triplet Loss L = max(0, d(anchor, pos) - d(anchor, neg) + margin) Pulls anchor closer to positive, pushes away from negative Use: face recognition, image similarity, early recommendation embedding work Problem: hard to mine good triplets NT-Xent Loss (SimCLR / Contrastive) L = -log( exp(sim(z_i, z_j)/τ) / Σ_k exp(sim(z_i, z_k)/τ) ) In-batch negatives: all other samples in the batch are negatives τ = temperature (lower = sharper, higher = softer) Use: self-supervised pretraining, two-tower models, sentence embeddings More efficient than triplet loss (no triplet mining needed) In-Batch Softmax (used in two-tower models) Same idea as NT-Xent but applied to user-item retrieval All other items in batch = negatives for each user Watch out: popular items appear often as negatives → popularity bias in training, correct with logQ correction (subtract log sampling probability from the logits) # Knowledge Distillation KL Divergence L = Σ p(x) · log(p(x)/q(x)) Measures how distribution p (teacher soft labels) differs from q (student predictions) Student loss = task loss + α·KL(teacher || student) Use: compressing large models to smaller ones for serving # Quick Lookup Situation Loss Binary, balanced Binary cross-entropy Binary, imbalanced (fraud, safety) Focal loss Multi-class Categorical cross-entropy Regression, clean data MSE Regression, noisy/outliers Huber or MAE Pairwise ranking (implicit feedback) BPR loss Listwise ranking (optimize NDCG) LambdaRank / ApproxNDCG Embedding learning NT-Xent (in-batch) or Triplet Model compression KL divergence Multi-task Weighted sum of per-task losses
